/glossary.title: Glossary · LLM Dojo
/glossary.description: Every term used in the lessons, with a short definition and where it is taught.

Models read and write tokens, not characters.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#token","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Tokenizer","description":"The component that cuts text into tokens and maps each to an integer ID, and turns IDs back into text.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#tokenizer","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Token ID","description":"The integer a tokenizer assigns to a token: its position in the vocabulary. IDs only mean something within the vocabulary that produced them.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#token-id","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Vocabulary","description":"The fixed list of every token a tokenizer knows. Its size is a design choice made before training.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#vocabulary","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Byte pair encoding (BPE)","description":"A way to learn a subword vocabulary: start from single symbols and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair. Encoding replays the learned merges in order.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#bpe","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Subword","description":"A token that can be a whole word or a fragment of one. Common words get one token; rare words are built from several.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#subword","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Special token","description":"A vocabulary entry with a control meaning rather than text, such as end-of-text or a chat-role marker. User text must never become one.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#special-token","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Embedding","description":"A vector of numbers that represents a token or a text, arranged so that similar meanings end up close together.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#embedding","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Embedding table","description":"The learned matrix with one row per vocabulary entry. Embedding a token ID means reading its row.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#embedding-table","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Cosine similarity","description":"How closely two vectors point the same way, from −1 to 1, ignoring their lengths. The usual way to compare embeddings.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#cosine-similarity","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Dot product","description":"Multiply two vectors element by element and add the results. Grows with both their alignment and their lengths.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#dot-product","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Contextual embedding","description":"A token's vector after the transformer layers have mixed in the surrounding text, so the same word gets different vectors in different sentences.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#contextual-embedding","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Semantic search","description":"Finding documents by comparing embeddings of the query and the documents, so matches can share meaning without sharing words.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#semantic-search","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Attention","description":"The mechanism that lets each token take in information from other tokens, weighted by how relevant they score.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#attention","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Query, key and value","description":"Three learned projections of each token's vector. A query is compared with every key to get attention weights; the weights then mix the values.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#qkv","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Attention head","description":"One independent attention computation. Models run many heads in parallel, each free to look for a different relationship.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#attention-head","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Causal mask","description":"In GPT-style models, the rule that a token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens, never later ones.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#causal-mask","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Softmax","description":"Turns a list of scores into probabilities: exponentiate each score, then divide by the total so they sum to 1.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#softmax","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Transformer block","description":"The repeated unit of a transformer: attention and a feed-forward network, each wrapped in a layer norm and a residual connection.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#transformer-block","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Residual connection","description":"Adding a sub-layer's output back onto its input, so each block refines the token vectors instead of replacing them.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#residual-connection","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Layer norm","description":"Rescales each token's vector to a standard spread before a sub-layer, which keeps training stable.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#layer-norm","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Feed-forward network (MLP)","description":"The part of a transformer block that processes each token's vector on its own, after attention has mixed information between tokens.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#mlp","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Logit","description":"A raw score the model gives each vocabulary token for being next. Softmax turns logits into probabilities.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#logit","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"LM head","description":"The final layer that turns the last position's vector into one logit per vocabulary token.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#lm-head","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Autoregressive generation","description":"Writing one token at a time, appending each to the input before predicting the next.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#autoregressive","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Greedy decoding","description":"Always picking the single most likely next token. Deterministic, but prone to repetition.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#greedy-decoding","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Temperature","description":"A number that divides the logits before softmax: below 1 sharpens the distribution, above 1 flattens it, 0 means greedy.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#temperature","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Top-k","description":"Sampling only among the k most likely tokens, after renormalising their probabilities.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#top-k","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Top-p (nucleus sampling)","description":"Sampling only among the smallest set of most-likely tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#top-p","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Seed","description":"The starting value of a random number generator. The same seed and settings reproduce the same samples on the same setup.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#seed","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Logprob","description":"The natural log of a token's probability. Useful for debugging, but not a measure of whether an answer is true.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#logprob","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Context window","description":"The maximum number of tokens a model can process at once: prompt and output together.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#context-window","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Position embedding","description":"A vector added to each token's embedding so the model knows where the token sits in the sequence.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#position-embedding","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Prefill","description":"Processing the whole prompt in one parallel pass before the first output token can be produced.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#prefill","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Decode","description":"The sequential phase of generation: one forward pass per new token.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#decode","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"KV cache","description":"Stored keys and values of earlier tokens, so each decode step only computes them for the new token. Exact, but costs memory.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#kv-cache","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Hallucination","description":"Fluent, confident output that is false or not supported by the input.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#hallucination","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Grounding","description":"Giving the model relevant, trusted text in its context so its answer can be based on that text rather than memory alone.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#grounding","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Time to first token (TTFT)","description":"How long from sending a request until the first output token arrives. Mostly the prefill, so it grows with the prompt's length.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#ttft","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Time per output token (TPOT)","description":"The average time between output tokens after the first one: how fast a streamed reply flows.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#tpot","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Inter-token latency","description":"The gap between two consecutive output tokens. Its average is the time per output token.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#itl","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Percentile (p50, p99)","description":"pN is the value N% of measurements fall at or below: p50 is the median, p99 is beaten by all but the slowest 1%. Used for latency because the mean hides the tail.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#percentile","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Throughput","description":"Work done per second across all requests, usually output tokens per second. Not the same as how fast any one user's reply arrives.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#throughput","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Goodput","description":"The rate of requests that meet the latency objective (SLO). Slow requests count toward throughput but not goodput.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#goodput","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Service level objective (SLO)","description":"A target a service promises to meet, such as 'first token within 100 ms and at most 10 ms per token after that'.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#slo","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Time to publish","description":"Time until the first token the user can see. Later than time to first token when the model first generates hidden steps such as a plan.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#time-to-publish","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Compute-bound","description":"Work whose time is set by how much arithmetic it needs; a chip with more operations per second speeds it up.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#compute-bound","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Memory bandwidth-bound","description":"Work whose time is set by how fast data moves from memory to the arithmetic units; more memory bandwidth, or fewer bytes to move, speeds it up.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#bandwidth-bound","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Arithmetic intensity","description":"Operations done per byte read from memory. Low intensity means bandwidth is the limit; high intensity means compute is.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#arithmetic-intensity","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Roofline","description":"A chart of achievable operations per second against arithmetic intensity: a sloped roof set by memory bandwidth and a flat roof set by peak compute, meeting at the ridge.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#roofline","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Model bandwidth utilization (MBU)","description":"The share of peak memory bandwidth inference uses: parameters × bytes per parameter × tokens per second, over the peak, for one sequence.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#mbu","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Continuous batching","description":"Batching that re-decides the batch before every decode step: finished replies leave at once and waiting requests take their seats.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#continuous-batching","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Quantization","description":"Storing a model's numbers in a format with fewer bits, such as FP16, INT8 or INT4, to cut memory and the bytes each step reads. Strictly it means converting to integers, but in practice it covers any precision reduction.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#quantization","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"BF16 (bfloat16)","description":"A 16-bit float with 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 fraction bits. It has the same range as FP32 but less precision than FP16.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#bf16","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Post-training quantization","description":"Quantizing a model after it has been fully trained. It is the most common approach, and the one application developers use.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#ptq","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Quantization-aware training","description":"Simulating low precision during training so the model learns to work well in it. It does not make training faster.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#qat","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Prompt caching","description":"Keeping the KV cache of a prompt's shared opening, such as a system prompt or long document, so later requests that start with the identical prefix skip prefilling it.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#prompt-caching","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Exact caching","description":"Storing whole answers and returning one only when exactly the same query is asked again.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#exact-caching","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Semantic caching","description":"Returning a stored answer when a new query's embedding is similar enough to a stored query's, above a threshold. Raises the hit rate, but can return the answer to a different question.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#semantic-caching","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Cost per request","description":"What one request costs end to end: input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price for an API, or machine time × hourly price when self-hosting. Comparable across models with different tokenizers, unlike a price per token.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#cost-per-request","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Batch API","description":"An inference API that returns results later (often hours) in exchange for a lower price, for work that doesn't need an answer straight away.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#batch-api","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Utilization","description":"The share of a resource's capacity actually in use. A rented machine that sits idle still bills by the hour, so low utilization raises the cost per request.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#utilization","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Cost per useful answer","description":"Total spend divided by answers that were both on time (met the SLO) and correct. Retries, late replies and wrong answers all raise it.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#cost-per-useful-answer","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Warm-up","description":"Untimed runs before a benchmark starts timing, so one-off costs such as loading and kernel compilation don't land in the results.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#warm-up","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"MLPerf Inference","description":"MLCommons' public inference benchmark. Its rules fix the model, dataset and accuracy target; the Server scenario reports the highest Poisson arrival rate that meets the latency limits.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#mlperf","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Chat template","description":"The model-specific rule that turns a list of role-tagged messages into the one token sequence the model was fine-tuned on, with special markers around each turn. A wrong template fails silently.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#chat-template","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"System prompt","description":"The developer's instructions, sent as the first message with the system role. The model gets it in the same sequence as the user's text; it carries more weight only through position and training.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#system-prompt","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Instruction hierarchy","description":"A trained priority order for conflicting instructions (Wallace et al., 2024): system over user over model and tool output. Lower-level instructions that conflict with higher ones are ignored; ones that agree are followed.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#instruction-hierarchy","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"In-context learning","description":"Teaching a model a task through instructions and examples in the prompt, with no change to its weights. Each example is a shot: zero-shot uses none, few-shot several.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#in-context-learning","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Structured output","description":"Model output in a fixed machine-readable format, such as JSON with known keys or one label from a list, so code can parse and use it.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#structured-output","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Constrained sampling","description":"At each generation step, masking every token that would break a rule, grammar or schema, then renormalising the remaining probabilities before sampling. Guarantees format, not correctness.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#constrained-sampling","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Tool calling","description":"A model emits a structured request (a tool name and JSON arguments) instead of text; the application checks and runs the function, then returns the result into the model's context.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#tool-calling","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Lost in the middle","description":"The finding (Liu et al., 2023) that language models often use information at the start or end of a long context better than information in the middle, giving a U-shaped accuracy curve.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#lost-in-the-middle","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Needle in a haystack","description":"A long-context test: insert a piece of information at different positions in a long prompt and check whether the model can find and use it.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#needle-in-a-haystack","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Reciprocal rank fusion","description":"Combining several retrievers' rankings by summing 1 / (k + rank) for each document, with k typically 60.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#reciprocal-rank-fusion","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"BM25","description":"A keyword-search scoring function that ranks documents by the query words they contain, weighting rare words more and long documents less.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#bm25","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Prompt version","description":"One exact, named revision of a prompt. It is logged with every output it produces so results can be traced and compared; any edit, even a typo fix, makes a new version.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#prompt-version","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Test set","description":"A fixed collection of inputs with known expected answers, run unchanged against every version so their results can be compared case by case.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#test-set","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Exact match","description":"A scorer that passes an output only if it equals the expected answer exactly. Suits short, exact answers; fails correct answers that are formatted differently.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#exact-match","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Prompt injection","description":"Text that gets a model to follow instructions its developer never intended, possible because instructions and data reach the model as one token stream.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#prompt-injection","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Indirect prompt injection","description":"Prompt injection delivered through data the model reads later, such as a web page, email, document or tool result, rather than typed by the user.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#indirect-prompt-injection","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Jailbreaking","description":"Getting a model past its safety features. OWASP treats it as a form of prompt injection.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#jailbreak","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"},{"@type":"DefinedTerm","name":"Trust boundary","description":"The line between context written by the developer or the user being served, and context anyone else controls, which must not be allowed to give orders.","url":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#trust-boundary","inDefinedTermSet":"https://llmdojo.dev/glossary#terms"}]}

children.children: MLCommons' public inference benchmark. Its rules fix the model, dataset and accuracy target; the Server scenario reports the highest Poisson arrival rate that meets the latency limits.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: The share of peak memory bandwidth inference uses: parameters × bytes per parameter × tokens per second, over the peak, for one sequence.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: A long-context test: insert a piece of information at different positions in a long prompt and check whether the model can find and use it.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: pN is the value N% of measurements fall at or below: p50 is the median, p99 is beaten by all but the slowest 1%. Used for latency because the mean hides the tail.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A vector added to each token's embedding so the model knows where the token sits in the sequence.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Quantizing a model after it has been fully trained. It is the most common approach, and the one application developers use.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Processing the whole prompt in one parallel pass before the first output token can be produced.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Keeping the KV cache of a prompt's shared opening, such as a system prompt or long document, so later requests that start with the identical prefix skip prefilling it.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Text that gets a model to follow instructions its developer never intended, possible because instructions and data reach the model as one token stream.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: One exact, named revision of a prompt. It is logged with every output it produces so results can be traced and compared; any edit, even a typo fix, makes a new version.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: Storing a model's numbers in a format with fewer bits, such as FP16, INT8 or INT4, to cut memory and the bytes each step reads. Strictly it means converting to integers, but in practice it covers any precision reduction.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Simulating low precision during training so the model learns to work well in it. It does not make training faster.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Three learned projections of each token's vector. A query is compared with every key to get attention weights; the weights then mix the values.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: Combining several retrievers' rankings by summing 1 / (k + rank) for each document, with k typically 60.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Adding a sub-layer's output back onto its input, so each block refines the token vectors instead of replacing them.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A chart of achievable operations per second against arithmetic intensity: a sloped roof set by memory bandwidth and a flat roof set by peak compute, meeting at the ridge.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: The starting value of a random number generator. The same seed and settings reproduce the same samples on the same setup.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Returning a stored answer when a new query's embedding is similar enough to a stored query's, above a threshold. Raises the hit rate, but can return the answer to a different question.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Finding documents by comparing embeddings of the query and the documents, so matches can share meaning without sharing words.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A target a service promises to meet, such as 'first token within 100 ms and at most 10 ms per token after that'.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Turns a list of scores into probabilities: exponentiate each score, then divide by the total so they sum to 1.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A vocabulary entry with a control meaning rather than text, such as end-of-text or a chat-role marker. User text must never become one.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Model output in a fixed machine-readable format, such as JSON with known keys or one label from a list, so code can parse and use it.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A token that can be a whole word or a fragment of one. Common words get one token; rare words are built from several.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: The developer's instructions, sent as the first message with the system role. The model gets it in the same sequence as the user's text; it carries more weight only through position and training.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: A number that divides the logits before softmax: below 1 sharpens the distribution, above 1 flattens it, 0 means greedy.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A fixed collection of inputs with known expected answers, run unchanged against every version so their results can be compared case by case.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Work done per second across all requests, usually output tokens per second. Not the same as how fast any one user's reply arrives.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: The average time between output tokens after the first one: how fast a streamed reply flows.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: How long from sending a request until the first output token arrives. Mostly the prefill, so it grows with the prompt's length.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Time until the first token the user can see. Later than time to first token when the model first generates hidden steps such as a plan.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A piece of text from a model's fixed vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a character or a byte sequence. Models read and write tokens, not characters.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: The integer a tokenizer assigns to a token: its position in the vocabulary. IDs only mean something within the vocabulary that produced them.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: The component that cuts text into tokens and maps each to an integer ID, and turns IDs back into text.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: A model emits a structured request (a tool name and JSON arguments) instead of text; the application checks and runs the function, then returns the result into the model's context.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Sampling only among the k most likely tokens, after renormalising their probabilities.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: Sampling only among the smallest set of most-likely tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: The repeated unit of a transformer: attention and a feed-forward network, each wrapped in a layer norm and a residual connection.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline

children.children: The line between context written by the developer or the user being served, and context anyone else controls, which must not be allowed to give orders.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: The share of a resource's capacity actually in use. A rented machine that sits idle still bills by the hour, so low utilization raises the cost per request.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: The fixed list of every token a tokenizer knows. Its size is a design choice made before training.

children.className: font-medium text-foreground underline-offset-4 transition duration-200 hover:underline
mt-3 divide-y divide-border rounded-3xl bg-surface px-2

children.children: Untimed runs before a benchmark starts timing, so one-off costs such as loading and kernel compilation don't land in the results.

/interview.title: AI Engineer & ML Engineer Interview Questions with Answers · LLM Dojo
/interview.description: Interview questions for AI engineers, ML engineers and applied AI engineers, with model answers: transformers, KV cache, sampling, RAG, fine-tuning, agents, inference and evals.

entries.question: When you send a prompt to a language model, what does the model actually receive?
entries.answer: A list of integer IDs, not the string. A tokenizer swaps each piece of text for an ID from a fixed vocabulary; the model reads IDs and writes them one at a time. With GPT-4o's o200kbase, "Tokenizers turn text into integers." is seven tokens: Token + izers, and the period on its own.

entries.question: What is a token, and why do most models use subword tokens rather than whole words or single characters?
entries.answer: A token is a piece of text from the tokenizer's fixed vocabulary, stored as an integer ID. Subwords are the compromise: whole words need a huge vocabulary and miss new words; characters make sequences several times longer. Rare words are built from frequent fragments, and a byte-level base like GPT-2's encodes any input.

entries.question: How does byte pair encoding learn a vocabulary, and how does it then encode a word it never saw in training?
entries.answer: Training repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols into a new one, giving an ordered merge list. Encoding splits new text into base symbols and replays the merges in order, so an unseen word becomes several known pieces. GPT-2's 50,257 entries are 256 byte tokens, 50,000 merges and one end-of-text token.

entries.question: A colleague estimates next month's API bill by counting the words in a batch of English and Hindi support tickets and multiplying by the price per token. What's wrong with the estimate, and how would you do it instead?
entries.answer: Prices are per token of one specific tokenizer, and words-to-tokens isn't constant. The rule of about 100 tokens per 75 words is for English prose with GPT-4's tokenizer. With cl100kbase, an English sentence took 6 tokens and a Hindi one saying roughly the same took 21, so the Hindi tickets would be badly underestimated. Sample real tickets, count them with the tokenizer of the model you'll call, and budget for output tokens.

entries.question: You're moving a product from a model that uses cl100k_base to one that uses o200k_base. Nothing crashes in staging. What could still be broken, and what goes into the migration plan?
entries.answer: Anything that stores tokens, because tokenizer mismatches fail silently: decoding IDs with the wrong tokenizer returns plausible garbage, not an error. The plan: - Cached token IDs: rebuild them. - Chunks sized in tokens: re-chunk and re-index. - Token budgets and cost estimates: recount; the same text gives different counts. - Throughput dashboards: tokens per second now means a different amount of text, so old and new numbers don't compare. Keeping the old tokenizer isn't an option: model and tokenizer were trained together.

entries.question: A ticket summariser crashes because tiktoken raises ValueError on a ticket that contains the literal end-of-text marker. A teammate's fix is to pass allowed_special='all'. What's your review comment?
entries.answer: Block it: that change is the injection. Special tokens like carry control meaning, so with allowedspecial="all" a user who types the marker can end a turn early or forge a boundary. The ValueError is the defence working. Encode untrusted text with encodeordinary() or disallowedspecial=(), so the marker stays plain characters; allowed, it becomes ID 199999, a real end-of-text signal. Add special tokens only from your own code. And catching the error to drop the ticket isn't a fix either: it silently loses data.

entries.question: Compare the main NLP tokenization approaches. Then, how would you design a recommender that uses an LLM?
entries.answer: Word vocabularies are huge and fail on unseen words; characters never fail but make sequences long. Subword methods, BPE, WordPiece and unigram, sit between: frequent words stay whole and rare ones split, so nothing is out of vocabulary. For the recommender, keep a classic retrieval stage over item and user-history embeddings, and use the LLM to rerank and explain a short candidate list, since item IDs make poor tokens and catalogues change daily.

entries.question: How would you design a subword tokenizer for a new LLM? And separately, what is KL-regularised supervised fine-tuning, and why use it?
entries.answer: Train byte-level BPE on a sample of the real mix of languages and code, so nothing is unknown. Vocabulary size trades shorter sequences against bigger embedding and output tables. Add digit and whitespace rules and chat tokens. KL-regularised SFT adds β times the KL divergence from a frozen base model's next-token distributions to the cross-entropy loss. It limits drift and forgetting; β sets how far it may move.

entries.question: What is subword tokenization, what does SentencePiece add, and what are the main transformer variants?
entries.answer: Subword tokenizers keep common words whole and split rare ones into frequent pieces: no unknown words, short sequences. SentencePiece trains on raw text, spaces included, so it needs no language-specific pre-splitting. Variants: encoder-only like BERT for understanding, decoder-only like GPT for generation, and encoder-decoder like T5 for input-to-output tasks such as translation.

entries.question: Implement a byte-pair encoding tokenizer with train, encode and decode, where training keeps merging the most frequent adjacent pair until counts fall below a threshold.
entries.answer: Work on bytes so any text encodes. Training merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new ID until its count falls below the threshold. python from collections import Counter def pairs(ids): return zip(ids, ids[1:]) def merge(ids, pair, new): out, i = [], 0 while i 1: pair, n = Counter(pairs(ids)).mostcommon(1)[0] if n 1: cand = [p for p in set(pairs(ids)) if p in merges] if not cand: break p = min(cand, key=merges.get) earliest merge ids = merge(ids, p, merges[p]) return ids def decode(ids, merges): vocab = {i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)} for (a, b), i in merges.items(): in merge order vocab[i] = vocab[a] + vocab[b] return b"".join(vocab[i] for i in ids).decode( "utf-8", errors="replace") Encoding applies merges in training order, always the earliest-learned pair present; decoding concatenates byte strings. Interviewers check the round trip, overlapping pairs like aaa, and the stopping rule.

entries.question: Before coding a BERT keyphrase span-extraction task, what would you clarify about the interface, tokenizer offsets, valid spans and the outputs?
entries.answer: Interface: one keyphrase per text or several, overlapping or not, labelled as offsets or strings? Tokenizer: which vocabulary, cased or not. Map character labels to token start and end with the fast tokenizer's offset mapping, and decide what happens when a label cuts through a subword. Texts over 512 tokens need sliding windows. Valid spans: end not before start, a maximum length, a no-answer case. Outputs: top spans as character offsets with scores.

entries.question: What is an embedding table, and what does it mean for two embeddings to be similar?
entries.answer: It's a learned matrix with one row per vocabulary entry, and embedding a token just reads its row. all-MiniLM-L6-v2's table is 30,522 × 384, about half its parameters. No single coordinate means anything; training shapes which vectors land near which. "Similar" means pointing the same way, usually measured with cosine similarity.

entries.question: People say 'embedding' for three different things. What are they, and why does the difference matter?
entries.answer: Only the last two change with context: - Static token embedding: a table row, identical in every sentence: river "bank" and money "bank" score cosine exactly 1. - Contextual token embedding: the transformer's output at one position, so it depends on context. - Text embedding: one vector per text; MiniLM averages its token outputs, then normalizes.

entries.question: Your vector database only supports dot-product search, but your embedding model's documentation says to compare vectors with cosine similarity. What do you do, and why does it work?
entries.answer: Normalize every vector, documents and queries alike, to length 1. Cosine is the dot product divided by both lengths, so on unit vectors the two are the same number. Without that, the dot product also rewards length, so a long document can outrank a closer short one. Verify rather than assume: for the lesson's sentences, MiniLM's vectors were 4.86 to 6.46 long until its final normalize step.

entries.question: You're building search over medicine leaflets with a small English embedding model, and you plan to reply 'no answer found' whenever the top cosine score is below 0.5. What risks do you raise before this ships?
entries.answer: Three risks. First, similarity tracks topic, not truth: in our MiniLM data, "This medicine is safe for children." and its negation scored 0.936, far above the best real paraphrase pair at 0.645. For medicine, negation needs explicit tests. Second, 0.5 means nothing universal. Scores aren't calibrated and there's always a nearest neighbour, so pick the threshold from labelled real queries and recheck it when the model changes. Third, MiniLM truncates after 256 word pieces according to its model card, so chunk long leaflets.

entries.question: Your team switches to a newer embedding model with the same 384 dimensions and starts embedding incoming queries with it. Search quality collapses, but nothing errors. Explain what happened and how you'd run the migration.
entries.answer: Each model arranges its own space, so matching dimensions only means the dot product can be computed. New-model queries against old-model documents give effectively random scores, with no error. Migrate by re-embedding the whole collection, cutting queries and documents over together, and re-checking every threshold, since thresholds are model-specific. Even a preprocessing change invalidates stored vectors. Budget for it: generating embeddings costs money, and storage grows with dimension. At 4-byte floats, a million documents is about 1.5 GB at 384 dimensions against 12.3 GB at 3,072.

entries.question: Embedding models return 1,536 or 3,072 numbers per text. What do those sizes mean?
entries.answer: That's the vector's dimension: each text becomes a point with that many coordinates. More dimensions can hold finer distinctions, but every vector costs more memory and search time. The numbers mean nothing alone: vectors compare only with others from the same model.

entries.question: An input embedding table is too large for one device. Compare sharding it by vocabulary with sharding it by hidden dimension.
entries.answer: By vocabulary, each device owns a range of rows, looks up the tokens it owns, writes zeros for the rest, and an all-reduce sum assembles full vectors. It pairs with a tied output head sharded the same way, but popular tokens can make one shard hot. By hidden dimension, every device holds all rows but a slice of the width. Lookups are local, then an all-gather concatenates the slices. Both move about batch × tokens × width numbers; choose by what the next layer wants.

entries.question: Your assistant's semantic search over user content is slow and expensive. How do you optimise it: embedding choice, ANN indexing and sharding?
entries.answer: Embeddings: shortlist models on public retrieval benchmarks, then pick on your own queries; smaller dimensions or int8 vectors cut memory and latency. Index: HNSW gives high recall at low latency but holds full vectors in memory; IVF with product quantisation compresses billions of vectors. Tune the recall-latency trade with ef or nprobe, then rerank a shortlist exactly. Sharding: partition by user or tenant, since an assistant searches one person's content, which also enforces isolation; otherwise scatter-gather across shards and merge top-k. Add replicas for throughput.

entries.question: Design an API that serves text embeddings and classification, for both interactive and batch requests.
entries.answer: Two endpoints, one encoder: classification is a light head on the embedding. Interactive calls are synchronous, with dynamic batching to a latency target. Batch is an async job: submit a file, get a job id, poll or take a webhook, read results from storage, trading latency for cost. Every response names the model version, because vectors from different versions aren't comparable.

entries.question: Design a system that returns a meaningful distance between any two employees to power people search and collaboration recommendations.
entries.answer: Build a collaboration graph: edges from shared documents, meetings, messages, code reviews and the org chart, weighted by frequency and recency. Learn node embeddings, with node2vec or a graph neural network, combine them with text embeddings of each person's work, and use cosine distance. Validate by predicting held-out future collaborations, then by people-search clicks. Respect permissions: only use signals the viewer could see.

entries.question: In your recommendation project, did you use embeddings, what counted as a positive label, and how did you retrain without exposure bias or leakage?
entries.answer: Yes: a two-tower model with user and item embeddings, trained with in-batch negatives. A positive should mean value: a click with real dwell time or a save, never a bare impression. Retrain on a time-based split, computing features only from data before each label's timestamp, so nothing leaks from the future. Exposure bias: the logs only hold what the old model chose to show, so keep a small exploration slice of randomised items, correct for popularity in sampled negatives, and weight by inverse propensity. Validate on the following day, then A/B test.

entries.question: Compare PCA and autoencoders as ways to fight the curse of dimensionality, and explain how you'd tell which compression helps downstream.
entries.answer: In high dimensions data gets sparse and distances concentrate, so models need far more data. PCA finds the linear projection that keeps the most variance: fast, deterministic, and easy to size from explained variance. An autoencoder learns a nonlinear encoder and decoder by minimising reconstruction error. A linear autoencoder with squared loss spans the same subspace as PCA, so it only wins on nonlinear structure with enough data. Judge them on the downstream task, not reconstruction: train the same model on each representation, sweep the dimension, and compare held-out accuracy and stability across seeds.

entries.question: In a notebook, implement embedding retrieval with cosine similarity. How does cosine relate to the dot product, and when would you choose each?
entries.answer: python import numpy as np def topkcosine(q, docs, k=5, eps=1e-12): n = np.linalg.norm(docs, axis=1, keepdims=True) d = docs / np.maximum(n, eps) qn = q / max(np.linalg.norm(q), eps) scores = d @ qn idx = np.argsort(-scores)[:k] return idx, scores[idx] Cosine is the dot product of unit-length vectors, so normalise once at indexing and any dot-product index ranks by cosine. Raw dot product also rewards vector length. Follow how the embedding model was trained: cosine for most sentence-embedding models, dot product when the model puts meaningful signal, such as popularity, in the norm. Guard against zero vectors.

entries.question: Design user and visual-item embeddings for retrieval when a user's history can hold 160,000 events. Cover time-correct training data, cold start and freshness.
entries.answer: A two-tower model. The item tower embeds image and text content, so new items get vectors immediately. The user tower runs a transformer over recent actions plus pooled summaries of older history, since 160,000 events won't fit attention. Build each example as of its timestamp: only earlier events, split train and test by time. For freshness, refresh user embeddings daily and add recent actions at request time. New users fall back to onboarding interests.

entries.question: Implement a local training pipeline for a text-embedding recommender built from member profiles, item text and click or skip interactions, with leakage-resistant splits and reproducible inference.
entries.answer: Join each impression to the profile as of that timestamp, label clicks positive and skips negative, then split by time: train on the past, validate on the next window, and keep anything fitted, like vocabularies or normalizers, to the training slice. Model: a two-tower text encoder for member and item, trained contrastively with in-batch negatives plus skips as hard negatives. Evaluate recall at k against a popularity baseline. For reproducibility, pin seeds, model versions and a data-snapshot hash in one config, ship preprocessing with the model, and test that inference reproduces the training embeddings.

entries.question: Design a service that computes and stores embeddings for user-uploaded documents, images and videos. Cover ingestion, chunking, frame sampling, idempotency and multi-tenant privacy.
entries.answer: Uploads land in object storage and enqueue a job. Workers per modality: documents are parsed and chunked by structure; images are embedded directly; videos are sampled at intervals and scene changes, with the audio transcribed and embedded as text. Batch on GPUs. Idempotency: key each output by content hash, model version and chunking config, and upsert, so retries never duplicate. Failures go to a dead-letter queue. Store vectors with tenant and offsets. Tenant isolation is enforced server-side: per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant keys, and deletes that propagate to vectors. Model upgrades re-embed into a new index.

entries.question: Design a streaming system that tokenizes arriving text, embeds it, trains a classifier and serves low-latency predictions.
entries.answer: Text arrives on a log. Stream workers tokenize with the tokenizer pinned to the encoder version, embed in GPU micro-batches, and store vectors with ID, timestamp and version. Train a light head, logistic regression or an MLP, on frozen embeddings, joining labels by time; retrain periodically and promote only after validating on the newest window. Serving latency is mostly the encoder: use a small distilled one, batch, and cache repeated texts. Keep training and serving on one embedding version, and backfill when it changes.

entries.question: Walk me through scaled dot-product attention. What are queries, keys and values, and why divide by the square root of d?
entries.answer: Score each token's query against every visible key, divide by √d, softmax, and weight the values. The query is what a token looks for, the key what it offers, the value what it hands over. Dot products grow with d, and large scores push softmax onto one token, where gradients get tiny.

entries.question: What's inside one transformer block, and where do most of its parameters sit?
entries.answer: Two sub-blocks, each layer norm, then the sublayer, then a residual add: first multi-head attention, then an MLP. Attention moves information between tokens; the MLP transforms each token on its own and holds most parameters. In GPT-2 small's first block, the MLP has 4,722,432 against attention's 2,362,368, and the model stacks 12 blocks.

entries.question: What does the causal mask do, and what does it imply for a decoder model reading 'The ladder did not reach the window because it was too short'?
entries.answer: It hides later tokens: before softmax, every score whose key comes after the query becomes minus infinity, so those weights are exactly 0 and the rest still sum to 1. So a decoder disambiguates only from the past: whether the ladder sentence ends "too short" or "too high", GPT-2 small's attention rows up to and including " it" were identical in all 12 layers and 12 heads. That also makes the KV cache exact.

entries.question: A teammate shows you a GPT-2 head that puts most of a pronoun's attention on the right noun and concludes that the head resolves pronouns. How do you respond?
entries.answer: It's a lead to test, not a conclusion. Head 4.3 puts 0.659 on " ladder" from " it", but " did", " not" and " reach" also look mostly at " ladder", and the subject always sat in the first two tokens. That can't separate "finds the subject" from "likes an early position". Attention weights show where a head reads from, not what the values carry or how 144 heads combine. I'd test sentences with the noun in different positions.

entries.question: Product wants to double the context you support, from 1,000 to 2,000 tokens. From the attention side, what gets more expensive, and what families of fixes would you weigh?
entries.answer: Attention compute grows quadratically. Each head scores an n × n grid, so doubling n roughly quadruples that work; the paper puts self-attention per layer at n² · d. GPT-2's 1,024-token window is about a million scores per head. The KV cache grows linearly, with context and batch size, and with learned positions the window is a hard cap. Fixes trade flexibility for speed and memory: a local attention window, keys and values shared across heads, a cache in fewer bits, or architectures that scale linearly. I'd measure latency and memory at both lengths first.

entries.question: Implement batched multi-head self-attention with a causal mask.
entries.answer: Project once, split into heads, attend in each head, merge. python def mhsa(x, wqkv, wo, h): x: (B, T, d) B, T, d = x.shape q, k, v = (x @ wqkv).split(d, -1) heads = lambda t: t.view(B, T, h, -1).transpose(1, 2) q, k, v = heads(q), heads(k), heads(v) (B, h, T, d/h) s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / (d // h) 0.5 future = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).triu(1) s = s.maskedfill(future, float("-inf")) y = s.softmax(-1) @ v return y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d) @ wo Interviewers watch for the mask before softmax, scaling by the head size, not d, and the transpose before the final reshape.

entries.question: A pre-norm transformer block trains badly. What do you check around the norms and residuals?
entries.answer: Pre-norm should read x + attn(norm(x)), then x + mlp(norm(x)): normalise each sublayer's input and add its output to the un-normalised stream. Common bugs: adding to the normed tensor, so the residual path stops being an identity; normalising the sublayer's output instead of its input; one norm shared where two are meant; and no final norm before the output layer. A quick test: zero both output projections, and the block must return x exactly.

entries.question: How does RMSNorm differ from LayerNorm, and why do recent models use it?
entries.answer: LayerNorm subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation, then applies a learned scale and shift. RMSNorm skips the mean: it divides by the root mean square and keeps only the scale. That's less computation with comparable quality in the paper's experiments, so models like Llama use it, in the same pre-norm positions.

entries.question: Implement scaled dot-product attention in PyTorch, then tell me where it can go wrong numerically.
entries.answer: python def sdpa(q, k, v, mask=None): mask True = may attend s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / q.size(-1) 0.5 if mask is not None: s = s.maskedfill(~mask, float("-inf")) s = s - s.amax(-1, keepdim=True) p = s.exp() return (p / p.sum(-1, keepdim=True)) @ v Scale by √d so scores don't saturate softmax. Subtract the row max before exp so nothing overflows; torch's softmax does this internally. A fully masked row gives NaN, since max minus max is inf minus inf, so guard it. In FP16, compute scores and softmax in FP32. FlashAttention does the same blockwise with a running max.

entries.question: Implement self-attention, give its time and memory complexity, and describe the efficient variants.
entries.answer: python def selfattn(x, wq, wk, wv): x: (T, d) q, k, v = x @ wq, x @ wk, x @ wv s = q @ k.T / q.shape[-1] 0.5 (T, T) s = s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True) p = np.exp(s) return (p / p.sum(-1, keepdims=True)) @ v Time is O(T² d) and the score matrix takes O(T²) memory, against O(T d²) for projections, so long sequences are attention-dominated. FlashAttention stays exact but tiles the work so the T-by-T matrix never reaches HBM. Sliding-window and sparse patterns make it linear in T; linear and low-rank attention approximate; MQA and GQA shrink the KV cache.

entries.question: Using only plain Python loops, implement a numerically stable sigmoid, a stable softmax and single-head scaled dot-product attention.
entries.answer: python import math def sigmoid(x): if x = 0: return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-x)) e = math.exp(x) x is negative: no overflow return e / (1 + e) def softmax(xs): m = max(xs) shift so the largest exp is 1 es = [math.exp(x - m) for x in xs] s = sum(es) return [e / s for e in es] def attention(Q, K, V): d = len(Q[0]) out = [] for q in Q: scores = [] for k in K: dot = 0.0 for a, b in zip(q, k): dot += a b scores.append(dot / math.sqrt(d)) w = softmax(scores) row = [0.0] len(V[0]) for wi, v in zip(w, V): for j in range(len(v)): row[j] += wi v[j] out.append(row) return out The trap is overflow: exp of a large number blows up. Branch sigmoid on the sign, and subtract the max before softmax, which leaves the result unchanged. Attention is then dot products, scaled by √d, a softmax per query, and a weighted sum of values.

entries.question: Quick-fire: explain self-attention, LoRA, Adam versus SGD, and the Vision Transformer.
entries.answer: Self-attention: each token scores its query against every key, softmaxes, and sums the values by weight. LoRA: freeze the weights, train a low-rank update. Adam tracks running averages of each parameter's gradient and squared gradient, giving per-parameter step sizes: the transformer default. SGD uses one global rate and less memory; it often generalises well in vision. ViT cuts an image into patches, embeds each as a token, and runs a standard transformer encoder.

entries.question: With no starter code, implement a GPT-style transformer decoder from scratch in about 30 minutes.
entries.answer: python import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F class Block(nn.Module): def init(self, d, h): super().init() self.h = h self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d) self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d) self.qkv = nn.Linear(d, 3 d) self.proj = nn.Linear(d, d) self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(d, 4 d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 d, d)) def attn(self, x): B, T, C = x.shape q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(C, dim=-1) q, k, v = (t.view(B, T, self.h, -1) .transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v)) s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / k.shape[-1] 0.5 m = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).tril() s = s.maskedfill(~m, float("-inf")) y = s.softmax(-1) @ v y = y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C) return self.proj(y) def forward(self, x): x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x)) return x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x)) class Decoder(nn.Module): def init(self, vocab, d, h, n, maxlen): super().init() self.tok = nn.Embedding(vocab, d) self.pos = nn.Embedding(maxlen, d) self.blocks = nn.ModuleList( Block(d, h) for in range(n)) self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(d) self.head = nn.Linear(d, vocab, bias=False) def forward(self, idx, targets=None): pos = torch.arange(idx.shape[1], device=idx.device) x = self.tok(idx) + self.pos(pos) for b in self.blocks: x = b(x) logits = self.head(self.ln(x)) if targets is None: return logits loss = F.crossentropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), targets.flatten()) return logits, loss Interviewers watch the causal mask, head reshapes that keep batch and heads apart, pre-norm residuals, and targets shifted by one token outside the model.

entries.question: In a recommender that uses cross-attention between a user's behavior sequence and a candidate item, what exactly are the query, key and value?
entries.answer: The candidate item is the query; the user's behaviour sequence supplies the keys and values. Each past item is embedded from its ID, category and context like time gap, then projected into a key and a value; the candidate's embedding is projected to the query. Softmax over query-key scores weights the history, so the output is a candidate-specific interest vector, the target attention DIN introduced. Cost grows with history length per candidate, so long histories are truncated or filtered first.

entries.question: Write pseudocode for single-head scaled dot-product self-attention with masks and tensor shapes, and for the cross-entropy loss.
entries.answer: State shapes as you go: x is T by d, scores T by T. Mask before the softmax, and normalise stably. python def attention(x, Wq, Wk, Wv, mask): x: (T, d) q, k, v = x @ Wq, x @ Wk, x @ Wv (T, dk), (T, dv) s = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(k.shape[-1]) (T, T) s = np.where(mask, s, -1e9) mask: True = keep s = s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True) p = np.exp(s) p /= p.sum(-1, keepdims=True) return p @ v (T, dv) def crossentropy(logits, y, ignore=-100): (N, V), (N,) keep = y != ignore z, t = logits[keep], y[keep] m = z.max(-1, keepdims=True) lse = m[:, 0] + np.log(np.exp(z - m).sum(-1)) return (lse - z[np.arange(len(t)), t]).mean() Cross-entropy is log-sum-exp minus the target logit, averaged over non-ignored tokens. Interviewers check the scale by the key width, masking scores rather than zeroing probabilities, and that padding labels are skipped.

entries.question: Compare RNNs, LSTMs and Transformers for sequence modeling, which Transformer variant you used and why, and how model predictive control fits in.
entries.answer: RNNs carry one hidden state step by step: cheap per step, but sequential, and gradients vanish over long spans. LSTMs add gates and a cell state so information survives longer. Transformers attend over all steps in parallel, train faster and capture long range, at cost quadratic in length; for streaming prediction I'd pick a causal decoder. MPC is different: it uses a dynamics model to optimise actions over a short horizon, applies the first and replans. A learned sequence model can be that dynamics model or forecaster, while MPC enforces constraints.

entries.question: Implement scaled dot-product multi-head attention and a Transformer block from scratch, including the backward pass for attention, without autograd.
entries.answer: Have the forward pass cache what the backward pass needs: the softmax probabilities P. python def attnfwd(Q, K, V): (T, d) each S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(Q.shape[-1]) S = S - S.max(-1, keepdims=True) P = np.exp(S) P /= P.sum(-1, keepdims=True) return P @ V, P def attnbwd(dO, Q, K, V, P): dV = P.T @ dO dP = dO @ V.T dS = P (dP - (dP P).sum(-1, keepdims=True)) dS /= np.sqrt(Q.shape[-1]) return dS @ K, dS.T @ Q, dV dQ, dK, dV The key line is the softmax backward: each row's gradient is P times dP minus its P-weighted mean. Multi-head attention reshapes into heads around this, and a block adds residuals, LayerNorm and an MLP, each with its own backward. Prove it with a finite-difference gradient check.

entries.question: Compare convolutional networks and Transformers on inductive bias, data and compute needs, and long-range dependencies. Where do hybrids fit?
entries.answer: Convolutions build in locality and translation equivariance: each layer sees a small neighbourhood so they learn well from less data, but long-range links need depth or pooling. Self-attention connects every position to every other in one layer with few built-in assumptions, so it needs more data or pretraining, and its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Hybrids take both: a convolutional stem feeding transformer layers, or convolution stages early and attention later, as in CoAtNet.

entries.question: Walk me through Transformer attention: causal and padding masks, cross-attention, why a KV cache helps at inference, and how mixed-precision training works.
entries.answer: Masks set scores to minus infinity before the softmax. The causal mask hides future positions; the padding mask hides pad keys, and pads are excluded from the loss. In cross-attention, queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder. At decode time, past keys and values never change, so the KV cache stores them; each step computes projections for one new token instead of re-running the prefix. Mixed precision runs matmuls in FP16 or BF16, keeps FP32 master weights and optimizer state, and with FP16 scales the loss so small gradients don't underflow.

entries.question: Implement sinusoidal or learned positional encodings in PyTorch, explain the equations and tensor shapes, and say what you'd see if positional information were missing.
entries.answer: python import math import torch def sinusoidalpe(T, d): pos = torch.arange(T).float()[:, None] (T, 1) i = torch.arange(0, d, 2).float() (d/2,) freq = torch.exp(-math.log(10000.0) i / d) pe = torch.zeros(T, d) d even pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(pos freq) pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(pos freq) return pe x: (B, T, d); x = x + sinusoidalpe(T, d).to(x) learned: x = x + nn.Embedding(maxlen, d)(posids) Dimension pair 2i gets sin and cos of pos divided by 10000 to the power 2i/d. A learned table is simpler but can't go past maxlen. Without positions, attention is permutation-equivariant: an encoder sees a bag of words, so shuffled inputs give shuffled outputs and order-dependent tasks fail. A causal decoder recovers some position from its mask.

entries.question: What are logits, and how does a model go from them to a whole sentence of output?
entries.answer: Logits are the raw scores the LM head gives every vocabulary token, 50,257 for GPT-2, from the last position's vector. Softmax turns them into probabilities: after "Thank you very", " much" got 0.992. For a sentence, loop: pick a token, append it, run the model again. So 25 new tokens means 25 passes.

entries.question: Explain temperature, top-k and top-p. Why would you usually reach for top-p rather than a fixed k?
entries.answer: Temperature divides every logit by T before softmax: low T sharpens, high T flattens, and T near 0 approaches greedy. Top-k keeps a fixed number of top tokens; top-p keeps the smallest set whose probabilities reach p, so the cut adapts to the distribution's shape. At top-p 0.9, GPT-2 kept 1 token after "Thank you very" but 417 for an open-ended prompt. No single k suits both: Holtzman et al.'s argument.

entries.question: Greedy decoding on a small model gives fluent text that soon repeats itself word for word. Why does that happen?
entries.answer: It's a feedback loop: once a phrase has appeared, the model rates it more likely to appear again, and greedy always takes the top choice. Continuing "I opened the box and found", GPT-2 small picked " amount" at 0.027 the first time and 0.988 on the repeat. Holtzman et al. report the same for most phrases they tested: decoding that maximizes probability tends to give bland or looping text.

entries.question: Your integration tests call a hosted model at temperature 0 and compare the output with an exact string. They fail now and then. What's going on, and what do you change?
entries.answer: The test assumes a determinism a hosted API doesn't promise. Temperature 0 is greedy and uses no random numbers, and our sampling script gave byte-identical output across two runs, but on one machine. AI Engineering notes that even with temperature, top-p, top-k and seed fixed, hardware can change the output, and with an API the hardware is the provider's choice. So stop asserting exact text from live calls: cache known answers where you need exact strings, or parse the output and compare fields, labels or structure. A seed won't fix it.

entries.question: A PM wants to show users a 'confidence' percentage computed from the answer's token probabilities. What's your position, and what would you build instead?
entries.answer: Against it: a token probability says how typical the text is after the prompt, not whether it's correct. Asked for the largest planet, GPT-2 small rated " Earth" at 0.0282, slightly above " Jupiter" at 0.0270. The number also moves with sampling settings, and the GPT-4 report found the model much less calibrated after post-training. Instead, use logprobs internally: log them, flag low-probability answers for review, and check on a labelled set that the flag actually catches errors.

entries.question: Write beam search that returns each sentence with its probability. How does it differ from greedy decoding?
entries.answer: Keep the k best partial sentences. Each step, extend every one with its likely next tokens, score by the sum of log-probabilities, and keep the top k. A sentence's probability is the exponent of that sum. Greedy is beam width 1, so it misses sequences whose first token wasn't the best. Longer sentences collect more negative terms, so normalise by length when comparing finished beams.

entries.question: Build a bigram next-word predictor that samples the next word in proportion to how often it followed.
entries.answer: Count each word's successors, then sample in proportion to the counts. python import random from collections import Counter, defaultdict def train(words): counts = defaultdict(Counter) for a, b in zip(words, words[1:]): counts[a][b] += 1 return counts def nextword(counts, w): nxt = counts.get(w) if not nxt: return None unseen word ws, cs = zip(nxt.items()) return random.choices(ws, weights=cs)[0] Interviewers check the unseen-word case and whether you can sample without random.choices: a cumulative sum plus binary search.

entries.question: Cover the fundamentals: self- versus cross-attention, autoregressive decoding and sampling, where RL fits, and how you evaluate the result.
entries.answer: Self-attention draws queries, keys and values from one sequence; cross-attention takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from another source, like an encoder's output. Decoding is a loop: score the next token, pick one greedily or by temperature and top-p, append, repeat, with a KV cache. RL then tunes those sampled outputs against a reward, held near a reference model. Evaluate with perplexity, task benchmarks and human or judge preferences.

entries.question: Given logits from a toy language model, implement greedy, top-k and top-p decoding in NumPy.
entries.answer: Greedy takes the argmax. Both samplers sort the probabilities, keep a prefix, renormalise it and sample. python import numpy as np def softmax(z): e = np.exp(z - z.max()) return e / e.sum() def pick(logits, rng, mode="greedy", k=5, p=0.9, temp=1.0): if mode == "greedy": return int(np.argmax(logits)) probs = softmax(logits / temp) order = np.argsort(probs)[::-1] high to low if mode == "topk": keep = order[:k] else: topp cum = np.cumsum(probs[order]) keep = order[:np.searchsorted(cum, p) + 1] q = probs[keep] / probs[keep].sum() return int(rng.choice(keep, p=q)) Interviewers check the max subtracted in softmax, that top-p keeps the token that crosses p, and the renormalisation before sampling.

entries.question: What is a context window, and why can't GPT-2 small take a 1,025th token even with plenty of memory?
entries.answer: It's the most tokens a model can read at once, shared by prompt, history and output: 1,024 for GPT-2 small. Attention alone ignores order, so GPT-2 adds a learned position vector from a table with exactly 1,024 rows. Position 1,025 has no row; on our CPU run it raised an IndexError.

entries.question: Users say your summariser 'takes ages to start' on long documents but then writes quickly. Explain what's happening in terms of prefill and decode.
entries.answer: The wait is prefill. Prefill runs the whole prompt in one parallel pass and sets the time to first token; decode then writes one token per step, each costing about the same. On our test machine, GPT-2 small prefilled 16 tokens in 15.3 ms and 960 in 219.6 ms, while a decode step stayed between 8.0 and 9.6 ms. The lever is how much text goes into the prompt.

entries.question: What does the KV cache store, why is using it exact rather than an approximation, and how much does it save?
entries.answer: It stores every processed token's keys and values, per layer and head, so each decode step computes only the new token's. It's exact because of the causal mask: earlier tokens never depend on later ones, and greedy output was identical with and without the cache. After a 960-token prompt on our test machine, a step took 9.6 ms with the cache against 228.8 ms without, about 24 times faster.

entries.question: You're sizing GPUs for a chat service. How do you estimate KV-cache memory, and which levers would you pull if it doesn't fit?
entries.answer: Multiply it out: 2 (key and value) × layers × heads × head dimension × tokens × bytes per number × batch. GPT-2 small in 32-bit floats needs 72 KiB per token; a full 1,024-token window at batch 64 is 4.50 GiB, nearly ten times the weights. Cache, not weights, can cap context length and concurrent users. Each factor is a lever: fewer bytes (a lower-precision cache), fewer tokens (a local window, trimmed history), keys and values shared across heads, a smaller batch. I'd model the real mix of context lengths and batch sizes before buying hardware.

entries.question: Request A has a 960-token prompt and 10 output tokens. Request B has a 16-token prompt and 200 output tokens. Same model and machine: which finishes first, and what does that tell you about a chat app that resends the full history every turn?
entries.answer: A. On our GPT-2 small measurements, A is about 220 ms of prefill plus 10 steps of about 10 ms, roughly 0.3 s; B is about 15 ms plus 200 sequential steps of about 8 ms, roughly 1.6 to 1.7 s. Output tokens run one after another, while prompt tokens are processed together. Resending the history re-prefills more every turn, so time to first token and cache memory grow turn by turn; once history won't fit the window, apps drop or summarise old turns. APIs typically bill input and output tokens, so trim both.

entries.question: What are multi-head and grouped-query attention, and what does GQA do to the KV cache?
entries.answer: In multi-head attention every head has its own queries, keys and values. Grouped-query attention lets a group of query heads share one key-value head. The cache holds keys and values per key-value head, so fewer of them means a proportionally smaller KV cache: Llama 2 70B's 64 query heads share 8, an 8× cut, with little quality loss.

entries.question: Here's a small transformer with a few bugs. Fix them, then add a KV cache for decoding.
entries.answer: Usual planted bugs: the mask applied after softmax, scaling by d instead of head size, a missing transpose before merging heads.
