entries.answer: Assume anything in the context can steer the model, so enforce security outside it. Tools run with the end user's permissions, checked server-side on every call; writes need confirmation. Retrieval filters by access control before text reaches the model, and no secrets go in prompts. Outputs are scanned for personal data, and links or images are rendered safely to block exfiltration. Add injection classifiers, rate limits, redacted logs and ongoing red-teaming.

entries.question: What is evaluation-driven development?
entries.answer: Writing down how you'll evaluate an application before you build it, the way test-driven development writes tests before code. You decide the criteria, and how each is scored, first. Otherwise you ship something that costs money to run and that nobody can say is working.

entries.question: What kinds of criteria would you use to evaluate an LLM application?
entries.answer: Four kinds, scored separately: domain capability (does it understand the subject?), generation (coherent, faithful, safe), instruction following (the requested format and length), and cost and latency. A summary can be faithful but too long, so one overall score would hide what to fix.

entries.question: Two annotators grading the same chatbot replies keep disagreeing. What do you change?
entries.answer: The instructions, not the annotators. Turn each criterion into a rubric with examples: what a reply that earns each score looks like, and why. Then have two people grade the same sample: their disagreements show where the rubric is ambiguous. Agreement alone isn't enough, since both can pass a reply that invents a price unless the rubric checks facts.

entries.question: Your support bot's factual consistency is 90%. Is that good enough to automate support?
entries.answer: It depends on the slices and the bar. Map the score to a business outcome: what share of requests can be automated at this level? Then check each slice: an overall 90% can hide a much lower score on billing questions, below your usefulness threshold there, while product questions are well above it.

entries.question: Version B has a higher pass rate than version A on last week's production logs. Do you ship B?
entries.answer: Not on that evidence. Each version served different traffic: if B got the easy self-serve tickets, its overall rate is flattered by its mix. That's Simpson's paradox: A can win every slice and still lose overall. Compare slice by slice, or better, run both on one fixed test set with the same mix, then check the slices you care about.

entries.question: How would you design the evaluation for a two-step résumé parser: PDF to text, then text to current employer?
entries.answer: Score the end-to-end answer and each step on its own: step 1 by similarity of the extracted text to the true text, step 2 by accuracy when it's given correct text. Then a failure points at a step, not the whole system. Add slices such as file formats and layouts, include out-of-scope inputs, and log each step's output so failures can be traced.

entries.question: The prompt mixes a regression target with precision and recall: untangle it, and pick metrics and a modeling plan tied to the real decision.
entries.answer: Ask what decision the output drives. Approve or decline is binary, so use precision and recall at the operating threshold, set by error costs. How much, like a loss amount, is regression, judged by MAE or RMSE. Often it's both: predict the probability of default and the loss if it happens, and combine them into expected value per decision. Agree the metric with stakeholders before modelling, and validate on a time-based split.

entries.question: When would you use unsupervised methods for fraud detection, and how would you evaluate them without reliable labels?
entries.answer: Use them when labels are scarce, delayed or blind to new attacks: isolation forests, autoencoder reconstruction error or graph clustering flag what's unusual, not what's known fraud. Evaluate by proxy. Backtest on the labels you do have with precision at the top k, since investigators can review only so many. Send flagged and random cases to analysts to estimate precision and lift. Inject synthetic anomalies to check recall, and track alert volume and stability over time. Unusual isn't fraud, so feed confirmed cases into a supervised model.

entries.question: You add a fixed amount to a logistic regression's intercept. What happens to the decision boundary, recall, precision, ranking metrics and calibration?
entries.answer: It adds the same constant to every logit, a monotonic shift, so the order is unchanged and ranking metrics like AUC stay identical. At a fixed threshold the boundary moves: a positive shift labels more examples positive, so recall rises or holds and precision usually falls. Calibration breaks, since predicted probabilities no longer match observed rates. It's equivalent to moving the threshold, which is how prior correction after resampling works.

entries.question: You're shipping a classifier for 7-day purchase with 3% positives, a 10-day label delay and asymmetric business values. How do you calibrate it and pick the threshold?
entries.answer: Validate out of time, only on examples whose labels have matured. With 3% positives, report PR-AUC, not accuracy. Calibrate with Platt or isotonic regression on a recent held-out window, check reliability curves and log loss, and undo any resampling first. Then act when expected value is positive: with gain G from a true positive and cost C from a false positive, the threshold is C / (C + G). Better still, sweep thresholds for expected profit with confidence intervals under capacity limits. Until labels arrive, monitor score distributions.

entries.question: What's the difference between exact and subjective evaluation?
entries.answer: Exact evaluation gives the same verdict every time: code passes its tests or it doesn't; an answer matches or it doesn't. Subjective evaluation depends on the judge, a person or a model, and can change between graders or runs. Prefer exact where the task allows, so a moving score means the system moved.

entries.question: What is pass@k?
entries.answer: For code generation: generate k samples per problem; a problem counts as solved if any of them passes all its tests; pass@k is the share of problems solved. It can only rise with k, so always report k: 80% at k = 10 is much weaker than 80% at k = 1.

entries.question: Why can BLEU or ROUGE mislead you when evaluating a model?
entries.answer: They measure how much the output looks like the references, not whether it's right. A correct rewording can score low because no reference matches it, and a wrong answer that changes one number can score near the top. References can also be incomplete or wrong. On HumanEval, OpenAI found BLEU similar for correct and incorrect solutions.

entries.question: When would you use semantic similarity instead of word overlap, and what does it depend on?
entries.answer: When many phrasings are right. Embeddings compare meaning, so a rewording can score high without sharing words, and “the dog bit the man” isn't scored as identical to its reverse. But it's only as good as the embedding model, which may not represent your domain, and it costs compute on every output.

entries.question: How do you choose a scoring method for a new LLM feature?
entries.answer: Take the most exact method the task allows. If the output can be run and checked, use functional correctness. One short right answer: exact match after normalising. Many valid phrasings and good references: lexical or semantic similarity. Otherwise, a judge with a rubric. Then check the metric itself by reading outputs it scores high and low.

entries.question: Can perplexity tell you which of two chat models is better?
entries.answer: Not on its own. Perplexity measures how predictable a text is to a model. It's a rough capability proxy, and useful for spotting contamination, when it's suspiciously low on a benchmark, or odd text. But post-training such as SFT and RLHF typically raises perplexity while making models better at tasks, so judge chat models on task metrics.

entries.question: Implement AUC-ROC with correct tie handling, a numerically stable softmax, and logistic regression trained with cross-entropy and L2 regularization.
entries.answer: AUC is the chance a random positive outscores a random negative, so compute it from average ranks, which counts ties as half. python def auc(y, s): order = np.argsort(s, kind="mergesort") ss = s[order] ranks = np.empty(len(s)) i = 0 while i < len(s): average rank per tie group j = i while j + 1 < len(s) and ss[j + 1] == ss[i]: j += 1 ranks[order[i:j + 1]] = (i + j) / 2 + 1 i = j + 1 pos = y == 1 npos, nneg = pos.sum(), (~pos).sum() u = ranks[pos].sum() - npos (npos + 1) / 2 return u / (npos nneg) def softmax(z): z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True) e = np.exp(z) return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) def fitlogreg(X, y, lam=0.1, lr=0.1, steps=2000): w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0 for in range(steps): z = X @ w + b p = 0.5 (1 + np.tanh(z / 2)) stable sigmoid g = p - y w -= lr (X.T @ g / len(y) + lam w) no L2 on b b -= lr g.mean() return w, b Interviewers check ties, overflow on large logits, which subtracting the max prevents, and that the bias isn't regularised.

entries.question: Build a lightweight evaluation harness for a model served through Ollama: run a dataset of prompts, score the answers against references and report the results.
entries.answer: Keep it small: a JSONL dataset, a client that calls Ollama's generate endpoint with temperature fixed, a scorer, and a report. python import json, requests URL = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" def ask(model, prompt): body = {"model": model, "prompt": prompt, "stream": False, "options": {"temperature": 0, "seed": 0}} r = requests.post(URL, json=body, timeout=120) r.raiseforstatus() return r.json()["response"] def norm(s): return " ".join(s.lower().split()) def run(model, path): rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open(path)] hits = 0 for row in rows: ok = norm(ask(model, row["prompt"])) \ == norm(row["answer"]) hits += ok print(json.dumps({"id": row["id"], "ok": ok})) print(f"accuracy {hits / len(rows):.3f} " f"n={len(rows)}") Normalised exact match suits short answers; swap in a numeric tolerance or a judge for free text. Log each output with model and prompt version so runs stay comparable.

entries.question: What is LLM-as-a-judge, and why is it so widely used?
entries.answer: Using a model to score outputs. It's fast, cheap next to human graders, works without reference answers so it can run on live traffic, and can judge any criterion you can describe. A judge is the model plus its prompt and settings: change any one and you have a different judge.

entries.question: How would you write the prompt for an LLM judge?
entries.answer: State the task, the criteria in detail, and the scoring system. Prefer labels, or a short discrete scale like 1 to 5, over wide or continuous ranges, and include an example of each score with the reason. Ask for the reasoning too, so verdicts can be audited.

entries.question: Your judge gives the same reply different scores on different runs. What do you do?
entries.answer: Reduce the randomness: fix the sampling settings, such as temperature 0, and add scored examples to the prompt. Zheng et al. raised GPT-4's consistency from 65% to 77.5% that way. But consistent isn't accurate, and examples make every call longer and costlier, so check the judge against human labels too.

entries.question: A vendor reports “faithfulness 4.2” and your pipeline reports “faithfulness 0.8”. Which system is more faithful?
entries.answer: You can't tell. Judge criteria aren't standardised: tools ship a criterion called faithfulness with different prompts and scales, such as 1 to 5, 0 or 1, or yes or no. A score is defined by its judge model, prompt and settings, so compare only scores from the same judge, and re-score a baseline whenever the judge changes.

entries.question: What biases do LLM judges have, and how do you mitigate them?
entries.answer: Self-bias: favouring its own outputs, so don't let a model judge itself against a competitor. First-position bias: favouring the first answer, so judge each pair in both orders and call disagreements ties. Verbosity bias: preferring longer answers, even ones with errors, so compare verdicts with length and ask for brevity in the rubric. Different judges have different biases: measure yours.

entries.question: Your judge agrees with human graders 80% of the time. Can you use it as a quality gate?
entries.answer: Agreement alone can't say. Break it down: of the replies people called bad, how many does the judge let through? Easy good replies inflate agreement, so a lenient judge can agree 80% and still pass most bad ones. Decide which mistake costs more, fix the rubric or examples where they disagree, and re-check whenever the judge's model, prompt or settings change.

entries.question: Design a hybrid evaluation platform that combines human reviewers with LLM judges. How do you calibrate the judges and measure agreement between evaluators?
entries.answer: Layer it. Deterministic checks run on everything, LLM judges score the rest, and humans label a stratified sample plus cases where judges are unsure or disagree. Humans are the reference. Each judge, meaning model, prompt and settings, is calibrated against a gold set and promoted only when its agreement with humans, by Cohen's kappa, nears the agreement between humans. Low inter-annotator agreement means the rubric is unclear. Re-validate judges on fresh labels regularly and whenever the judge or product changes, and report per slice with confidence intervals.

entries.question: Design an evaluation platform for a design-editing agent that handles both exact property changes and open-ended visual requests, combining hard assertions, rubrics and calibrated evaluators.
entries.answer: Split tasks by verifiability. Exact requests, like setting a padding, get hard assertions on the document diff: the target property changed, and nothing else did. Open-ended requests get a multimodal judge over before and after renders, scored per rubric criterion: intent followed, content preserved, layout intact. Calibrate each judge against designer labels and track agreement over time. The platform: versioned files and instructions, sandboxed runs, stored traces, per-slice results, and a regression gate.

entries.question: Why does every evaluation result need a baseline?
entries.answer: A score means little until you know what it beats. Random guessing is the floor (25% on four-option multiple choice), then the simplest approach that could work, the version you run today, and sometimes a person doing the job. Most real decisions are against what you'd replace.

entries.question: What is an ablation study, and when would you run one?
entries.answer: Remove one part at a time, such as retrieval, a reranker or prompt examples, and re-run the same evaluation. The drop is what that part is worth. A part whose removal costs nothing measurable can go: it's pure cost in tokens, latency and upkeep. Change one thing at a time, or you can't tell which change mattered.

entries.question: Version B scores 4 points higher than A on 100 test cases. Is B better?
entries.answer: Not yet: bootstrap it. Resample the 100 cases with replacement many times, the same cases for both versions, and look at B's lead each time. If the 95% interval includes zero, the set can't tell them apart. Four points on 100 cases is four cases; on 1,000 cases the same lead can be clearly real.

entries.question: What is benchmark contamination, and how would you detect it?
entries.answer: A model scoring well because it saw the test in training, usually by accident through web scraping. Detect it with n-gram overlap against the training data, accurate but needing the data and compute, or unusually low perplexity on the test, cheaper and less accurate. For your own decisions, a private test set avoids it.

entries.question: How many test cases do you need to compare two LLM systems?
entries.answer: Start from the smallest difference that would change your decision. A rough rule reported from OpenAI: about 100 cases to detect 10 points, about 1,000 for 3, about 10,000 for 1. Every 3× smaller difference needs about 10× more cases. If a 2-point gain is worth real money, budget for thousands of cases.

entries.question: How should you use public leaderboards like Chatbot Arena when choosing a model?
entries.answer: As a shortlist, not a decision. Rankings come from crowd votes on many simple prompts, with few votes per pair, and they assume transitivity. Elo even depends on match order, one reason Arena moved to Bradley–Terry. And a win rate says which is better, not whether either is good enough for your tasks, in your setup, at its cost.

entries.question: You only have small counts. How would you statistically compare two rare-event detection models and decide which is better?
entries.answer: Accuracy hides rare events; compare counts on the same cases. If both models saw the same data, use McNemar's paired test, which uses only cases where they disagree. For rates like detections per thousand miles, compare Poisson rates with an exact test. With few events, report the wide intervals too.

entries.question: What is error analysis?
entries.answer: Reading real failures, grouping them into failure modes, counting each, fixing the one that matters most, and turning those failures into test cases. Metrics tell you how often something goes wrong; reading the outputs tells you what goes wrong.

entries.question: Your pass rate dropped five points this week. What do you do first?
entries.answer: Read a sample of the new failures and note what went wrong in each, in plain words, before trying a fix. Then group the notes and count them. Read some passing outputs too: scorers and judges can pass things for the wrong reason.

entries.question: How do you decide which failure mode to fix first?
entries.answer: Weigh how often it happens by how much harm it does, and both against the cost of the fix. A rare failure that gives customers wrong prices can outrank a common one that only makes them ask again. Write the severities down and agree on them, like a rubric.

entries.question: How do you make sure a fixed failure doesn't come back?
entries.answer: Turn it into a test case: the original input, the expected answer, and a check a program can run, in a known-failures set that runs on every change. Keep that set separate from the production-like one, or a growing pile of hard cases makes an improving system look worse.

entries.question: A RAG assistant gave a wrong answer. How do you find the cause?
entries.answer: Check the steps in order, from the logs. Was the right passage retrieved? If not, fix retrieval. Was it there but ignored or contradicted? Fix the prompt or the model. Was the source itself wrong or stale? Fix the docs. Without each answer's retrieved passages and prompt version logged, you can't tell which.

entries.question: What is criteria drift, and what does it mean for your evaluation?
entries.answer: You need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs is how you discover what the criteria should be. So the rubric is never finished: add criteria as new failure modes appear, version it, and re-score a baseline after each change so results stay comparable.

entries.question: A recommender ranked mostly by distance raised add-to-cart rate but lowered revenue per session: diagnose why and design a replacement with experiments to separate causes.
entries.answer: Sorting by distance favours cheap, nearby items, so carts fill more often but with smaller baskets. Decompose revenue per session into conversion times order value and slice by category and price band to see which term moved. Replace it with a ranker scoring expected revenue: relevance times conversion times basket value, with distance as one feature. To separate causes, A/B test old, new, and a distance ranking reweighted to the old price mix.

entries.question: What is retrieval-augmented generation?
entries.answer: A retriever finds the passages most relevant to a question in your own data, and a generator answers with them in its prompt. It builds context per query, so answers can use current, per-user data and cite where they came from.

entries.question: Your knowledge base is 150,000 tokens. Do you need RAG?
entries.answer: Maybe not. Anthropic's guidance: under about 200,000 tokens you can put the whole knowledge base in the prompt. The trade-off is per-query cost and how well the model uses a long context: sending 150,000 tokens instead of 5 chunks of 300 is 100× the input on every request. Large or fast-changing data needs retrieval.

entries.question: Which changes force you to re-index, and which don't?
entries.answer: The index belongs to the retriever. Re-index when the chunking, the embedding model, or the tokenizer you chunk by changes. Swapping the generator doesn't require it: it reads whatever text retrieval hands it.

entries.question: Retrieval finds the right passage 70% of the time. Is a better generator or better retrieval worth more?
entries.answer: Usually retrieval. A generator only helps on the questions where it has the passage. Illustratively, with 90% accuracy given the passage and 20% without: start at 0.69; a 95% generator gives 0.725; 90% retrieval gives 0.83. With perfect retrieval, the generator's accuracy is the ceiling.

entries.question: How would you decide where a question should be answered from in a RAG system?
entries.answer: Route before retrieving: - No search for messages like “thanks”: a search always returns something, which then competes for attention. - Documents for how things work. - Tables for numbers: text-to-SQL from the schema, run it, answer from the result; with many tables, first predict which ones. - Multi-query or multi-hop when one search can't answer it. A wrong route fails before any ranking happens, so evaluate the router too.

entries.question: When is RAG the wrong tool?
entries.answer: When the knowledge fits comfortably in the prompt and rarely changes, a retriever adds work without adding much. When the answer must be computed, like a sum over a sales table, text search can't find it: use SQL. And when failures are about format or behaviour rather than missing facts, retrieval won't fix them. Long contexts don't make RAG obsolete, though: data outgrows windows, and long contexts aren't always used well.

entries.question: What do TF and IDF measure?
entries.answer: Term frequency: how often a term appears in a document. Inverse document frequency: how rare it is across the collection, the total count divided by the documents containing it, usually logged. TF-IDF sums IDF × TF over the query's terms, so rare query words count most.

entries.question: What does BM25 add to TF-IDF?
entries.answer: Two corrections to term frequency: - Saturation: the tenth mention adds less than the first (parameter k1). - Length normalisation: long documents contain terms by chance, so their counts are discounted (parameter b; 0 turns it off). It's still a strong baseline. On the course's help-centre data, length alone decides which of two equally matching toy articles wins.

entries.question: Why is term-based search fast, and what does it never return?
entries.answer: An inverted index maps each term to the documents containing it, with counts, so only documents on the query terms' lists are scored. The flip side: a document sharing no term with the query is never a candidate, however well it answers. Paraphrase is term search's blind spot.

entries.question: How does embedding retrieval work, and what's its catch?
entries.answer: Embed every chunk once; at query time embed the query with the same model and return the k nearest vectors. The catch: there's always a nearest neighbour, so it returns k results even when nothing is relevant. A similarity threshold helps, but it's model-specific. It can also struggle outside the domain its model was trained on.

entries.question: Exact k-NN is too slow at your scale. What do you give up with an ANN index, and how do you choose one?
entries.answer: Recall: approximate search looks at only some vectors, so a true neighbour can be missed. Indexes differ in how they trade: IVF searches the nearest clusters; HNSW walks a graph, accurate and fast to query but slow and memory-hungry to build; LSH hashes, cheap to build but less accurate. Compare on recall, queries per second, build time and index size, and weigh build time heavily if the data changes often.

entries.question: Term-based or embedding retrieval for a support search full of error codes and paraphrased questions?
entries.answer: Both. Term search is faster, cheaper and strong out of the box, and exact codes like EADDRNOTAVAIL are where it's most reliable; embeddings can blur them. Embeddings handle paraphrase and can be improved by fine-tuning, but cost more to compute, store and search. Also check term tokenization: splitting can create false matches (“two-year-old” matching “two-factor”) or destroy identifiers. Then measure both on real queries.

entries.question: What is hybrid search?
entries.answer: Combining term-based and embedding-based retrieval, because they fail differently. Either in sequence (a cheap retriever fetches candidates, a precise step orders them) or in parallel (both rank, then the rankings are fused).

entries.question: How does reciprocal rank fusion work, and why use ranks rather than scores?
entries.answer: Each retriever gives a document 1 / (k + rank); sum across retrievers. BM25 points and cosine similarities aren't on the same scale, but ranks always are. k = 60 keeps one retriever's first place from dominating, so agreement wins. Cormack et al. found k = 60 near-optimal but not critical.

entries.question: When can fusion make retrieval worse?
entries.answer: When one retriever returns noise for a class of queries. On the course's six queries, BM25 matched a single common word (“every”, “phone”) in unrelated articles, those spurious matches got votes, and fusion ranked the right article first for 3 of 6, against 5 of 6 for embeddings alone. Fusion is only as good as its inputs: measure it on your queries.

entries.question: What's the difference between an embedding model and a reranker?
entries.answer: An embedding model encodes query and document separately, so document vectors are precomputed and search scales to millions. A reranker is typically a cross-encoder: it reads query and candidate together and scores relevance. More precise, but one model run per candidate at query time, so it only sees a shortlist.

entries.question: How do you size the candidate pool for a reranker?
entries.answer: From where the right chunk usually lands. A reranker can only reorder what it's given: if relevant chunks typically sit at rank 8, a pool of 3 can't help. Each extra candidate is another model run, so the pool trades quality against latency, as Nogueira et al. note for multi-stage ranking. Measure recall at the pool size, then precision at the top after reranking.

entries.question: A reranker fixes most of your misses but still prefers “safe for children over three” to “not safe for children under three”. What do you conclude?
entries.answer: A reranker is a better ranker, not a reasoner. On the course's data it ranked the right article first for 5 of 6 queries, but scored the reassuring toy article 4.66 against 3.89 for the one that answers. So keep more than one candidate, instruct the generator to read carefully and answer only from the passages, and keep negation cases in the evaluation set.

entries.question: Why do RAG systems chunk documents?
entries.answer: Embedding models and generators have input limits, and one vector for a whole document blurs every topic in it. Chunks give each idea its own vector, so a specific question finds the specific passage, and only that passage spends prompt tokens.

entries.question: How much overlap should chunks have?
entries.answer: Enough to keep whole what must stay whole. A span of L words always lands inside some chunk when overlap ≥ L − 1: for a 9-word answer, overlap 8. The cost: more chunks to embed and store (13 instead of 7 in the course's example), and repeated text when neighbours are both retrieved.

entries.question: Fixed-size or recursive chunking?
entries.answer: Recursive, usually: split by section, then paragraph, then sentence, until each piece fits. Cuts land where the author put them. Fixed sizes ignore meaning, so whether a fact survives is luck. Some documents suggest their own unit: a question-and-answer pair, or a code-aware splitter.

entries.question: A chunk is whole and correct but never retrieved. What's the fix?
entries.answer: Give it its context. Cut from its document, it may never say what it's about: “It usually arrives in 5 to 7 business days” doesn't say “refund”. Prepend the title and section, add keywords or entities, list questions it answers, or generate a short context with a model, as Anthropic's contextual retrieval does.

entries.question: How do you choose a chunk size?
entries.answer: By experiment. Smaller chunks let more distinct pieces fit (halve the size, fit twice as many) but split information and double the vectors to compute, store and search. Larger ones keep context together but carry more irrelevant text. Both are bounded by the embedding model's and generator's limits. The book says there's no universal best: measure retrieval on real questions with known answers at a few sizes.

entries.question: Anthropic reports large gains from contextual retrieval. What exactly did they measure, and what does it cost?
entries.answer: 1 − recall@20: the share of relevant chunks missing from the top 20. Contextual embeddings cut it 35% (5.7% → 3.7%); adding contextual BM25, 49%; adding a reranker, 67% (to 1.9%), on their evaluation sets. The cost is a model call per chunk at indexing time, repeated whenever documents change, plus longer chunks to embed and store.

entries.question: What are context precision and context recall?
entries.answer: Precision: of the documents retrieved, the share that's relevant. Recall: of the relevant documents, the share retrieved. Recall is harder in production: it needs every document judged for each query, so some frameworks report precision only.

entries.question: Two systems each retrieve one relevant result in their top three, at positions 1 and 3. How do rank-aware metrics tell them apart?
entries.answer: Average precision averages precision at each relevant position: 1/1 = 1.0 for the first system, 1/3 ≈ 0.33 for the second. MAP averages AP over queries; with one relevant document per query it equals MRR. nDCG goes further, allowing graded relevance and discounting gains lower down.

entries.question: Why score retrieval and answers separately?
entries.answer: To know where a failure happened. Retrieved but wrong points at generation; missed and wrong at retrieval; missed but right means the model answered from memory, unverifiable. The book: evaluate component by component and end to end.

entries.question: What's the difference between faithfulness and citation precision?
entries.answer: Faithfulness (Ragas): claims supported by any retrieved passage ÷ all claims. Citation precision: citations that support the sentence they're attached to. A true sentence citing the wrong passage is faithful but fails citation precision. Liu et al. found only 74.5% of generative search engines' citations supported their sentence.

entries.question: Your RAG answers score faithfulness 1.0, yet users report wrong answers. How?
entries.answer: Faithfulness measures loyalty to the evidence, not the evidence. A perfect summary of an outdated or irrelevant passage scores 1.0. Check what was retrieved: is the source current, was the right chunk returned, is the answer relevant to the question? Pair faithfulness with retrieval metrics, answer relevance and end-to-end correctness, and audit the judge.

entries.question: How do you make a RAG system say “I don't know”, and how do you know it's working?
entries.answer: Two guards: a similarity threshold so weak matches never reach the prompt, and instructions to answer only from the passages and say when they don't contain the answer. Then measure both sides: abstention on questions you know are unanswerable, and refusals on answerable ones. Every guard trades hallucinated answers for false refusals.

entries.question: What is an AI agent?
entries.answer: Something that perceives its environment and acts on it, defined by that environment and the actions its tools allow. In an AI agent the model plans the next step, reads the results, and decides when the task is done. By that definition, a RAG system is a simple agent.

entries.question: Walk me through the agent loop.
entries.answer: The model reads the context and writes a step: a thought and a tool call, or a final answer. The harness parses and runs the call and appends the result as an observation. Repeat. It ends when the model answers or the harness stops it: step limits, budgets, errors.

entries.question: What kinds of tools can an agent have, and which need the most care?
entries.answer: Knowledge augmentation (retrievers, SQL, web search), capability extension (calculators, code interpreters), and write actions (send email, update a database, move money). Reads change what the agent knows; writes change the world, so writes need the most trust and guarding.

entries.question: Each step of your agent is 95% reliable. How reliable is a 10-step task?
entries.answer: About 60%, if every step must succeed and failures are independent: 0.95¹⁰. At 100 steps, about 0.6%. The levers: fewer model decisions (fixed code where judgment isn't needed), checks between steps, and limits on how far it runs alone.

entries.question: Where does an agent's reliability come from?
entries.answer: Mostly the harness: the code that defines the tools, validates and runs calls, handles failures, manages the context, enforces limits and records everything. A prompt makes a mistake rarer; a check in code makes it impossible. Anthropic's principles point the same way: keep it simple, make planning visible, and design the agent-computer interface carefully.

entries.question: How do you decide whether a task needs an agent at all?
entries.answer: Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when needed. If the steps are known in advance, fixed code can run them, with the model doing only the parts that need judgment. An agent earns its extra cost, latency and compounding risk when the path can't be written down beforehand.

entries.question: What's the difference between a workflow and an agent?
entries.answer: Who chooses the next step. In a workflow, predefined code paths orchestrate the model and tools. In an agent, the model directs its own process and tool use. Workflows suit well-defined tasks; agents, open-ended ones where the number of steps can't be predicted.

entries.question: Name some workflow patterns you'd try before an agent.
entries.answer: - Prompt chaining: fixed steps, with checks between. - Routing: classify, then a specialised path. - Parallelisation: independent parts at once, or voting on repeated runs. - Orchestrator–workers: a model splits the task and delegates. - Evaluator–optimiser: generate, critique, revise.

entries.question: Why separate planning from execution?
entries.answer: So a bad plan is rejected before anything runs. Otherwise a plan that can't reach the goal can burn hours of calls, or perform a write you can't undo. Validate with heuristics in code (every tool exists, under a step limit) or a model judge; regenerate on rejection.

entries.question: Which planning failures can you catch before execution, and which can't you?
entries.answer: Catchable from the plan: an invalid tool, invalid parameters, too many steps, or a forbidden order like a refund before a policy check. Not catchable: wrong parameter values, like refunding the original charge instead of the duplicate. Those values come from earlier results, so check them at call time.

entries.question: Your agent loops “until the tests pass”. What does the harness need?
entries.answer: Its own limit: maximum attempts, time and cost. When a model judges a loop's exit condition, nothing guarantees it's ever met. In ordinary software conditions are exact; in agents the model decides them, so every loop gets a bound enforced in code.

entries.question: How do you put people into an agent without making it useless?
entries.answer: Decide the level of automation per action, in advance: reads run; small refunds run; large refunds wait for approval; deletions never. Enforce it in the tool wrapper. Approval pauses need durable state so the task resumes later. Often the best design runs a workflow for known cases and sends only the rest to an agent.

entries.question: What kinds of memory does an AI agent have?
entries.answer: Internal knowledge (the weights), short-term memory (the context, limited and gone after the task), and long-term memory (external stores reached by retrieval, persistent and editable). Place information by how often it's needed.

entries.question: What goes wrong if the harness just drops the oldest messages when the context fills?
entries.answer: The oldest message is often the task itself. FIFO assumes early messages matter least, and the book warns that can be fatally wrong, especially when they state the purpose. In the course's 12-step run, dropping the oldest loses the task at step 6 while the context still looks fine.

entries.question: How do you keep a long run within its context without losing what matters?
entries.answer: Pin what must stay (task, instructions, constraints) and summarise older steps instead of dropping them: Anthropic calls it compaction. A summary keeps only what its prompt asks for, so test that later steps still find what they need.

entries.question: What belongs in harness state rather than the context?
entries.answer: Anything that must be exact or must survive: IDs processed, refunds already issued, lists, queues. Structured data stays structured in code; in a context it's just text. Load details just in time with tools, keeping lightweight identifiers in the context.

entries.question: Your context fits the window. Why might you still manage it?
entries.answer: Context rot: as tokens grow, the model's ability to recall information from the context decreases; Anthropic calls the context an attention budget. And every step re-reads, and pays for, the whole context. So keep it to what the next decision needs, well before the hard limit.

entries.question: How would you design a handoff to a sub-agent?
entries.answer: The sub-agent knows only its brief. Send the goal, specific inputs, constraints and the shape of the result. Ask for a condensed summary back (Anthropic cites 1,000–2,000 tokens) that includes what it couldn't do or wasn't sure of. Clean contexts keep each agent focused; the risk is information lost at each boundary.

entries.question: Which tool failures should a harness retry automatically?
entries.answer: Transient ones: timeouts and dropped connections, with backoff. Not permanent ones like invalid arguments: return those to the model so it can fix the call. Overload responses mean slow down, not retry harder.

entries.question: A refund call times out. What does the harness know?
entries.answer: Nothing certain: the request may have been lost, may still be running, or may have succeeded with the response lost. They look identical. For reads, retry. For writes, retry only if the operation is idempotent, or check its effect first.

entries.question: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
entries.answer: Clients that failed together retry together. Backoff alone keeps them in step, so a recovering service gets all of them at once: in the course's simulation, 100 calls in one 100 ms window. Random waits spread them out: peak 11.

entries.question: How do retries multiply, and how do you stop it?
entries.answer: Attempts per layer raised to the number of layers: five layers of 3 is 243 attempts at the bottom. Retry at one layer, cap retries per request, keep a process-wide retry budget, and count the model's own re-calls against it.

entries.question: How do you make an agent's write actions safe to retry?
entries.answer: Idempotency keys: the server stores the first result for a key and returns it to repeats, so a retried refund happens once. The harness derives the key from task and step (or saves it in the checkpoint), so retries reuse it; a key the model invents each time protects nothing. Without API support, record completed writes and check before repeating.

entries.question: Your agent runs for an hour and sometimes crashes midway. How do you resume safely?
entries.answer: Checkpoint after every step: task, context or summary, results, completed side effects, keys in flight. On restart, load it and continue; the harness, not the model, decides which steps are done, so completed writes are skipped. The same mechanism makes pauses for human approval cheap.

entries.question: What is a trace, and what should it capture?
entries.answer: The linked record of one request's path through the system, every step, so a failure can be pinned to the exact step. Log everything: model and settings, prompt version, inputs and outputs, every tool call with its arguments and result, timings and costs.

entries.question: How do you debug an agent run that claims success but did the wrong thing?
entries.answer: Walk the trace from the start and find the first step whose inputs don't follow from earlier results. In the course's example, the agent refunded ch1 when the duplicate was ch2: a valid tool with a wrong value. Its claim of success is a separate reflection error.

entries.question: What failure modes are specific to agents?
entries.answer: - Planning: invalid tool, invalid parameters, wrong values. - Goal: misses the task or breaks a constraint, including time. - Reflection: claims it's done when it isn't. - Tools: right tool, wrong output, or a missing tool. - Efficiency: right result, too many steps or too costly.

entries.question: How should you judge whether an agent's task succeeded?
entries.answer: By the end state of the environment, not the agent's claim. τ-bench compares the database after the conversation with an annotated goal state. Run in a sandbox reset before each trial, and include what must not change, so side effects count as failures.

entries.question: Your agent succeeds 87.5% of the time on a task. Is it ready to run unattended?
entries.answer: Measure pass^k: the chance that all k trials succeed, unlike pass@k (at least one). On the course's illustrative trials, pass@8 is 0.833 but pass^8 is 0.167. τ-bench found even gpt-4o under 50% on its tasks, with pass^8 below 25% in retail. Unattended agents need consistency, not just a success rate.

entries.question: Your logs show most bad tool calls go to one tool. What do you do?
entries.answer: Improve its description and examples, fine-tune if needed, and if it's still misused, change the tool: simpler parameters or a narrower purpose. Also look at the tool-use distribution and ablate: if removing a tool doesn't hurt, remove it. Then rerun the test harness on every change.

entries.question: What is excessive agency?
entries.answer: An application that can take damaging actions when model output is unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated. OWASP names three causes: excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy.

entries.question: What stopping conditions would you put on an agent?
entries.answer: Limits on steps, cost, wall-clock time, repeated identical calls and consecutive failures, all checked by the harness. Anthropic recommends stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations. When one fires, checkpoint, report what was and wasn't done, and hand over.

entries.question: How do you apply least privilege to an agent's tools?
entries.answer: Only the tools it needs, each doing only what's needed; narrow tools over open-ended ones like a shell; read-only where possible; actions run as the user; authorisation enforced downstream on every request. A tool that can't express a harmful action can't be talked into it.

entries.question: Where should “refunds over $100 need approval” be enforced?
entries.answer: In the harness, in the refund tool's wrapper, checking the argument before the call runs. The prompt can describe the rule so the model explains the wait, but code decides what runs. A policy uses facts the model doesn't control, like the customer's address from the ticket system.

entries.question: How do you defend an agent against instructions hidden in tool output?
entries.answer: Treat every tool result as untrusted input. Detection is unreliable, so block outcomes: a recipient rule stops an injected email without anyone noticing the injection. Don't let tool output widen permissions, and be wary of chains that give a stranger's text a route to write tools.

entries.question: What is the lethal trifecta, and how do you break it?
entries.answer: Private data, untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally, in one agent. Then injected instructions can exfiltrate data. Willison's advice: avoid the combination; a filter catching 95% of attacks is a failing grade against an adversary who retries. Remove a leg, fix the recipients, or split the work across agents.

entries.question: How do you choose a model for an application?
entries.answer: Filter on hard attributes you can't change (licence, model size, privacy, control), narrow with public benchmarks, run your own evaluation balancing quality, latency and cost, then monitor in production. You want the best model for your application, not the leaderboard.

entries.question: Why pin model versions when using an API?
entries.answer: The model behind an API name can change, sometimes without notice. The book cites Voiceflow reporting a 10% drop between GPT-3.5-turbo versions. Pin a dated version where offered, and treat any switch as a release: rerun the evaluation and regression suites.

entries.question: What does a router in front of your models do?
entries.answer: Usually an intent classifier: sends each query to the best solution, a specialised model, a cheaper model, a person, or a stock reply for out-of-scope requests with no model call. It can also ask for clarification. It must be small and fast, since it runs on every query.

entries.question: Router or cascade?
entries.answer: A router decides before answering, from the question. A cascade lets the cheap model answer, checks the answer, and escalates failures, so it decides with more evidence. Cascades win when most queries stop at step one and a cheap, reliable check exists: a schema, a test, a validator. Escalated queries pay for both.

entries.question: How do you set a difficulty router's threshold?
entries.answer: Trace its cost–accuracy curve on your evaluation set and pick the cheapest point meeting your quality bar. In the course's illustrative example, one threshold matched the large model's 90% at about half its cost; RouteLLM reports over 2× savings in some cases. Moving the threshold moves the borderline queries, so re-measure, broken down by query type.

entries.question: What does a model gateway give an organisation?
entries.answer: One interface to every model, so a provider change happens in one place. Plus access control instead of shared provider keys, usage limits and cost tracking, fallbacks when a provider fails, and logging; some add caching and guardrails.

entries.question: What is graceful degradation?
entries.answer: When parts fail or load is too high, return lower-quality, cheaper results instead of nothing: a smaller model, no reranker, a cached answer, the raw passages, or an honest message. Never a hang.

entries.question: Your primary is 99% available and a fallback 99.5%. What's combined availability?
entries.answer: If outages are independent, both are down 1% × 0.5% = 0.005% of the time: about 2 minutes a month instead of about 432. If they share half their outages (same provider or region), it's about 217 minutes. Pick fallbacks by how they fail.

entries.question: What does a circuit breaker do?
entries.answer: Counts failures on a call; past a threshold it opens, failing fast or going straight to the fallback with no timeout wait. After a cool-down it lets one trial through; success closes it. In the course's example, users wait 80 s in total instead of 1,000 s during an outage.

entries.question: Demand is twice capacity. Why shed load instead of queueing everything?
entries.answer: Queueing everything makes every request slow until most time out: nobody is served. Load shedding rejects some requests fast with a clear “busy”, so the rest are served well. The SRE book's example: return 503 to new requests once too many are in flight.

entries.question: You fall back to a model you've never evaluated with your prompt. What can go wrong?
entries.answer: It's a different model: format reliability, refusals and quality may all change, turning an outage into a quality incident. Give the fallback path its own prompt version if needed, its own evaluation run, and metrics split by which model answered.

entries.question: Retry after a bad output, or send two requests in parallel?
entries.answer: Depends which budget is tighter. Retrying after failure is cheap but can double latency. Parallel requests keep latency near one call but pay for redundant calls every time. Either way, write the failure behaviour down and exercise it: unused fallback paths rot.

entries.question: What three budgets does an AI feature have?
entries.answer: Cost, rate and latency. Each is a requirement enforced in code with a planned behaviour when it's hit. A provider's spend cap stops every feature on the account until it resets.

entries.question: Your feature costs too much. Which levers do you compare?
entries.answer: Prompt caching of a shared prefix, routing easy requests to a smaller model, shorter outputs, and fewer input tokens. In the course's illustrative model, caching or routing roughly halves a $27,000 month; both together reach about $8,000. Each has a quality side: measure it before shipping.

entries.question: When is caching whole answers dangerous?
entries.answer: When the answer depends on who asked. The book's example: a return-policy answer built from user X's membership, cached as generic, then served to user Y. Key the cache on everything the answer depended on, skip user-specific and time-sensitive queries, and invalidate on prompt or data changes.

entries.question: You're under 60 requests a minute but still get 429s. Why?
entries.answer: Limits use a token bucket: capacity refills continuously, so short bursts can be rejected even when the per-minute total is fine. Smooth bursts, wait at least retry-after with backoff, separate batch from live traffic, and use prompt caching, which for most Claude models doesn't count toward input-token limits.

entries.question: How would you structure usage limits across an organisation?
entries.answer: Nested: provider limits for the organisation; per-application limits in the gateway so one can't starve others; per-user limits against abuse and compromised accounts; per-request caps on tokens and agent steps. Track spend daily, project the month, and act before the hard cap.

entries.question: Your answers must start within one second. How do you budget it?
entries.answer: Add up the stages before the first token: router, retrieval, reranker, the model's time to first token. Streaming hides generation, but not for answers needed whole, like JSON or output-guardrail checks. Parallelise independent stages, skip optional ones under load, and budget percentiles, not averages.

entries.question: What are MTTD, MTTR and change failure rate?
entries.answer: Mean time to detection: how long until you notice. Mean time to response: how long to resolve. Change failure rate: the share of changes needing a fix or rollback. Together they measure how observable a system is.

entries.question: How do you design production metrics for an AI feature?
entries.answer: Start from the failures you want to catch, not what's easy to plot: format failures, factual consistency, safety and refusals, user signals, latency and cost. Make every metric breakable by user, release, prompt version and time.

entries.question: Quality dropped after a canary rollout. How do you find what broke?
entries.answer: Break the metric down: by release on the same days, then by query type. In the course's synthetic incident, only how-to questions on the new release got worse, 3% to 12% thumbs-down. Then read traces of affected requests to find the failing step: there, retrieval returned a chunk cut off mid-procedure.

entries.question: What implicit feedback signals would you track in a chat product?
entries.answer: Early termination; error corrections like “No, …” or “I meant, …”; rephrasing; requests like “Are you sure?” or “Show me the sources”; and users editing outputs. They're noisier than thumbs but far more plentiful. And they're user data, with privacy obligations.

entries.question: Metrics are stable, yet you suspect drift. What drifts in an AI system?
entries.answer: - Prompts: a template changes, someone fixes a typo. - Users: phrasing and topics shift; the book's example is shrinking response lengths as users ask for concise answers. - Models: an API's model is updated. Version everything, watch slow trends and new input slices, and rerun the evaluation set on a schedule.

entries.question: Walk me through handling an AI incident.
entries.answer: Detect; mitigate first (roll back, flag off, fall back); then diagnose with breakdowns and traces; fix and add the failures to the test set; write a blameless postmortem covering impact, timeline, causes and follow-ups, asking why the system allowed it, not who erred.

entries.question: What are input and output guardrails?
entries.answer: Input guardrails stop private data leaking to external APIs and bad prompts compromising the system. Output guardrails catch failures (format, facts, toxicity, private data, brand risk) and apply a policy: retry, repair, block or hand to a person.

entries.question: How do you keep users' personal data out of a third-party model API?
entries.answer: Detect it in the assembled prompt, including retrieved passages and tool results, then block or mask it with placeholders, keeping a reverse map to restore values in the reply. It isn't airtight: detectors miss things, and the model can't use what it can't see.

entries.question: How do you choose an output guardrail's threshold?
entries.answer: Count both errors on a labelled sample: harmful outputs let through and good outputs blocked. The book stresses tracking false refusals: a system can be too secure. Pick the threshold whose mistakes you can best afford.

entries.question: Why don't output guardrails mix well with streaming?
entries.answer: Partial responses are hard to evaluate, so an unsafe part may already be on screen; holding the answer for a check gives up streaming's fast first token. Choose per feature: stream casual chat, hold back high-stakes answers.

entries.question: How would you ship a prompt change safely?
entries.answer: Offline evaluation and regression suite; behind a feature flag so turning it off is seconds, not a deploy; shadow on copies of traffic; a small canary compared with control on a few user-facing metrics; then ramp in steps.

entries.question: Why canary, and how many users does it protect?
entries.answer: Exposure scales with share: the workbook's example is a 5% canary at 20% errors adding about 1% overall. Comparing canary with control on the same days also catches problems sooner. In the course's illustrative example, 25 extra bad answers instead of 1,500.

entries.question: When should you fine-tune instead of prompting?
entries.answer: Usually after systematic prompting, examples and retrieval. Fine-tuning needs far more data, compute and expertise. It's for behaviour failures prompting can't fix. Set up evaluation first so you know whether it helped.

entries.question: RAG or fine-tuning?
entries.answer: Classify the failures. Information failures (missing or outdated facts) call for RAG; behaviour failures (wrong format, style or relevance) for fine-tuning. The book: fine-tuning is for form, RAG is for facts. With both, start with RAG.

entries.question: Give good reasons to fine-tune.
entries.answer: Output structure or a rare syntax, like an uncommon SQL dialect; task-specific behaviour; bias mitigation; and a small, specialised model that's cheaper to serve, possibly distilled. The book's example: Grammarly's fine-tuned Flan-T5 beat a GPT-3 text-editing variant at 60× smaller.

entries.question: Why does full fine-tuning need so much memory, and what does LoRA change?
entries.answer: Besides the weights, you store gradients and optimizer states for every trained parameter: a 7B model in 16-bit with Adam is 14 GB plus 42 GB. LoRA trains small low-rank matrices instead, merged back without inference latency, so training memory shrinks.

entries.question: Make the case against fine-tuning for a team that wants to.
entries.answer: It can degrade other tasks; it needs data, expertise, serving and maintenance as new base models arrive. Often prompt experiments weren't systematic. The book's cautionary tale: BloombergGPT, about 1.3M A100 hours, was outperformed on financial benchmarks by GPT-4-0314, released the same month.

entries.question: How would you assess whether an AI feature is ready for production?
entries.answer: Check each layer with evidence: evaluated and pinned models, routing and a gateway; independent fallbacks and degraded modes; enforced budgets; metrics, traces and an incident process; guardrails and flagged, canaried releases. Turn gaps into a list ranked by likelihood × harm against effort, each with an owner, a date and the evidence that will show it's done.

entries.question: What is retrieval-augmented generation, and how does it reduce hallucination?
entries.answer: Before the model answers, retrieve relevant passages from your documents and put them in the prompt, so it answers from evidence in its context, not memory alone. It cuts hallucination when retrieval finds the right passage and the prompt says to answer only from it, cite it, and admit when it isn't there.

entries.question: How do you choose a chunking strategy for RAG?
entries.answer: Chunks should be small enough to be specific and big enough to stand alone. Split on the document's own structure first, like headings and paragraphs, then cap the size in tokens with a little overlap so no sentence loses its context. Prefix each chunk with its title or section path. Then pick the size by measuring retrieval on real questions, not by rule of thumb.

entries.question: Why combine keyword and embedding search, and where does a reranker fit?
entries.answer: Embeddings catch paraphrases; keyword search such as BM25 catches exact terms like product codes, names and error messages. Hybrid search runs both and merges the rankings, for example with reciprocal rank fusion. A reranker, a cross-encoder that reads the query and a passage together, then rescores the top few dozen: too slow for the whole corpus, much sharper on a shortlist.

entries.question: How do you evaluate a RAG pipeline?
entries.answer: Score the two halves separately. Retrieval: on questions with known source passages, does the right one land in the top k? Generation: is the answer faithful to the retrieved passages, and does it answer the question? Use a judge model checked against human labels, on a fixed set run after every change. Bad retrieval and bad generation need different fixes.

entries.question: Your RAG chatbot keeps giving wrong answers. How do you find out why, and fix it?
entries.answer: Sort failures by stage before changing anything: log the retrieved passages for every bad answer. Right passage missing: fix retrieval with better chunking, hybrid search, query rewriting, metadata filters, or more candidates plus a reranker. Passage present, answer wrong: fix generation by putting it first, trimming distractors, and asking the model to quote and to abstain. Source wrong or stale: fix the data. Then add each failure to the eval set, so the fix stays fixed.

entries.question: Design a RAG system that has to meet strict latency and cost targets while serving many tenants.
entries.answer: Start by splitting the latency budget across retrieval, reranking and generation. I'd use hybrid retrieval, BM25 plus dense vectors, with a tenant filter applied inside the search, never after it. A small cross-encoder reranks, and only the best few chunks enter the prompt, which keeps prefill short. For cost: cache embeddings and answers per tenant, keep the system prompt a stable prefix for prompt caching, stream tokens, and route easy questions to a smaller model. Track recall and p95 per tenant, with rate limits so no tenant starves the rest.

entries.question: Design an agent for searching internal documents that respects permissions, cites sources and abstains when it should.
entries.answer: Permissions first: store each chunk with its source's access-control list and filter by the user's identity inside the retrieval call, so the model never sees what the user can't open. Sync ACL changes fast; stale permissions are a leak. The agent plans searches, reformulates and opens documents, but every answer must cite passages, and a checker verifies claims against them. With no relevant evidence, or conflicting evidence, it abstains and suggests owners. Evaluate recall, citation accuracy, correct abstention, and permission tests with users of different access.

entries.question: Design a production RAG system end to end, from ingesting documents to serving answers.
entries.answer: Offline: parse documents, chunk on their structure, embed, and index chunks with metadata and permissions in a vector and keyword index, updated incrementally. Online: rewrite the query, run hybrid search filtered by the user's access, rerank, and pack the best passages into a prompt that says to cite them and abstain when the answer isn't there. Around it: an eval set scoring retrieval and faithfulness separately, logged passages, caching, and a per-stage latency budget.

entries.question: Design a RAG-based agent system: how it retrieves, how it grounds its answers, and how it enforces access control.
entries.answer: Retrieval becomes tools the agent calls, a search per source, so it can reformulate and search again. Grounding: answers cite passages, a checker flags claims the passages don't support, and the agent abstains when evidence is missing. Access control lives in retrieval, not the prompt: filter every search by the user's permissions, and run tools with that user's credentials and least privilege. Retrieved text is untrusted, a vector for indirect injection, so write actions need confirmation. Log every retrieval and action for audit, and evaluate retrieval, faithfulness and leakage separately.

entries.question: You're designing retrieval for a coding agent. What do you index, how do you chunk and rank, how do you keep noise out, and how do you measure it?
entries.answer: Index more than files: parsed symbols with signatures and docstrings, the import and call graph, tests, docs and recent diffs. Chunk on syntax boundaries, a whole function with its path and class, not fixed windows. Rank with several signals: exact identifier search, embeddings for intent, and graph expansion from symbols in the open file or stack trace, then a reranker. Cut noise by skipping vendored, generated and build files. Measure recall of the files the real fix touched, then task success: do the tests pass?

entries.question: A coding agent writes SQL and notebooks over a company's data platform. How would you retrieve and rerank the right tables and notebooks for a request?
entries.answer: Turn each asset into a searchable card: a table's name, columns and comments, tags, owner, sample values and lineage; a notebook's title, cell summary, and the tables it reads and writes. Retrieve with exact match on table and column names plus embeddings on descriptions, filtered by access permissions first. Rerank with a cross-encoder and usage signals: query popularity, freshness, certified status, and lineage closeness to tables already in the session. Evaluate on logged requests: recall at k of the table the user really queried, then whether the SQL runs correctly.

entries.question: Users search an enterprise catalogue of tables, columns and dashboards by exact name and by meaning. How would you design hybrid retrieval over that metadata?
entries.answer: Queries mix exact identifiers, like a table name or catalogue path, with intent, like churn by region. Run a keyword index over names, paths and column names, and embeddings over descriptions and comments. Normalise identifiers first, splitting snakecase and camelCase so custid matches customer id. Merge them with reciprocal rank fusion, but let an exact name match go straight to the top. Filter by permissions first, and tune on search logs.

entries.question: Design an enterprise research assistant where every claim in the answer carries a citation the user can verify.
entries.answer: Make citation part of generation, not decoration. Retrieve with hybrid search and a reranker, respecting document permissions, and give each passage an id. Have the model write claim by claim, each with the supporting span as structured output. Then verify every claim: an entailment model or judge checks it against its cited span, and unsupported claims are dropped or flagged. Show citations as quotes that open the source. Evaluate citation precision and recall: is each claim supported, and is each citation needed?

entries.question: Using the Mistral API, how would you build a RAG agent end to end: ingestion, chunking, embeddings and retrieval?
entries.answer: Ingest: parse documents to text, keep metadata like source, date and permissions, and split by structure into chunks of a few hundred tokens. Embed them in batches and store vectors with the metadata. At query time, embed the question with the same model, retrieve the top k with filters, and give the chat model chunks with ids to cite. Make retrieval a tool, so the agent can search again with a rewritten query.

entries.question: Compare tokenization choices and dense versus sparse retrieval for search and RAG, then design and evaluate a hybrid retriever.
entries.answer: Sparse retrieval like BM25 matches tokens, so its tokenization matters: words with stemming suit English prose, while code, part numbers and other languages need subwords or character n-grams. Dense retrieval embeds meaning, so it catches paraphrases but misses rare exact strings. A hybrid fuses both rankings, say with reciprocal rank fusion, then reranks the top. Evaluate on labelled queries with recall at k and NDCG, broken down by query type, against each retriever alone.

entries.question: Build a minimal embedding-based RAG pipeline: chunk, index, retrieve and assemble the prompt. How do you evaluate retrieval, resist injected instructions and abstain when unsure?
entries.answer: python import numpy as np def chunk(text, size=200, overlap=40): w = text.split() step = size - overlap stop = max(len(w) - overlap, 1) return [" ".join(w[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, stop, step)] def buildindex(chunks, embed): E = np.array([embed(c) for c in chunks], float) return E / np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True) def retrieve(q, E, embed, k=4): v = np.asarray(embed(q), float) s = E @ (v / np.linalg.norm(v)) top = np.argsort(-s)[:k] return top, s[top] def hitrate(results, gold): hits = [bool(set(r) & g) for r, g in zip(results, gold)] return sum(hits) / len(hits) Normalise embeddings so retrieval is a dot product. Evaluate on questions labelled with their relevant chunk ids: hit rate or recall at k, plus MRR. The prompt wraps chunks as quoted evidence, says nothing inside them is an instruction, and requires a chunk id per claim. Delimiters reduce injection without stopping it, so the model gets no tools. If the top score falls below a threshold tuned on the eval set, abstain.

entries.question: Design a question-answering agent over a law firm's legal memos, from ingestion and chunking to grounded, cited answers at scale.
entries.answer: Ingest memos with the metadata lawyers filter on, such as matter, client, jurisdiction and date, plus ethical-wall permissions enforced inside the retrieval query. Chunk along the memo's structure, issue, analysis, conclusion, keeping the heading path, so citations land on a paragraph. Use hybrid search, since case names and statute numbers need exact match, then a reranker. The model answers only from retrieved passages with pinpoint citations, and a verifier checks each claim against its cited span. Flag memos the law may have overtaken, and abstain on conflicting evidence.

entries.question: Design a RAG system that reads company policies and writes step-by-step, cited instructions for a human support agent. How do you check a policy applies, and debug a wrong instruction?
entries.answer: Index policies as versioned documents with metadata: region, product, user type, effective dates. Extract the case facts from the ticket first, retrieve policies whose metadata matches, then run an applicability check: does each candidate cover this region, date and booking type? The model writes numbered steps, each citing a policy clause, or says none applies. Log policy versions, retrieved chunks and prompt version with every answer. When an agent reports a wrong instruction, replay it against that exact policy set to see whether retrieval, applicability or generation failed.

entries.question: Design an MVP RAG assistant that answers employee questions across Jira issues and Confluence pages, covering ingestion, retrieval, ranking and permissions.
entries.answer: Ingest through the product APIs and webhooks so edits and deletions arrive fast. Chunk pages by heading; treat an issue as summary, description and comments, with project, status and assignee as metadata for filters. Hybrid search, since issue keys need exact match, then a reranker boosting recent items. Store each item's permissions and filter by user inside the query, re-syncing when access changes. Answers cite links; evaluate on real employee questions.

entries.question: Design the retrieval and ranking pipeline behind a RAG assistant, including indexing, access control and the metrics you'd evaluate it with.
entries.answer: Index chunks with metadata and their source's access-control list, kept in sync. At query time, rewrite the query, run BM25 and dense retrieval with the permission filter inside both, fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, then a cross-encoder reranks the top few dozen. Measure each stage on labelled queries: recall at k for candidates, NDCG and MRR for the final order, then answer faithfulness and permission-leak tests.

entries.question: Design a chatbot for a single enterprise customer and domain that holds multi-turn conversations and answers only from that customer's approved documents.
entries.answer: RAG over the approved corpus only, versioned so removed documents disappear. Hybrid retrieval plus a reranker. For multi-turn, rewrite each follow-up into a standalone query using the history, and keep a short conversation summary. The prompt says answer only from the passages and cite them; when support is weak, the bot abstains or hands off to a human. Evaluate on real customer questions: faithfulness, correct abstention and resolution rate.

entries.question: Design an AI-powered document search pipeline with OCR, metadata and keyword extraction, indexing, retries and reprocessing.
entries.answer: Stages, each tracked per document: detect type, OCR scans while keeping page and box positions with confidence, extract metadata and keywords, chunk, embed, and write to a hybrid index with access-control fields. Each stage is idempotent, keyed by document hash and stage version, and persists its output, so a failure retries only that stage with backoff, and poison documents land in a dead-letter queue. Reprocessing is a version bump: a new OCR model reruns affected stages, then the index swaps over. Queries: hybrid retrieval, metadata filters, a reranker. Monitor OCR confidence and search quality.

entries.question: Prompting, RAG or fine-tuning: how do you choose?
entries.answer: Start with prompting: cheapest, and often enough. Add RAG when the model lacks knowledge, especially private or changing facts. Fine-tune when it has the knowledge but not the behaviour, like a format, tone or narrow skill that prompt examples can't fix. They combine, and fine-tuning is the costliest to change.

entries.question: What is LoRA, and why is it so much cheaper than full fine-tuning?
entries.answer: LoRA freezes the original weights and learns a small low-rank update for chosen matrices: W + BA, where B and A are thin, rank 8 or 16, say. Only A and B train, so gradients and optimizer state are a tiny fraction of the model's, and one base model can serve many adapters. After training you can merge BA into W, so inference costs nothing extra.

entries.question: You're handed fine-tuning code whose loss behaves oddly. What do you check?
entries.answer: Start with what the model actually sees: decode a batch back to text. Usual suspects: a chat template that differs from the base model's; labels shifted twice or not at all; a loss not masked to the answer tokens, so the model learns to predict prompts; padding counted in the loss; new special tokens missing from the tokenizer; a learning rate too high for the batch. Then overfit ten examples: if the loss won't approach zero, the bug is in the pipeline, not the data.

entries.question: Compare RLHF with a reward model to DPO.
entries.answer: Both learn from preference pairs, a chosen and a rejected answer. RLHF trains a reward model on them, then optimises the policy against it with PPO, held near a reference model: powerful, but several models and a touchy RL loop. DPO drops the reward model and the RL: one loss on the pairs raises the chosen answer's probability relative to the reference. Simpler and steadier.

entries.question: Debug a GRPO training loop. What is the probability ratio, and what goes wrong with it?
entries.answer: GRPO samples a group of answers per prompt, scores them, and uses each answer's reward minus the group mean, over the group's standard deviation, as its advantage: no value model needed. The ratio is the new policy's probability of a token over the old policy's that sampled it, clipped near 1 as in PPO. Typical bugs: the ratio built from the wrong log-probs, such as the reference model's, or not detached; a missing exp of the log difference; padding left unmasked; advantages normalised over the batch instead of the group.

entries.question: Design a platform for fine-tuning LLMs on AWS, covering distributed training and security between tenants.
entries.answer: A control plane accepts jobs, base model, dataset in the customer's S3, method and hyperparameters, validates them and schedules onto GPU pools. Default to LoRA: adapters train on few GPUs and many tenants share one served base model. Full fine-tunes use FSDP or ZeRO across EFA-linked nodes, checkpointing to S3 so spot interruptions resume. Isolation is the hard part: a per-tenant KMS key for data and weights, jobs in tenant-scoped IAM roles with no cross-tenant network path, no shared caches holding tenant data, and every access audited.

entries.question: How do you detect and prevent reward hacking during LLM post-training?
entries.answer: Reward hacking is the policy finding outputs the reward model scores highly but people wouldn't: longer answers, sycophancy, a format the grader likes, or edited tests in code tasks. Detect it when reward keeps rising while held-out human or stronger-model judgments flatten; track length and other proxies, and read the top-reward samples. Prevent it with a KL penalty to the reference model, early stopping as overoptimisation begins, reward-model ensembles, retraining the reward model on fresh policy samples, and verifiable rewards with graders the policy can't tamper with.

entries.question: Design an asynchronous RL post-training system for a production chat model.
entries.answer: Split actors from the learner. Inference workers on a fast serving engine generate rollouts from a recent policy snapshot; reward workers score them with reward models or verifiers; the learner trains from a buffer and pushes weights periodically. Asynchrony keeps GPUs busy despite rollouts of very different lengths, but samples go off-policy: track and cap policy lag, and correct with importance ratios and clipping, as in PPO. Keep a KL penalty to the reference model, version every weight and rollout, and gate releases on held-out helpfulness, safety and regression evals.

entries.question: Explain GRPO for reinforcement learning on LLMs, and how it differs from PPO.
entries.answer: Both maximise reward with a clipped probability ratio. PPO estimates advantages with a learned value model, often policy-sized. GRPO drops it: it samples a group of answers per prompt and uses each answer's reward, normalised by the group's mean and standard deviation, as the advantage. GRPO also puts the KL penalty in the loss, not the reward. It saves memory and suits checkable rewards like maths, but needs several samples per prompt.

entries.question: Walk me through the main LLM post-training methods: SFT, RLHF and preference optimisation. What are the trade-offs?
entries.answer: SFT imitates demonstrations: simple and stable, but can't exceed its data. RLHF trains a reward model on preferences and optimises against it with PPO: it can beat the demos, but is costly, unstable and prone to reward hacking. DPO-style methods learn from preference pairs directly: cheap and steady, but offline. For checkable tasks like maths and code, RL with verifiable rewards, such as GRPO, skips the reward model. SFT usually comes first.

entries.question: An enterprise customer wants a 7B model that's better at coding in their codebase. Design the post-training pipeline.
entries.answer: Start with the target: an execution-based eval built from the customer's real tasks, with unit tests that pass or fail, plus public coding benchmarks to catch regressions. Data: their repositories, internal libraries and review history, scrubbed of secrets, plus synthetic tasks kept only if they run. Then stages: continued pretraining on their code if it's unusual, SFT on instruction and solution pairs, then RL from execution feedback or DPO on passing versus failing samples. Gate every stage on the eval and watch for forgetting. LoRA adapters keep many customers on one base.

entries.question: Walk me through an LLM's lifecycle: pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, RL, and how each stage is evaluated.
entries.answer: Pretraining learns language and knowledge by next-token prediction on trillions of tokens, most of the compute. SFT trains on curated prompt-response pairs so the model follows instructions and a format.
