children.children: A vector of numbers that represents a token or a text, arranged so that similar meanings end up close together.

children: , working vector search, a reliable similarity metric and a threshold that takes trial and error. A wrong match returns a wrong answer.

children.question: Embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, which pair scores higher: 'My wifi keeps dropping every few minutes.' / 'Our wireless network disconnects all the time.', or 'The Earth orbits the Sun.' / 'The Sun orbits the Earth.'?

children.children: The opposite claims score 0.982. The Wi-Fi pair, which means the same thing, scores 0.645, the highest of all 21 Wi-Fi pairs. Embeddings like this capture topic and wording more than truth.

These are the 19 sentences from Module 01's embedding explorer, standing in for queries. We count a hit as right only when both sentences are Wi-Fi complaints. At a threshold of 0.50, 5 of the 21 Wi-Fi pairs hit, and so do 2 wrong pairs: "This medicine is safe for children." returns the answer cached for "…is not safe for children." (0.936).

Try to find a threshold that catches a paraphrase without a wrong hit. There isn't one in this data: both opposite pairs score above every paraphrase. Above 0.982 the wrong hits stop, and then nothing hits at all.

children.question: What should you do before adding a semantic cache?
options: Set the threshold to 0.5 and ship
Lower the threshold until the hit rate is high
Measure, on your own queries, how often hits are wrong as well as how often they happen

children.children: The book says to evaluate efficiency, cost and quality risks first. Semantic caching is worth it only if the hit rate is high and the wrong-hit rate is acceptable.

children.children: A piece of text from a model's fixed vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a character or a byte sequence. Models read and write tokens, not characters.

children: 's keys and values depend on every token before it. Change one early token and every later value changes, so only an identical prefix gives identical values to reuse.

. OpenAI's guide says to "put stable developer instructions and shared reference material first". Anthropic caches in a fixed order, tools, then system, then messages, up to the block you mark. In practice:

children.children: Instructions and tool definitions that never change.

Caching saves repeated work, so it does nothing when there isn't any. Look for these first:

Providers won't cache below a minimum: 1,024

children.question: CPU estimate: 128 shared + 64 unique prompt tokens, 400 output tokens. Caching the prefix makes the first token about 48% sooner. How much sooner does the full reply finish?

children.children: About 1%: 3.32 s becomes 3.30 s, because 400 decode steps take nearly all the time. Even with a 768-token prefix, 64 unique tokens and 192 output tokens (GPT-2's full 1,024), the total goes from 2.04 s to 1.87 s, only 9%.
For answer caches, the limits are the ones on the previous pages: personal, time-sensitive or one-off queries, and semantic matches you can't trust.

children.question: A code assistant sends a 2,000-token, rarely changing system prompt, then a short question, and writes long answers. Users complain the answers take too long to finish. Will a prefix cache fix it?
options: Mostly not: the first token comes sooner, but finishing is set by decode
No: the prefix is too short to matter for TTFT

children.children: Caching the system prompt helps the first token, but long answers are decode-bound. To finish sooner, change decode: shorter outputs, faster hardware, or fewer bytes per weight.

children.children: What one request costs end to end: input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price for an API, or machine time × hourly price when self-hosting. Comparable across models with different tokenizers, unlike a price per token.

children: stays roughly flat. A machine's daily cost is fixed, so its cost per request falls as traffic grows. They cross at the

children.children: break-even requests per day = machine cost per day ÷ API cost per request
provided one machine can serve that many requests. If even a fully busy machine costs more per request than the API, self-hosting never wins on price.

children.question: An always-on machine costs $48 a day. The API costs $0.0023 per request. Roughly where is the break-even?

children.children: $48 ÷ $0.002304 ≈ 20,800 requests a day. With the batch API's 50% discount it doubles to about 41,700.

children: The calculator's defaults are illustrative: Sonnet 5.5 list prices, a $2-an-hour machine, and the speed of GPT-2 on a laptop.

children.question: An illustrative request sends 2,000 input tokens and gets 500 output tokens back, at $2 and $10 per million. What share of its cost is the reply?
options: About 20%: it is a fifth of the tokens

children.children: Input costs 2,000 × $2 / 1,000,000 = $0.004 and output 500 × $10 / 1,000,000 = $0.005: $0.009 in all. The reply is 20% of the tokens and 56% of the bill.

children.question: (Illustrative numbers.) Each request costs $0.01, and 80% of answers are correct. Failed ones are retried until they succeed. What does a correct answer cost on average?

children.children: $0.0125. Each attempt succeeds 80% of the time, so a correct answer takes 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25 attempts on average. Without retries you get the same figure: $0.01 for every request, but only 80% of them are useful.

children.question: We served 120 mixed requests (prompts of 16 to 896 tokens) one at a time on the laptop CPU, with an SLO of TTFT ≤ 100 ms and ≤ 10 ms per token. About how many met it?
options: All 120: the CPU averages under 10 ms per token

children.children: 83 of 120. 36 of the 37 misses were long prompts (512 or 896 tokens) whose first token took over 100 ms; only one missed on token gaps alone. Throughput was 136.8 requests per minute of busy time; goodput was 94.6.
Each dot is one measured request: how long its first token took (across) and its average time per token (up). The shaded box is the SLO. Try:

children: : CPU goodput falls to 61 of 120 requests, even though throughput hasn't changed.

children.children: Find the SLO the CPU passes in full

children: , then ask whether your users would accept it.

children.children: Why it is the better target

children: Goodput turns a vague "faster" into a number you can optimise against, and it exposes trade-offs that throughput hides. Batching more requests raises throughput, but if it pushes requests past the SLO, goodput can
. When we model batching in lesson 2, goodput is the number to watch.

children.question: Service A completes 100 requests per minute with 30 meeting the SLO. Service B completes 60 per minute with 55 meeting it. Which has the higher goodput?
options: A, because it completes more requests
B: 55 requests per minute meet the SLO, against A's 30

children.children: Goodput only counts requests that met the objective, so B wins despite its lower throughput. (The 100 and 30 echo the book's example.)

children: request twice and you get two different times. Send it 200 times and you get a distribution: what happens to the processor and memory at that moment shifts each result a little, and occasionally a lot.

children.question: We sent the same request (256-token prompt) to GPT-2 on the laptop CPU 200 times in a row. Most first tokens came in around 61 ms. What did the slowest one take?
options: About 62 ms: identical requests take identical time
About 176 ms, nearly three times the median

children.children: 176.2 ms. Four of the 200 runs took over 100 ms. Nothing about the request changed; the machine did. Every real service has a tail like this, usually a longer one.

children.children: pN is the value N% of measurements fall at or below: p50 is the median, p99 is beaten by all but the slowest 1%. Used for latency because the mean hides the tail.

children: (the median) is the time half the requests beat: 61.3 ms.
is 112.8 ms: one request in a hundred was slower than that. Now switch to the
: the same request is tight, from 26.0 to 28.3 ms. A different processor, a different shape.
The mean, 65.0 ms here, sits above the median: a few slow runs drag it up, yet it tells you nothing about how slow they were.

(Ch. 9) gives a starker example: nine requests near 100 ms and one at 3 seconds average out to almost 400 ms, a number that matches no request at all. The book recommends watching percentiles, typically p50, p90, p95 and p99, and looking into the outliers, since they are often symptoms of something wrong.

children.children: The tail matters more than its size suggests. A page that makes several model calls is as slow as its slowest call, and a user who sends 100 messages a day will hit the p99 about once a day.

children.question: A dashboard shows mean TTFT steady at 300 ms all week, while support tickets about 'the bot freezing' double. What should you look at?
options: The p99 (and p95) TTFT: a growing tail can leave the mean almost unchanged

children.children: A small number of very slow requests can grow while the mean barely moves. Percentiles show the tail directly.

children.question: In our CPU stream, the median gap between tokens was 8.6 ms. Were all 63 gaps close to 8.6 ms?
options: Yes, every gap was exactly 8.6 ms
Mostly, but the slowest gap was 11.5 ms, a third longer
No, the gaps doubled as the reply got longer

children.children: Gaps ranged from 8.2 to 11.5 ms. Each step attends over one more token, which costs a little more, and the laptop is doing other things too. An average hides that; keeping every timestamp doesn't.
Three traps make timings wrong without any error message:

children.children: Untimed runs before a benchmark starts timing, so one-off costs such as loading and kernel compilation don't land in the results.

children: The first call is slow: weights load into caches, and GPU code gets compiled the first time it runs. We ran three warm-up requests before timing anything.
the GPU has finished. Stop the clock then, and you time the request to start work, not the work. Our script reads each token back to the CPU before taking the timestamp, which forces the wait.
Timing inside the server leaves out the network and the queue. Timing in the client includes them, which is what users feel. Say which one you measured.

children.children: Our numbers in this lesson are all from one laptop (Apple M5), GPT-2 small, one request at a time, with nothing in between. A hosted model adds network and queueing on top.

children.question: You time a GPU request by reading the clock right after calling the model, without waiting for any output. The result is 0.3 ms per token. What happened?
options: The clock stopped when the work was queued, not when it finished; GPU calls return before the GPU is done
The KV cache made it free

children.children: GPU work is asynchronous. Wait for a result (or synchronise the device) before stopping the clock; otherwise you are measuring how fast work gets queued.

children.question: On the laptop's CPU, a 16-token prompt got its first token in 12.8 ms. The GPU did it in 8.0 ms. For a 960-token prompt, the CPU took 223.3 ms. What did the GPU take?

About 220 ms: no difference on long prompts
About 8 ms: the GPU's time doesn't grow

children.children: 96.1 ms, 2.3 times faster than the CPU, against only 1.6 times at 16 tokens. A long prefill is a big batch of parallel work, which is what a GPU is built for. A 16-token prompt doesn't give it enough to do.

children.question: On the CPU, decoding one request ran at 125 tokens/s. We then decoded 16 requests at once (a batch of 16). What happened?
options: 16 × 125 = 2,000 tokens/s in total, each user still at 125
About 860 tokens/s in total, but each user dropped to about 54
Still 125 tokens/s in total, shared by 16 users

children.children: 863 tokens/s in total, about 7 times more work done, but each step took 18.5 ms instead of 8.0, so each user's reply came out at 54 tokens/s instead of 125. More for everyone together, less for each one.

children: On the GPU, the same move takes total throughput from 179 to 1,349 tokens/s while each user drops from 179 to 84. Both devices show the same trade-off:

children: ). This lesson is about measuring that properly: what to time, how to summarise many requests, and which numbers a product should actually promise.
Start with the user. They don't feel "the model's speed". They feel two waits: how long until
appears, and how long until the answer is complete.

children.question: We streamed one reply from GPT-2 on a laptop CPU: 64 output tokens after a 256-token prompt. The last token arrived at 633 ms. Roughly when did the first one arrive?

children.children: 67.5 ms. Prefill took the first ~60 ms, then 63 more tokens followed about 8.6 ms apart. With streaming the user sees text after 67.5 ms. Without it, they would stare at nothing for 633 ms, nine times longer, and then get everything at once.

children: and watch the ticks arrive at their measured times (10× slower, so you can see them). Then switch to
: the same reply on the same laptop's GPU starts at 26 ms and finishes at 382 ms.

(Ch. 9, "Inference Performance Metrics") points out that two systems with the same total latency can feel very different: one starts instantly and trickles, the other pauses and then flies. Which one users prefer is a product question, worth testing with real users.

The same section gives a useful ceiling for the trickle: a very fast reader gets through roughly one token every 120 ms. Our CPU produced one every 8.6 ms, about 14 times faster than anyone can read. Once streaming, extra decode speed stops mattering
. It still matters for total latency, for answers nobody reads live (JSON for another program, say), and for cost.

children.question: A support bot streams its answers. Users say it 'feels slow', yet its tokens stream far faster than anyone reads. What is the most likely culprit?
options: Time to first token: a long pause before any text appears

children.children: If tokens already arrive faster than reading speed, speeding them up changes little. The visible wait is the pause before the first token: a long prompt (big system prompt, pasted history) or queueing on the server.

children: . If its time is set by bytes read, fewer bytes per weight should make it faster. We can estimate how much from lesson 2's measured FP32 steps. We did
measure it: we ran no FP16, INT8 or INT4 model.

children.question: Lesson 2 measured a 9.1 ms CPU decode step reading 507.2 MB (497.8 MB of FP32 weights plus a 9.4 MB KV cache). If time scaled with bytes, what would INT4 weights give?

children.children: INT4 weights take 62.2 MB; with the same 9.4 MB cache the step reads 71.7 MB, so 9.1 ms × 71.7 ÷ 507.2 ≈ 1.3 ms. Not 8 times faster, because the cache didn't shrink: it is now 13% of the bytes. Even at INT4 the step does about 3.5 operations per byte, still left of both ridges (16 and 27).
This is an estimate under one assumption, the same bytes per second as in FP32, not a forecast. Real results can land either side:

options: It grows about 20 times, because the one big value sets the step for everyone
Only the big value has an error

children.children: The step grows from 0.00271 to 0.0542. The largest error on the 12 real weights goes from 0.00126 to 0.027, the mean error is 29 times larger, and two weights become 0. children.question: Why do quantization schemes often keep a separate scale for each small block of weights?
options: So one large value only coarsens its own block, not the whole tensor

children.children: The scale is set by the group's largest value. Smaller groups keep a rare large value from widening the step for everything else, at the cost of storing more scales.

children.question: Llama 2 13B on an 80 GB accelerator, 2,048 tokens per conversation, KV cache in 16-bit. With FP16 weights, 32 conversations fit. With INT4 weights?
options: About 128: four times smaller weights, four times the conversations

children.children: The weights drop from 26 GB to 6.5 GB, which frees 19.5 GB. Each conversation's cache is 1.68 GB, so that buys 11 more conversations. FP32 weights would fit only 16.

Weights four times smaller did not give four times the conversations, because at this length the cache takes most of the memory. Try shorter conversations in the calculator and the weights matter more; try GPT-2 and they barely matter at all. The cache is the next thing to shrink: lesson 2 noted its size is linear in bytes per number.

children: Where weight format matters most is getting a model to fit at all.

(Ch. 7, "Model I/O: Loading Quantized Models with LangChain") uses an 8-bit version of Phi-3 instead of the 16-bit one, cutting memory almost in half. Its rule of thumb: look for at least 4-bit models; at 3 or 2 bits the loss becomes noticeable, and a smaller model at higher precision is the better choice.

children.question: Your 80 GB server holds 32 conversations of 2,048 tokens with FP16 weights. You quantize the weights to INT8 and nothing else. Roughly how many fit now?

children.children: The weights shrink from 26 GB to 13 GB; 13 GB more room at 1.68 GB per conversation is 7 more, so 39. The cache is unchanged.

children.children: A 16-bit float with 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 fraction bits. It has the same range as FP32 but less precision than FP16.

children: both use 16 bits but split them differently, and that decides what they get wrong.
: 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, 10 fraction bits (NVIDIA's mixed-precision guide). Its largest number is 65,504.
: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 7 fraction bits (Google Cloud blog). It keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits, so its range matches FP32's: the largest number is about 3.39 × 10³⁸.
More exponent bits buy range; more fraction bits buy precision.
(Ch. 7, "Numerical Representations") shows the trade with one table of values converted from FP32.

children.question: Convert 1234.56789 from FP32 to FP16 and to BF16. Which lands closer?
options: They land on the same number

children.children: FP16 gives 1235, a 0.035% change; BF16 gives 1232, a 0.208% change. Now try 123,456.789: FP16 can't reach it and returns infinity, while BF16 gives 123,392.

The book's warning (same section): load a model in the format it was meant for. Llama 2 shipped its weights in BF16; many teams loaded it in FP16 and found its quality much worse than advertised. Which format suits a workload depends, the book says, on the range of values it needs, how sensitive it is to small changes, and the hardware.

children.question: FP16 keeps more fraction bits than BF16. What does it give up for them?
options: Nothing: it is better in every way

children.children: FP16 spends 5 bits on the exponent where BF16 spends 8. That buys finer steps between nearby numbers but a far smaller largest number.

children.children: Storing a model's numbers in a format with fewer bits, such as FP16, INT8 or INT4, to cut memory and the bytes each step reads. Strictly it means converting to integers, but in practice it covers any precision reduction.

children: for a group of numbers, and one small integer per number. Multiply the integer by the scale and you get the number back, nearly.
The LLM.int8() paper (Dettmers et al., 2022, §2) calls
the most commonly used technique: divide by the largest magnitude in the group, multiply by 127, and round to the nearest integer. The largest value maps to ±127 and everything else lands in between.

children.question: After absmax quantization to INT8 and back, what is the most any value can be off by?
options: Half of one step, where a step is the largest magnitude ÷ 127

children.children: Rounding moves a number to the nearest integer, at most half a step away, and the step is the scale. The error is the same size for big values and small ones, so small values lose the most relative to their size.
With these 12 real GPT-2 weights the step is 0.00271, so no value moves more than 0.00135.

children: INT4 has 16 integers instead of 256. Applying the same rule with −7 to 7 (our extension of the 8-bit rule, for illustration) makes the step 0.344 ÷ 7 = 0.0491, eighteen times coarser. Real 4-bit schemes are cleverer:

children.children: Activations are harder partly because of outliers. LLM.int8() (§1) found hidden-state features up to 20 times larger than the rest; at around 6.7 billion parameters they appear in every layer. children.question: In a chat app, some replies are 8 tokens and some are 256. What does continuous batching fix compared with static batching?
options: It reduces the memory each conversation needs
Short replies no longer wait for the longest reply in their batch, and freed seats are refilled at once
It makes each decode step faster
It removes the need for a KV cache

children.children: Scheduling every step instead of every batch keeps the batch full and returns each reply when it is done. The step itself costs the same.
The next page puts numbers on this.

children.question: Llama 2 13B in 16-bit numbers on an 80 GB accelerator, each conversation 2,048 tokens. About how many conversations fit?

children: The weights take about 26 GB (13 billion × 2 bytes). Each conversation's cache is 2 × 40 layers × 5,120 × 2,048 tokens × 2 bytes = 1.68 GB, so the remaining 54 GB holds 32. That matches
's example (Ch. 9, "Calculating the KV Cache Size"): a batch of 32 at 2,048 tokens needs about 54 GB of cache.

children.children: Try halving the tokens per conversation in the estimator: about twice as many conversations fit. Switching to 4-byte numbers costs more than half of them, because the weights double as well as the cache. Real servers fit fewer than this estimate, because activations, the framework itself and fragmentation all take memory.

children.children: Measuring decode and prefill on a roofline

To judge a measurement, you need the ceiling it is up against. We measured two on each device: a large memory copy (the most bytes per second it reached) and a large matrix multiply (the most operations per second). Apple publishes 153 GB/s of memory bandwidth for the M5; our best copy reached 122.3 GB/s on the CPU and 129.6 GB/s on the GPU.

children: At batch 1, a step took 9.1 ms on the CPU: 507 MB in 9.1 ms is 55.7 GB/s, 46% of the measured copy ceiling. The GPU did 6.3 ms, 80.5 GB/s, 62%. Both sit at about 0.5 operations per byte, far left of either ridge. We did not break down where the rest of the time goes.

children.children: The share of a resource's capacity actually in use. A rented machine that sits idle still bills by the hour, so low utilization raises the cost per request.

children: ): parameters × bytes per parameter × tokens/s, over the peak bandwidth. Its example: a 7B model in 16-bit at 100 tokens/s uses 700 GB/s, 70% of an A100-80GB's 2 TB/s. The formula assumes one sequence; with a batch, the weights are read once for all of them.

children.question: Decode at batch 1 uses about half the measured bandwidth and a tiny fraction of the compute. Which upgrade would most likely speed it up?
options: A chip with twice the FLOP/s and the same memory
Memory with more bandwidth, or fewer bytes per weight

children.children: Decode sits on the bandwidth slope, so moving bytes faster, or moving fewer of them, is what helps. Fewer bytes per weight is quantization: lesson 3.

children.children: Three learned projections of each token's vector. A query is compared with every key to get attention weights; the weights then mix the values.

children: projections, so each can learn to look for something different.
describes this as letting the model attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. In GPT-2 small, the 768-number vector is split across

; every head runs the scaled dot-product calculation on its own slice, the 12 outputs are joined back into 768 numbers, and one more learned matrix (the output projection) mixes them. GPT-2 small has 12 layers, each with its own 12 heads: 144 heads in all.

children.question: In real GPT-2 small, what do you expect most of its 144 heads to do?
options: Each head finds the most meaningful related word, like a pronoun's noun
All heads produce nearly the same weights
Many heads follow simple, almost mechanical rules: the previous token, the first token, the token itself

children.children: Simple rules are common, and a few heads follow them almost perfectly. Look at the measured weights below before reading on: three of the clearest heads are in the list underneath the explorer.

children.children: Turns a list of scores into probabilities: exponentiate each score, then divide by the total so they sum to 1.

children: must give out a total weight of 1, and heads with nothing useful to collect for a token seem to park it on the first position. GPT-2 does not add a special start token here, so the first token is just the first word of each sentence.

children.question: Head 4.11 puts about 1.0 on the previous token for every token. What does that head contribute?
options: Each token's output carries the value vector of the token before it, so later layers can use pairs like “river” + “bank” together
Nothing: a head this simple must be useless
It decides the next token on its own

children.children: A previous-token head moves information one step to the right. Later heads can then combine "what I am" with "what came just before me", which simple rules like the repeated-name pattern on the next page rely on.

Why split key from value? Matching and content are different jobs. A token can be easy to find for one reason (it is the subject of the sentence) and pass along something else (what kind of thing it is).
uses a book picture: the key is like a page number, the value like the page's content.

It climbs: same direction gives the largest dot product
River's own output changes, but bank's weights do not

children.children: The score is the dot product of bank's query with each key, and for vectors of fixed length the dot product is largest when they point the same way. A bigger score becomes a bigger weight after softmax.

children.question: Take a token's scores and multiply all of them by 3 before the softmax. What happens to its weights?
options: Nothing: softmax only cares about which score is largest
They get flatter: closer to equal
They get sharper: the top token takes an even larger share

children.children: Softmax exponentiates, so stretching the gaps between scores stretches the gaps between weights much more. Large scores push softmax toward "all weight on one token". That is exactly why the formula divides by √d (next section). Check it in the lab with the query length slider.

children: products. With more dimensions, the sums tend to get larger in size, and softmax over large scores puts nearly all weight on one token. The paper's authors note that this pushes softmax into a region where training gets extremely small gradients, so they scale the scores by 1/√d to keep them in a workable range.

up toward 4. The scores grow, and the weights pile onto one token. Slide it to 0: every score becomes 0 and the weights become equal thirds. A longer query does the same thing as skipping the √d scaling: it sharpens the softmax.

children.question: GPT-2 reads “The ladder did not reach the window because it was too short.” and then “…because it was too high.” The sentences differ only in the second-to-last word. How much do the attention weights of the token “ it” differ between the two runs?
options: Not at all: “ it” cannot see words that come after it
A lot: “short” and “high” point to different nouns
A little: the last word nudges every token

children.children: Not at all. We ran both sentences through GPT-2 small (transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1): in every one of the 12 layers and 12 heads, every attention row up to and including " it" was identical, a maximum difference of 0.0. The rows for " short"/" high" and the final "." did change, by up to 0.41.

contrasts this quadratic scaling with Mamba, a newer architecture whose authors report that its inference computation scales linearly.

children.question: In each of GPT-2 small's blocks, which part has more parameters: the attention (query, key, value and output projections) or the MLP?
options: The MLP: roughly twice as many
Attention, by far: it is the famous part
Neither has parameters; only the embedding table does

children: The MLP. Counting GPT-2 small's first block with transformers 5.20.2: attention has 2,362,368 parameters, the MLP 4,722,432.

describes the feed-forward layers as housing most of the model's processing capacity, and as the likely home of much of what it memorizes. Attention moves information between tokens; the MLP does most of the per-token transforming.

children.children: The learned matrix with one row per vocabulary entry. Embedding a token ID means reading its row.

children: (which GPT-2 reuses to turn each final vector into next-token scores) and the 1,024 × 768 position table. Position is how the model knows word order: attention scores come only from vector contents, so each token's input vector is its token row plus a learned row for its position. Without it, the same word at position 2 and position 9 would enter the first block as the same vector. Large modern models keep this same block structure with tweaks, and simply have more and wider blocks.

children.question: What does the residual connection around attention do?
options: It skips attention entirely for unimportant tokens
It normalizes the vector to length 1
It adds attention's output to the token's incoming vector, so each block refines the running representation instead of replacing it

children.children: Output = input + attention(norm(input)). If a block has nothing useful to add, it can contribute little and the vector passes through mostly unchanged.

children.question: In “Maria called her brother, and then Maria called her mother.”, GPT-2 reaches the second “ her”. A head that has learned “find where this happened before and look at what came next” would attend most to which token?
options: The second “ called”, just before it
“ brother”, the token that followed the first “ her”

children: " brother": the token that followed the earlier copy of " her". This is the pattern behind

(Olsson et al., 2022): having seen A then B, when A appears again, look at B. It helps a model continue patterns it has seen earlier in the same text. In GPT-2, head 10.7 puts 0.869 on " brother" here. Check it below.

children.children: Attention weights show where a head reads from. They do not show what the value vectors carry, what the MLP layers do with it, or how 144 heads combine. A high weight is a clue to check, not proof that the model "understood" a relation. Studying what models actually compute is the field of interpretability.

children.question: A head gives 0.8 of a pronoun's weight to the right noun in one sentence. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: It is a lead worth testing: check many sentences, including ones where the right noun is in a different position or the head's other tokens look at the same word
Nothing at all: attention weights are random

children.children: One sentence cannot rule out simpler rules such as "attend to the subject" or "attend to position 2". Head 4.3 above is exactly that case.

children.children: GPT-2 small's config gives 12 layers and 12 heads, and a model dimension of 768, so 64 numbers per head. The cache we measured had exactly that shape: 12 layers, each holding keys and values shaped (batch, 12 heads, tokens, 64), stored as 32-bit floats (4 bytes).

children.question: GPT-2 small, a full 1,024-token context, 32-bit floats, one sequence. How big is the KV cache?
options: Exactly the size of the model

children.children: 2 × 12 × 12 × 64 × 1,024 × 4 bytes = 75,497,472 bytes, 72.0 MiB. That is 72 KiB per token. In 16-bit floats (2 bytes) it halves to 36.0 MiB. For comparison, GPT-2 small's roughly 124 million parameters take nearly half a gigabyte in 32-bit floats, so one sequence's cache is modest next to the weights.

Try this: in the memory panel, set tokens to 1,024 and fp32: 72.0 MiB. Switch to fp16: 36.0 MiB. Now raise the batch to 64 sequences at fp32: 4.50 GiB, nearly ten times the weights. Halve the tokens to 512 and the size halves too. Every factor in the formula multiplies the total.

children: The same arithmetic applies to every transformer, with bigger numbers.

works it through for Llama 2 13B (40 layers, model dimension 5,120): a batch of 32 sequences of 2,048 tokens in 16-bit numbers needs about 54 GB of KV cache before any optimisation. It also cites a Google paper (Pope et al., 2022) estimating 3 TB of cache for a 500B+ model at batch 512 and 2,048 tokens, three times that model's weights. Cache memory, not weights, can become the limit on how long a context or how many users a server can handle.
That is why so much engineering targets the cache: attending only to a local window of recent tokens, sharing keys and values across heads, and storing the cache in fewer bits (
, Ch. 9, "Attention mechanism optimization"). Each changes one factor in the formula.

children.question: You double the context length and switch the cache from 32-bit to 16-bit numbers. What happens to the KV cache size?
options: It stays about the same: ×2 for tokens, ÷2 for bytes

children.children: Size is linear in tokens and in bytes per number, so the two changes cancel. Unlike the n² attention score grid from lesson 3, the cache grows only linearly with context.

children.question: On our test machine (GPT-2 small, CPU), a 16-token prompt takes 15.3 ms to prefill. A 960-token prompt is 60 times longer. Roughly how long does its prefill take?
options: About 15 ms: one pass is one pass
About 220 ms: much more, but far less than 60 times

children.children: 219.6 ms: 60 times the tokens for about 14 times the time. Spread over 960 tokens that is about 0.23 ms per prompt token, while a single decode step on the same machine takes 8 to 10 ms. Processing tokens together is far cheaper per token than one at a time.

The four prompt lengths we measured took 15.3, 26.3, 61.4 and 219.6 ms to prefill, while a single decode step stayed between 8.0 and 9.6 ms (gpt2, transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1, CPU Apple M5, 4 threads, median of 7 runs). Your machine will give different numbers; the ratios are what to compare. You will see these as bars two pages from now, once the decode side has been explained.

On our machine, a 960-token prompt with 32 new tokens is about 220 ms before anything appears, then about 32 × 9.6 ≈ 310 ms of streaming. The book also notes that prefill tends to be limited by raw compute and decode by how fast weights can be moved through memory, which is why some production systems run the two phases on separate machines (Ch. 9, "Computational bottlenecks"). Our CPU numbers do not test that claim.

children.children: A long input means a long prefill, which shows up as a slow first token. Once decoding starts, each step costs about the same.

children: will happily produce more than 1,024 tokens. It prints a warning ("Running this sequence through the model will result in indexing errors") and leaves the length alone. Cutting is your job, or your framework's:

children: 1,024 tokens and drops the rest (its default truncation side is the right). The end of a long document, often where the question is, disappears.

children.children: Chat apps often cut the other way: they drop the oldest turns to keep the newest. Whichever end goes, the model simply never sees it.
What a hosted API does with an over-long request depends on the provider, so check its documentation. Either way, count tokens before you send.
Try this: paste a few paragraphs of an article into the lab and read GPT-2's count. Then work out how many pastes fit in 1,024 tokens, remembering the answer has to fit in the same window.

children.question: A prompt is 1,000 GPT-2 tokens and you ask for 100 new tokens. What goes wrong?

The model compresses the prompt automatically
The prompt plus the generated tokens need 1,100 positions, more than the 1,024 the model has, so something has to be cut or generation must stop early

children.children: Every generated token takes a position too. Prompt plus output must fit in the window, so leave room for the answer.

children.children: In GPT-style models, the rule that a token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens, never later ones.

children.question: Same model, same machine. Request A: 960-token prompt, 10 output tokens. Request B: 16-token prompt, 200 output tokens. Using our measured numbers, which finishes first?

children.children: A: about 220 ms of prefill plus 10 steps of about 10 ms, roughly 0.3 seconds. B: about 15 ms of prefill plus 200 steps of about 8 ms, roughly 1.6 to 1.7 seconds. children.question: On our test machine, a decode step with the KV cache takes 9.6 ms after a 960-token prompt. Without the cache, the model re-runs the whole sequence every step. Roughly how long does each step take then?

children.children: 228.8 ms per token, close to the 219.6 ms prefill of the same prompt. Without the cache, every new token pays for a fresh pass over almost 1,000 tokens. That is about 24 times slower per token.

Try this: read the "cache saves" label above each group. With a 16-token prompt, a step without the cache takes 20.8 ms against 8.0 ms with it, about 2.6 times as long. At 64 tokens it is about 3.8 times; at 256, about 8.2 times; at 960, about 23.8 times. The "cache on" bars stay between 8.0 and 9.6 ms across all four prompts; the "cache off" bars grow with the prompt. The longer the context, the more the cache matters.

children: The exact times belong to our machine (gpt2, transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1, CPU, Apple M5, 4 threads, median of 7); the trend is the lesson.

The overdraft sentence: shared words dominate
They tie: the model cannot tell

children.children: The stream sentence, by a wide margin: 0.465 against 0.210. The model places "riverside" sentences together even when they share no words, and keeps the money sense of "bank" well away. Check it yourself below.

children.children: "We fished from the muddy bank of the river."

children: As predicted, meaning beats the shared word. But look closer: the money-bank sentences score 0.20 to 0.22 against the river-bank ones, while "edge of the stream" scores only 0.14 to 0.16 against them. Shared surface words still leak a little similarity.

children.question: Vectors A and B point 50° apart. You double B's length without changing its direction. Which numbers change?
options: Dot product and Euclidean distance; cosine stays the same

children.children: The dot product doubles, because it scales with each vector's length. The Euclidean distance changes, because B's tip moves. Cosine does not move at all: it divides the length back out and only sees the angle. Check it in the lab below.
The numbers here are illustrative 2-D math, not output from a model. Try these in order:

children: with its length slider. Watch which of the three numbers stay put.
until it is perpendicular to A (the angle readout shows 90°). Dot product and cosine both hit zero, whatever the lengths. Keep rotating until B points the opposite way: cosine reaches −1.

children.children: Give A and B the same direction

children: but different lengths. Cosine says "identical" (1.000) while Euclidean distance says "far apart". Which answer you want depends on whether length means anything in your data.
and repeat steps 1 to 3. Now the length sliders are disabled, the dot product equals the cosine, and the Euclidean distance depends only on the angle.

Switch databases: dot product and cosine rank results differently
Multiply every dot product by the vector dimension
Nothing: dot product and cosine are always identical

children: On unit vectors the dot product

the cosine similarity, so normalizing both sides makes the two interchangeable. Without normalization a long document vector could outrank a closer but shorter one. Many embedding models already return unit vectors, but check rather than assume.

children.children:
vocabulary size:          30,522
embedding dimension:      384
token embedding table:    30,522 × 384 = 11,720,448 numbers
token ID of "bank":       2924

Every one of those 11.7 million numbers is a trained parameter. Before training, the table holds random values like the rest of the model's weights; training nudges each row until the vectors are useful for the task the model is trained on. A pretrained model ships with its table, which is why a model is tied to the tokenizer it was trained with: swap the tokenizer and the IDs point at the wrong rows.

children.question: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 has 22,713,216 parameters in total. Roughly what share of them is the 30,522 × 384 token embedding table?
options: About 1%: the table is just a lookup, the real work is elsewhere

children.children: About half: 11,720,448 of 22,713,216 is roughly 52% (counted with sentence-transformers 6.1.0). This is a deliberately small model with only six transformer layers, so the vocabulary table dominates. In large generative models the transformer layers are far bigger and the table is a much smaller share, but it still grows with every vocabulary entry. That is the "bigger vocabulary means a bigger embedding table" cost from the tokenization lesson, made concrete.

children.className: my-6 rounded-md border-l-4 px-4 py-3 text-sm border-info bg-info-soft

children.question: Take MiniLM's static embedding row for the token “bank” in “I opened a savings account at the bank.” and in “We fished from the muddy bank of the river.” What is the cosine similarity between the two rows?
options: Exactly 1: it is the same row
About 0.6: the model notices the different senses
It depends on the sentence length

children.children: Exactly 1. A static embedding is a table lookup: token ID 2924 reads row 2924, whatever sentence it came from. The lookup cannot tell a river bank from a savings bank. Telling them apart is the job of the transformer layers that run after the lookup.

children.children: From many token vectors to one text vector

children: A transformer produces one vector per token. Search and clustering need one vector per text, so a text embedding model adds a
step. The common choice, and MiniLM's, is
: average the token output vectors (ignoring padding), then normalize the result to length 1. Another option is to use the output at a special first token such as

children.className: rounded bg-surface-2 px-1 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

children: notes that averaging a plain BERT model's outputs, or taking its

children.className: rounded bg-surface-2 px-1 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

children: output, gave sentence vectors worse than simply averaging GloVe word vectors; good text embedding models are trained for the job, contrastively, as on the previous page. That was the motivation for Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019): comparing every pair of 10,000 sentences by feeding both into BERT together takes about 50 million model runs (around 65 hours, per the paper), while embedding each sentence once and comparing vectors with

children.question: Your search system embeds documents once and stores the vectors. Why is that only possible with text embeddings, and not by feeding the query and each document into a model together?
options: A joint model only produces a score for a specific pair, so it would have to run once per (query, document) pair at query time; separate embeddings are computed once and compared with cheap vector math
It is possible either way; storage is the only difference
Joint models cannot handle long documents
Text embeddings are more accurate than any joint model

children.children: A model that reads both texts together (a cross-encoder) outputs a similarity score, not a reusable vector, so nothing can be precomputed. Embedding each text independently lets you index documents ahead of time and compare a new query against all of them with dot products. Joint models are still useful later, for re-ranking a short list, which Module 05 covers.

children: Documents are embedded once and stored. Each query is embedded at search time with the same model and compared with cheap vector math. Change the model and every stored vector must be re-embedded.

children.children: Storage example is arithmetic, not a measurement: 1,000,000 vectors × 384 dims × 4 bytes (float32) ≈ 1.5 GB.
Fourteen help-centre articles, six real-sounding queries. Keyword search scores shared words; semantic search compares embeddings.

children.question: For the query “how do I stop paying every month”, which method puts the “Cancel your subscription” article first?

children.children: Semantic search only. The query shares no meaningful word with the cancel article, so keyword search falls back on the one word it can match, “every”, and ranks the Wi-Fi article first. The embedding of “stop paying every month” lands near “cancel your plan” anyway.

2. Changing the embedding model means re-embedding everything.

children: Upgrading the model, or even changing how you preprocess text before embedding, invalidates every stored vector. Budget for it:

points out that generating embeddings costs money, especially when data changes often, and that vector storage and search can be expensive too: a company's vector database bill can reach one-fifth or even half of what it spends on model APIs.

Bigger vectors can hold more distinctions, but every stored vector costs memory and every comparison costs time in proportion to its length. Simple arithmetic, assuming 4-byte floats and no compression: one million documents take about 1.5 GB at 384 dimensions (MiniLM) and about 12.3 GB at 3,072 (the size
lists for OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large). Pick the model by measured retrieval quality on your own data first, then weigh its size.

options: It works: same dimension means compatible vectors
Results are effectively random and nothing errors, because the two models' spaces are unrelated; you must re-embed the documents
Scores are slightly lower but rankings are preserved
The vector database rejects the queries

children.children: Matching dimensions only means the dot product can be computed, not that it means anything. Each model arranges its own space during training. Re-embed the whole collection with the new model, and re-check any similarity thresholds while you are at it.

children.children:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# 1. The embedding table: one row per vocabulary entry
table = model[0].auto_model.embeddings.word_embeddings.weight
print("table shape:", tuple(table.shape))

# 2. Sentence embeddings: unit length, so dot product = cosine
texts = [
    "How do I reset my password?",
    "I forgot my login credentials.",
    "How do I not reset my password?",
    "What time does the museum open?",
]
emb = model.encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True)
print("dimensions:", emb.shape[1])
for t, score in zip(texts[1:], emb[1:] @ emb[0]):
    print(f"{score:.3f}  {t}")

# 3. Truncation: text past the limit is never read
print("max_seq_length:", model.max_seq_length)
long = " ".join(["filler"] * 400)
a, b = model.encode([long, long + " The last sentence is about penguins."])
print(f"cosine(long, long + extra): {a @ b:.3f}")

children: A vector is just a list of numbers

The first 24 of the 384 numbers that represent “bank”. No single coordinate means “money” or “river”: meaning is spread across all of them, and only comparisons between whole vectors are interpretable.

children.children: Row 2924 of all-MiniLM-L6-v2's word-embedding table, rounded to 3 decimals (sentence-transformers 6.1.0).

children: Staring at them tells you nothing, and that is the point. Training never assigned a meaning to coordinate 3 or coordinate 200. What training shapes is the
: which points end up close to which. All the useful information lives in relationships between vectors, not in any single number.

children.children: That gives the whole lesson its working rule:
Similar meaning should mean nearby vectors.

children.question: A teammate finds that coordinate 17 of an embedding model's vectors is large for a few finance sentences and wants to filter documents by it as a “finance flag”. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: each coordinate encodes one topic
It would work, but only after normalizing the vectors
It would work, but only for models with fewer than 100 dimensions
Coordinates have no assigned meaning; information is spread across many of them and only relationships between whole vectors are designed to be meaningful

children.children: Training optimizes which vectors are near which, not what any single axis means. A large value in coordinate 17 for a handful of examples is a coincidence of this model's arrangement, not a feature you can rely on. Compare whole vectors instead (next page).

in the eyes of the model. That is not the same as meaning the same thing, and it is nothing like being true.

options: The Wi-Fi paraphrases: they mean the same thing
The medicine pair: it shares almost every word and topic

children: The medicine pair, and it is not close:

, against 0.645 for the best paraphrase pair in the set. One word flips the meaning, yet the two sentences share their topic, structure and almost every token, which is what this model mostly measures. Open the explorer on the previous page and pick "This medicine is safe for children." to see it.

children: High similarity is not the same meaning
Sentences that share words and topic score higher than real paraphrases, even when they say opposite things. Similarity measures topic and wording, not truth.
The other pair in that group is worse. "The Earth orbits the Sun." and "The Sun orbits the Earth." score

, the highest of any two different sentences in the set. Swapping subject and object reverses a fact, and the vectors barely move. (Measured with sentence-transformers 6.1.0, from the explorer's data.)

children.children: The failure modes to design around

children: A retrieval system built on embeddings will happily return a document that contradicts the query, or a false claim worded like a true one. Similarity finds candidates; something else has to judge them.

children.children: Negation and word order are weak signals.

children: "Safe" and "not safe" land almost on top of each other. If your application depends on that difference (medical, legal, policy), test it explicitly.

In this one small set, a reversed fact (0.982) beats every genuine paraphrase (0.444 to 0.645). There is no universal "0.8 means similar"; thresholds are specific to a model and to your data, and have to be chosen by measuring.

children.question: A support bot retrieves the help article most similar to the user's question, and you plan to answer “we don't have an article on that” when the top score is below 0.5. What is the problem with that plan?
options: Nothing: 0.5 is the standard cut-off for cosine similarity
The threshold is specific to the model and the data; you need to pick it by measuring scores on real relevant and irrelevant questions, and check it again whenever the model changes
Cosine scores are always above 0.5, so it never triggers
Thresholds only work with Euclidean distance

children.children: Cosine values have no fixed meaning across models. With MiniLM, paraphrases in this lesson scored as low as 0.444 while a contradicting sentence scored 0.936. Choose a threshold from labelled examples of your own traffic, and re-check it after any model change.

children: by hand. So how do vectors for "loan" and "mortgage" end up near each other?
The answer is an old idea from linguistics, the

: words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. Jurafsky and Martin trace it to linguists of the 1950s such as Joos, Harris and Firth. You rarely see "mortgage" next to "paddle", but you often see it near "rate", "bank", "approve" and "monthly", and so does "loan". If a training objective rewards vectors for predicting their contexts, words with similar contexts are pushed toward similar vectors.
word2vec (Mikolov and colleagues, 2013) turned this into a cheap training recipe. The version described in

children.question: Why does word2vec need the random “not neighbours” pairs? What happens if you train only on true neighbour pairs?
options: Training becomes slower but the vectors are the same
Nothing: negative pairs are an optional speed trick
The model can score every pair as “neighbours” and be right every time, so the vectors learn nothing useful

children: With only positive examples, the trivial answer "always yes" is perfect, so there is no pressure to separate related words from unrelated ones. The contrast between real neighbours and random pairs is what forces the geometry. Pushing similar things together

children: models are trained contrastively too, on pairs of texts instead of pairs of words: a question and its answer, a title and its article, two paraphrases. The MiniLM model in this lesson was fine-tuned with a contrastive objective on more than a billion sentence pairs, according to its model card. Its idea of "similar" is whatever those pairs taught it, a point worth remembering when it surprises you later in this lesson.

children.children: No machine learning background is needed. You should be happy with multiplying and adding numbers, and with the idea of a function: numbers in, a number out.

children: Every model in this course, from this lesson's tiny network to a large language model, is a function. Numbers go in, numbers come out, and what happens in between is set by a list of adjustable numbers called
. Training is the search for parameter values that make the function do what you want.
Hands-On Large Language Models describes neural networks as interconnected layers of nodes, where each connection has a weight; those weights are the model's parameters. The building block is one
: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with one extra number called the
, and passes the total through an

children.children: Stack neurons into layers and you have a network. Each neuron in a layer takes every output of the layer before, so the parameters add up quickly.

children.question: A network has 2 inputs, one hidden layer of 4 neurons, and 1 output neuron. Every neuron has one weight per input it receives, plus a bias. How many parameters does it have?

children.children: The hidden layer has 2 × 4 = 8 weights and 4 biases; the output neuron has 4 weights and 1 bias. That's 12 weights and 5 biases. This is the XOR network later in this lesson; the "big" network in the overfitting topic has 217.

The activation function matters more than it looks. Without it, a neuron is a weighted sum, and a weighted sum of weighted sums is still just a weighted sum: however many layers you stack, the network can only draw straight lines. The bend is what lets layers build curves, which you'll see happen in the XOR lab.

children.children: Backpropagation: a gradient for every weight

children: Gradient descent needs a gradient for every parameter, on every step.
is how a network gets them all at once, and AI Engineering splits each training step into two phases.
: compute the output from the input, layer by layer.

: compare the output with the expected one (the loss), then work out how much each parameter contributed to the mistake. That contribution is the parameter's gradient, the derivative of the loss with respect to it, and there is one per parameter. A parameter with a large gradient contributed a lot and gets adjusted more.

children.children: The backward pass works from the output towards the inputs. The output neuron's error is known directly; each earlier neuron's share of the blame is the error of the neurons it feeds, weighted by the connections between them. A weight's gradient is then its neuron's share of the blame times the input that weight saw. One pass backwards, and every weight has its gradient.

children: What happens to the gradients is the

's job. Plain SGD (stochastic gradient descent) subtracts learning rate × gradient, as in the last two topics. The book notes that Adam is by far the most widely used optimizer for transformer models; it also keeps running averages for each parameter, which is why training needs more memory than inference.

children.children: This lesson's network is written from scratch, and its tests check the backward pass the slow way: nudge one weight by a millionth, measure how much the loss changes, and compare that with the gradient backpropagation computed. They agree.

children.question: When you send a prompt to a trained model and it answers, which passes run?
options: The forward pass and then the backward pass, every time
Neither: answers are looked up, not computed

children.children: Only the forward pass. The backward pass exists to compute gradients for updating parameters, and answering a prompt doesn't change any parameters. That's one reason inference is so much cheaper than training.

children.children: A piece of text from a model's fixed vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a character or a byte sequence. Models read and write tokens, not characters.

children: at every position, so there's no labelling bottleneck and the training data can be enormous. A model trained that way is trained to minimise its cross entropy on that data.

children.question: Where do a language model's training labels come from during pre-training?
options: People label each sentence as good or bad
The text itself: each position's label is the next token
There are no labels; it doesn't use a loss

children.children: The text itself. AI Engineering's example: "I love street food." gives six training samples, each asking for the token that comes next. That's self-supervision, and it's why language models could scale to so much data.

children: has everything from this lesson in one place: four datasets, seven inputs, up to six hidden layers, four activation functions, the learning rate, batch size, noise and regularization. Some things to try:

children.children: Spiral with only x₁ and x₂: how many layers does it take?
Any dataset at a learning rate of 3 or 10: watch the loss curve.
ReLU against tanh on the circle.
A model is a function whose behaviour is set by parameters: weights and biases.
Loss is one number for how wrong the model is; training pushes it down.
Gradient descent moves each parameter a little against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate. Too small is slow; too big overshoots or blows up.
Backpropagation computes every parameter's gradient in one backward pass; an optimizer such as SGD or Adam applies them. Inference runs only the forward pass.
Hidden layers with nonlinear activations, or better inputs, let a network learn shapes a straight line can't.
Watch held-back data: training loss falling while test loss rises means overfitting. Stop earlier, add data or use a smaller model.

children.children: Gradient descent: downhill in small steps

Picture the loss as a landscape: every possible setting of the parameters is a place, and the loss is the height there. Training wants the lowest point. With millions of parameters you can't look at the whole landscape, but you can always feel the slope under your feet.

children: : how much the loss changes when a parameter changes a little.
takes a small step downhill, against the gradient, then measures the slope again. For one weight:

children.children: new weight = weight − learning rate × gradient

children: sets the step size. Start with the simplest landscape there is, loss = w², whose slope at any point is 2w.

children.question: At w = 2.5 the slope of loss = w² is 2 × 2.5 = 5. With a learning rate of 0.1, where is w after one step?

children.children: 2.0: 2.5 − 0.1 × 5 = 2.0. The next step is smaller, because the slope at 2.0 is only 4: the closer you get to the bottom, the flatter it is and the smaller each step.

A real network does exactly this, for every parameter at once. Its landscape has one dimension per parameter, so you can't draw it, but each weight still moves a little against its own gradient on every step.

children.question: With no hidden layer, the network is one neuron reading x₁ and x₂ directly. After 200 epochs, roughly what share of the test points does it classify correctly?
options: About 50%: no better than a coin flip
About 75%: three quadrants out of four

children.children: About 50% (50.5% here). One neuron can only split the plane with a straight line, and no straight line separates opposite corners from each other. Add a hidden layer of 4 neurons and it reaches 99.5%; give the single neuron the input x₁x₂ instead and it reaches 100%, because x₁x₂ is positive exactly where the answer is.

children: Two lessons in one picture. A
of neurons, each bending its own straight line through an activation function, can combine them into shapes no single line could make. And the right

can do the same job: the network can learn the feature x₁x₂ itself, or you can hand it over. Deep learning's advantage is that it learns useful features from raw data instead of needing someone to design them.

children.question: A network with no hidden layer has to separate points inside a circle from points around it, and it's only given x₁ and x₂. What would let it succeed without adding a hidden layer?
options: Adding x₁² and x₂² as inputs

children: The squares. A circle is x₁² + x₂² < r², a straight line in terms of x₁² and x₂², so one neuron reading them reaches 100% in this course's tests. With only x₁ and x₂ it stays stuck below chance, however long it trains or however much data it gets. Try it in the

children.children: The learning rate is the setting people tune most. AI Engineering calls it the step size: too small and training takes too long to reach the goal, too big and it can overstep the goal and never converge.
On the curve loss = w², each step multiplies w by (1 − 2 × learning rate), which makes the effect exact and easy to see.

children.question: Starting from w = 2.5, what does a learning rate of 1.05 do to w over 20 steps?
options: It reaches the minimum faster than any smaller rate
It settles slightly to one side of the minimum
It moves further from the minimum on every step

children.children: It blows up. Each step multiplies w by 1 − 2 × 1.05 = −1.1: the sign flips and the size grows by 10%, so after 20 steps w is about 16.8. At exactly 1.0 the factor is −1 and w bounces between 2.5 and −2.5 forever; at 0.5 the factor is 0 and w lands on the minimum in one step.

children: There is no universal best value. The book suggests experimenting, and reading the

: if it jumps around a lot, the learning rate is probably too big; if it's steady but slow to fall, probably too small. Many training runs also change the rate as they go, larger at the start and smaller near the end, using a

children.children: The size of the step isn't the only thing that decides where you end up. Gradient descent only knows the slope where it stands, so on a landscape with more than one valley, the starting point decides which valley it settles in.

children.question: A loss curve falls smoothly but very slowly over thousands of steps. What does that suggest?
options: The learning rate is probably too small
The learning rate is probably too big
The model has reached its best possible loss
The data has no pattern to learn

children.children: Too small: every step goes the right way, just not far. A rate that's too big shows the opposite, a loss curve that jumps around.

children.children: Loss: one number for how wrong

children: To improve a model you first need to measure how wrong it is, as a single number. That number is the
. AI Engineering defines it as the difference between the computed output and the expected output: if they differ, the model made a mistake and its parameters need adjusting.
The network in this lesson outputs a number between −1 and 1, and each training point's right answer is +1 or −1. Its loss for one point is half the squared distance between the two,
, and the loss over a dataset is the average across its points.

children.children: Squaring does two things. Every miss counts as positive, whichever side it falls on, and big misses cost far more than small ones, so training works hardest on the points the model gets most wrong.

children.question: For a point whose answer is −1, which output gives the larger loss: 0.5 or −0.2?
options: They're equal, because both are less than 1 away from zero
0.5, because it's 1.5 away from −1; −0.2 is only 0.8 away
Neither: loss is only counted when the sign is wrong

children.children: 0.5. Its loss is ½(0.5 − (−1))² = ½ × 2.25 = 1.125; for −0.2 it's ½(−0.2 − (−1))² = ½ × 0.64 = 0.32. Loss measures distance from the right answer, and wrong-side outputs are usually far.

children.children: Two more training settings matter as much as the learning rate. AI Engineering defines them:

children: : how many examples each update learns from. Very small batches (the book says fewer than eight) can make training unstable; larger ones give steadier updates but need more memory.
: an epoch is one pass over the training data, so the number of epochs is how many times each example is trained on.
More epochs aren't always better. A model can start memorising its training examples, including their noise, instead of learning the pattern. That's

, and the only way to see it is to keep some data back and measure the loss on that too. The book's rule: if training loss still falls while validation loss rises, the model is overfitting, and you might try fewer epochs.

children.question: A network with 217 parameters trains on just 30 noisy points. Its training loss falls to zero. What does its loss on 270 held-back test points do?
options: Rises from the very first epoch

children.children: It falls, then rises. Here the lowest test loss is 0.273 at epoch 16; by epoch 500 it has climbed to 0.547 and test accuracy is 68.5%, while training loss is 0. The network has fitted the 30 points exactly, noise included.
Three fixes, each visible in the lab:

children: The model at epoch 16 was the best one this run produced. Keeping the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss is called early stopping.
With 150 training points instead of 30, the same big network's lowest test loss is 0.185.
With 9 parameters there isn't room to memorise 30 points: final test loss 0.241 and 83.7% test accuracy, against 0.547 and 68.5% for the big network.
(L1 and L2), which pulls every weight towards zero a little on each step. On this example it helps less than the three fixes above, so try it there and compare.

children.question: Your fine-tuning run's training loss is still falling, but validation loss has started rising. What does AI Engineering suggest trying?

children.children: Fewer epochs: the model has started overfitting. More (or cleaner) data and a smaller model are the other levers this topic showed.

This is the end of Module 01. You have read GPT-2's numbers in tables and labs. Now you run the model yourself, in your own browser, and use everything from the six lessons on prompts you choose.

children.question: You type “The capital of Australia is the city of” into the browser model. Will its top-5 probabilities match the table from earlier in this lesson exactly?
options: Close, but not identical: the browser runs a quantized copy, stored with lower-precision numbers
Yes, to four decimals: it is the same model
No relation at all: it is a different model

children.children: Close, not identical. Quantization stores the weights with fewer bits (Module 02 covers it), which shifts every probability a little and can occasionally swap two close tokens. The GPT-2 numbers in this module come from the full-precision PyTorch model, so record your own numbers from the screen instead of expecting to match them.

children.question: In task 5, the temperature-0 run picks “ the” and the temperature-1.2 run picks “ a” at the same step. On screen, “ the” is 0.31 and “ a” is 0.12 at T = 1 (illustrative numbers). What is the best explanation?
options: Temperature changed which token is most probable
Greedy always takes the top token; at T = 1.2 the distribution is flatter and sampling can pick a lower-ranked token, here the second one

children.children: Temperature does not reorder the tokens; it changes how spread out the probabilities are. Greedy takes rank 1 every time. Sampling at a higher temperature gives lower ranks a bigger share, and once one pick differs, every later step sees different context.

The model is trained for likely text, not true text. It has no lookup, its knowledge is frozen, it copies patterns, and it builds on its own errors. Probability is a signal, not a guarantee.

children.question: The model has just written a wrong token. What does it do with that token at the next step?
options: Marks it as uncertain and avoids building on it
Reads it as part of the context, exactly like the prompt, and predicts what usually follows it
Ignores it: each step only reads the original prompt

children: It becomes context like any other token. Nothing marks it as the model's own guess. GPT-2's greedy run for “The capital of Italy is the city of” shows where this leads: “Milan, and the capital of the Italian Republic is Rome. The capital of the Republic is Rome.” Each sentence is locally likely, and nothing checks the paragraph as a whole for consistency (gpt2, transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1, from

children.children: Fluent, confident output that is false or not supported by the input.

children: (Ortega et al., DeepMind, 2021): the model does not separate the text it was given from the text it generated. Once it has written a slightly wrong claim, it expands on it.
(Zhang et al., 2023): after an early wrong assumption, a model keeps going to justify it, and can then fail questions it would otherwise get right.
Ji et al. (2022, section "Hallucination from Training and Inference") name a related training-time cause,
. During training the model always predicts from real text. During generation it predicts from its own earlier output, and errors can build up as the text gets longer.

children.children: A right first token does not protect the rest of the continuation. In GPT-2's greedy runs, each of these began with the correct answer:
Everest: “about 1,000 feet above sea level”. Its summit is about 29,031 feet (8,848.86 m).
Romeo and Juliet: “based on the play "The Tempest,"”. The story comes from an Italian tale by Matteo Bandello, which Arthur Brooke turned into a verse poem and William Painter retold in prose.
Pride and Prejudice: “a collection of essays by Austen”. It is a novel.
Mercury: “about 1.5 times the distance from the Sun to the Sun”, which does not mean anything.

children.question: Why does a long generated answer have more room for hallucination than a one-word answer?
options: Long answers use a higher temperature
Every token is conditioned on the model's own earlier tokens, so each step is another chance to go wrong, and early errors get built on
The context window fills up after 20 tokens

children: More steps mean more chances to go wrong, and each mistake becomes context for the rest. This is one reason
says that asking for concise answers seems to reduce hallucination: fewer tokens, fewer chances to make something up.

children.children: Lessons 1 to 5 followed a prompt all the way to text. Nowhere on that path is there a step that checks whether the text is true. This lesson is about what follows from that.

children.question: GPT-2 was trained on about 40 GB of web pages. During training, what was it rewarded for?
options: Answering questions the way a teacher would
Looking facts up in a database
Giving a high probability to the token that actually came next in the training text

children.children: Predicting the next token of real text. If a training page said something false, predicting that false next word was the "right" answer. GPT-2's model card puts it plainly: models like it do not tell fact from fiction, so uses that need the output to be true are not supported.

children.children: Fluent, confident output that is false or not supported by the input.

children: is fluent, confident-sounding output that is false or not supported by any source. Two definitions from the literature:
(Ch. 2, "The Probabilistic Nature of AI") describes it as a response that is not grounded in facts.
Ji et al. (2022), a survey of the field, use "content that is nonsensical or unfaithful to the provided source". They split it into
(cannot be checked against the source either way). They also note why it is hard to catch: hallucinated text reads as fluent and natural.

children.children: The fluency is the problem. A model that wrote wrong answers in broken grammar would be easy to distrust. A next-token predictor is very good at grammar, because grammar is exactly what makes text likely.

children.question: Which of these is a hallucination?
options: A summary that states a date the article never mentions, in a confident, well-formed sentence
A summary that leaves out a minor detail of the article
A reply in a different language than asked
A reply that is cut off at the token limit

children.children: An unsupported claim stated fluently. In Ji et al.'s terms, a date the source never mentions is an extrinsic hallucination: the source can neither confirm nor refute it. The others are quality problems, but not made-up content.

children.children: Larger, newer models do better, and this has been measured:

Kadavath et al. (2022), "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know", found that larger models are well calibrated on many multiple-choice and true/false questions when the questions are formatted the right way. Models can also be trained to predict whether they know an answer. That generalizes partly across tasks, and its calibration is weaker on new ones.

children: (OpenAI, 2023, "Limitations", Figure 8), already cited in lesson 4, found the pre-trained model well calibrated on a subset of a multiple-choice benchmark, and much less so after post-training.

children.children: A free-form answer spreads its claim over many tokens, so there is no single token probability to read. Kadavath et al.'s workaround is to ask the model a second question: is the answer it just proposed true? They report encouraging calibration for that probability, improving with model size. So: a low probability is a useful warning, and a high one is evidence, not proof.

children.question: You log the probability of the first token of every answer your app gives. Which use is justified?
options: Show it to users as “the chance this answer is correct”
Flag low-probability answers for review, and check against a labelled test set whether that flag actually catches errors for your model and prompts
Ignore it: probabilities carry no information

children: Use it as a signal and measure how well it works for your setup. GPT-2's right

children.question: A support bot answers from your company's policy documents, placed in the prompt. Which check is most practical?

children.question: For “The chemical symbol of sodium is Na and the chemical symbol of gold is”, GPT-2 puts “ Na” first (0.1334) and “ Au” at rank 47 (0.0031). What is the most likely reason?
options: GPT-2 has never seen the word gold
It continued the pattern in the prompt and copied the symbol it had just read

children.question: GPT-2 small continues “I opened the box and found” for 25 tokens with greedy decoding. What do you expect?
options: Fluent text that soon starts repeating itself

children.children: Fluent, then a loop. The measured greedy continuation is: “a small box with a small amount of paper. I opened it and found a small box with a small amount of paper.” The second half repeats the first, word for word.

children: Try this: select the box prompt and compare

with the other settings. Then look at the greedy run for “The largest planet in our solar system is”: it says the planet is “about 1.5 billion light years away”, then repeats that figure in the next sentence.

children.children: Once a phrase has appeared, the model finds it more likely to appear again. That makes the repeat the top choice, and greedy always takes the top choice. Measured on the box continuation (each token's probability at the moment greedy picked it):

token      first time   second time
" small"     0.030        0.235
" box"       0.088        0.593
" amount"    0.027        0.988

(Same script, gpt2, transformers 5.20.2, torch 2.14.1.) Holtzman et al. (2020) report this feedback loop for most phrases they tested: a repeated phrase becomes more probable with every repetition. They show that methods which maximize probability tend to produce text that is bland or stuck in repetitive loops, and that the highest-scoring long texts are often generic and awkward rather than human-like.

children.question: Look at the table again: “ small” was picked at probability 0.030 the first time. Why did greedy pick a token that unlikely?
options: It was still the single most probable token at that step; when many words are plausible, even the top one can have a small probability
Greedy picks at random among the top 50

children.children: Greedy only needs the top token, not a likely one. After “found a” many adjectives fit, so the top one held only 0.030. Picking the top token at every step does not mean the whole sequence is the most likely one, or the best.

children.question: Divide every logit by T = 0.5 (that is, double them) before softmax. What happens to the top token's probability?
options: It goes up: the distribution gets sharper
It goes down: the distribution gets flatter
It stays the same: dividing every logit by the same number cancels out

children: It goes up. Dividing by a small T stretches the gaps between logits, and softmax turns bigger gaps into a more lopsided distribution. A large T shrinks the gaps and flattens it. As T approaches 0, nearly all the probability lands on the top token, which is greedy decoding. That is why "temperature 0" means greedy:
(Ch. 2, "Temperature") notes that you cannot actually divide by 0, so in practice the top token is simply picked.

children.question: Top-p = 0.9. For a prompt where the top token alone has probability 0.95, how many tokens can be sampled?

children.children: The top token alone already reaches 0.9, so the nucleus is just that token, and sampling behaves like greedy for that step. On a flat distribution the same setting can keep hundreds.

When you split documents into chunks for a retrieval system, you can measure chunk size in tokens of your generation model's tokenizer. That makes it easy to guarantee chunks fit the context window. The cost, as
points out, is that switching to a model with a different tokenizer means re-chunking and re-indexing your data.
