children: A prompt is a token budget
Everything you send, plus the room you leave for the answer, has to fit the model's context window, counted in that model's tokens. Count each part before you send.

children.children: Illustrative numbers for an 8,000-token window, not a measurement.

children.question: A colleague estimates an API bill by counting words in a batch of support tickets written in English and Hindi, then multiplying by the price per token. What's wrong?
options: Nothing: one word is about one token
It overestimates, because tokens are longer than words
Prices are per token and the words-to-tokens ratio depends on language, so the Hindi tickets are badly underestimated
It's fine as long as they use the 100 tokens ≈ 75 words rule

import tiktoken

text = "Tokenizers turn text into integers."
for name in ["gpt2", "cl100k_base", "o200k_base"]:
    enc = tiktoken.get_encoding(name)
    ids = enc.encode(text)
    pieces = [enc.decode([i]) for i in ids]
    print(f"{name}: {len(ids)} tokens")
    print("  ids:   ", ids)
    print("  pieces:", pieces)
    assert enc.decode(ids) == text  # round-trips losslessly

children.children: A way to learn a subword vocabulary: start from single symbols and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair. Encoding replays the learned merges in order.

children: runs, a regular expression splits the text into chunks (roughly: words with their leading space, runs of digits, punctuation, whitespace), and merges never cross chunk boundaries. This is why a space attaches to the following word.

WordPiece (used by BERT) and Unigram (used by T5) build vocabularies differently, and the SentencePiece library trains BPE or Unigram directly on raw text without assuming spaces separate words. The output is the same kind of thing: a vocabulary and a fixed procedure for splitting text into it.

children.children: Measured with tiktoken 0.14.0: encoded with o200k_base, decoded with cl100k_base.

That is the dangerous part: a mismatch produces plausible-looking garbage instead of a crash. The same applies to caches of token IDs, token-based chunk boundaries and token-count budgets stored in a database.

Requests fail with an invalid-token error

children: Three ways to cut one word
Word-level vocabularies can't represent words they never saw; character-level ones can, but make sequences long. Subwords keep common words whole and spell out rare ones from pieces.

children.children: Subword split measured with tiktoken 0.14.0 (o200k_base). The [UNK] row is illustrative: it shows what a word-level vocabulary does with a missing word.
Vocabulary size is a dial the tokenizer designer sets:

children: : shorter sequences (cheaper, more text per context window), but a bigger embedding table and fewer training examples for each rare token.
: a smaller table, but longer sequences.

children.children: That is why vocabulary size is a deliberate design decision and differs from model to model.

children.question: A team doubles their tokenizer's vocabulary size. What is the most direct effect?
options: Sequences get longer and the embedding table gets smaller
The model can now represent words it could not before
Nothing measurable; vocabulary size only affects training speed
Sequences get shorter and the embedding table gets bigger

children.children: More entries means more text is covered by single tokens (shorter sequences), and every entry needs its own row in the embedding table. With a byte-level base, the old vocabulary could already represent any input, just in more pieces.

children.children: A piece of text from a model's fixed vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a character or a byte sequence. Models read and write tokens, not characters.

children: per request, and prices. The lab uses illustrative prices for a large and a small model, not any provider's list prices, so plug in your own.

children.children: The starting workload: 50,000 requests a day, 4,000 input tokens and 400 output tokens each, all on the large model. That's $0.018 a request, or $27,000 a month.

children.question: Your budget is $15,000 a month. Which single change gets closest?
options: Both of the last two are about equally effective
Caching a shared prefix that's 75% of every prompt
Routing half of requests to the small model

children.children: Halving the output saves about 17%: $22,500. Caching a 75% prefix brings it to $14,850; routing half to the small model to $14,625. Both together: about $8,000. Try them.
The levers, and where they come from in this course:

children.children: The developer's instructions, sent as the first message with the system role. The model gets it in the same sequence as the user's text; it carries more weight only through position and training.

children: . It only helps when the same prefix really repeats.
easy requests to a cheaper model: lesson 1. It only helps if quality holds on the routed share.
: often cheap to try, since output tokens cost more per token than input in this price list (and in many real ones), but they change the product.

children.children: Every lever has a quality side. A cost model tells you what each change saves; your evaluation suite tells you what it costs in quality. You need both numbers before deciding.

children.question: Routing 50% of traffic to the small model saves the most money in your model. What must you check before shipping it?
options: Quality on the routed share, with your evaluation set, because the saving is only real if those answers stay good enough

children.children: Cost per request is only meaningful next to quality. Module 02 called this cost per useful answer.

Alert with a projected run-out date, and shift some traffic to cheaper paths (more routing to the small model, tighter limits) before it runs out

children.children: At this rate the budget runs out around day 21. Acting now, in small steps, beats a hard stop later.

children.question: One sentence: what's the difference between a budget and a limit?

children.question: Users often ask “What's the return policy for electronics?” Your system answers it using the asking user's membership tier. Is it safe to cache the answer by question text?
options: No: the answer depends on who asked, so a cached copy can show one user's details, or the wrong policy, to another

children.children: This is the book's own warning. The question looks generic, but the answer was built from user X's information. Cached as generic, it's served to user Y, leaking X's data.
Rules for caching answers in production:
Key on everything the answer depended on

children: : the query, the user or their segment, the prompt and model version, the data version.

children.children: Don't cache user-specific or time-sensitive answers.

children: The book's examples are “What's the status of my recent order?” and “How's the weather?”, and it notes many teams train a classifier to decide which queries to cache.
: an eviction policy (the book lists least recently used, least frequently used, and first in, first out) and an expiry, so stale answers age out.

children.question: Answers are streamed. Before the first token: router 40 ms, retrieval 120 ms, reranker 180 ms, model's time to first token 450 ms. Your budget to first token is 1 second. What's the slack?
options: About 210 ms: the stages add up to 790 ms
It depends on the output length

children.children: 40 + 120 + 180 + 450 = 790 ms, leaving 210 ms. The whole 300-token answer takes 6.79 s, but with streaming, users start reading at 790 ms.

children.children: Your own limits: apps, users, requests
Provider limits apply to your whole organisation. Inside them, you need your own: otherwise one application, one batch job or one user can use up capacity everyone else needs.

children.question: One user scripts your AI feature and sends 50,000 requests overnight. With no per-user limit, what's at risk?
options: Your organisation's rate limit and spend for everyone, and possibly the monthly cap that stops all features

children.children: Without per-user limits, the heaviest user sets everyone's experience, and a stolen account or a buggy script can spend real money fast.

children.children: A piece of text from a model's fixed vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a character or a byte sequence. Models read and write tokens, not characters.

children: (Ch. 10, "Gateway") says can monitor and limit API usage to prevent abuse and manage costs. Anthropic's documentation describes the same idea for its workspaces: set lower limits on one so it can't use up capacity others need.
: requests, tokens or spend per hour or day, enforced by your application.
: maximum input and output tokens, and for agents, maximum steps and cost (Module 06).

children.children: Per-user limits are also a product decision. Free and paid tiers often differ by exactly these numbers. Whatever the limits, tell users when they hit one and when it resets, rather than failing silently.

children.question: Which limit best caps the damage of a single runaway agent task?
options: A per-request (per-task) limit on steps and cost, enforced by the harness

children.children: The innermost limit catches the problem closest to its source, before it touches anyone else's budget.

children.children: The minute's total isn't what's checked; what's in the bucket at each moment is. Spread the same 100 requests at 1 per second and all are accepted.

children: A feature that works in a demo can still fail in production by costing too much, by tripping a provider's rate limit at peak hours, or by being too slow for the people using it. These are the three budgets of an AI feature:

children.className: cursor-help underline decoration-muted decoration-dotted underline-offset-4 outline-none focus-visible:rounded focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring
absolute bottom-full left-0 z-50 mb-2 hidden w-72 max-w-[80vw] rounded-xl border border-border bg-surface p-3 text-sm leading-6 shadow-xl group-hover/term:block group-focus-within/term:block

children.children: What one request costs end to end: input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price for an API, or machine time × hourly price when self-hosting. Comparable across models with different tokenizers, unlike a price per token.

children: and what the latency numbers mean. This lesson is about controlling them in a running system: setting the budgets, enforcing them in code, and watching them.

children.question: Your organisation reaches its provider's monthly spend cap on the 24th. What happens to your AI features?
options: They stop: requests fail until the cap resets or is raised, for every feature on that account
Only the most expensive feature stops

children.children: Anthropic's rate-limits documentation describes it: once an organisation reaches its tier's monthly spend cap, API usage pauses, and requests return errors until the next month or a higher limit. Your own budgets should trigger long before that.

children: Each budget is a product requirement: what the feature may cost, how much traffic it must handle, and how fast it must respond. Like the requirements in
, they're set before launch and checked continuously.

children.children: And each needs a planned behaviour when it's hit, from lesson 2's ladder: route to a cheaper model, return a cached answer, queue, or refuse clearly.

children.question: Why is “we'll watch the bill” not a cost control?
options: A bill arrives after the money is spent; a control limits spending as it happens, in code, per user and per feature

children.children: Watching is necessary but not sufficient. Limits that act in real time are what stop a runaway agent or an abusive user from spending the month's budget in a day.

children: Write the plan down, and wrap-up

children.children: A fallback only helps if you reach it quickly. If every request first waits for the dead primary to time out, each user pays the full timeout before the fallback even starts.

children.question: During a 100-second outage, one request arrives per second, and each call to the dead primary waits 10 seconds before falling back. How much total waiting do users do on the primary?
options: 1,000 seconds: every one of the 100 requests waits the full 10 seconds

children.children: The fallback works, but every user meets the timeout first. A circuit breaker stops that.

children: Martin Fowler's "CircuitBreaker" (2014) describes the pattern. A breaker wraps the call and counts failures. Once they reach a threshold, it
: further calls fail immediately without reaching the failing service, so the fallback answers at once. After a timeout it lets one
through; success resets it, failure opens it again.

children.children: With a breaker that trips after 5 failures and tries again every 30 seconds, the primary gets 8 calls instead of 100, and users wait 80 seconds in total instead of 1,000. The struggling service also gets far less traffic while it recovers, which is Fowler's other reason for the pattern: without it, one unresponsive service can tie up resources and spread failure to everything that calls it.
Put breakers where the gateway calls each model, so every application behind the gateway benefits.

children.question: What does the half-open state protect against?
options: Staying on the fallback for ever: it periodically tests whether the primary has recovered, with a single request instead of all traffic

children.children: One trial request is a cheap probe. If the primary is back, traffic returns to it; if not, only one request paid the price.

children.children: Not every bad day is an outage. Sometimes the system is up but overwhelmed: a launch, a viral post, a batch job sharing your rate limit. Two techniques from Google's SRE book, "Addressing Cascading Failures", apply.

children: does less work per request: lower-quality, cheaper results. The book's example is a search that only looks through the subset of data in an in-memory cache. For an AI application, the equivalents are a smaller model, skipping the reranker, fewer retrieved passages, a shorter maximum output, or switching off an expensive optional feature.

refuses some requests outright, so the rest can be served. The SRE book describes returning HTTP 503 (service unavailable) to new requests once too many are in flight, or throttling based on CPU, memory or queue length.

children.question: Demand is twice your capacity. You queue every request instead of shedding any. What happens?
options: Everyone is served, just a little later
Queues grow, every request waits longer, and soon most time out: nobody gets an answer in time

children.children: Serving everyone slowly can mean serving no one. A fast, clear “busy, please try again” to some users keeps the system useful for the rest.

children: The SRE book adds two cautions for degraded modes. They should rarely trigger, typically only when capacity planning fails or load shifts unexpectedly. And they must be
, because the code path you never use is often the code path that doesn't work. A fallback you've never run is a hypothesis, not a plan.

children.question: Your degraded mode switches to a smaller model. It hasn't been triggered in eight months. What's the risk?
options: It may not work when needed: the model may be retired, its prompt outdated, or its credentials expired; test it on a schedule

children.children: Unused paths rot. Run the degraded mode on purpose, for example on a small share of traffic or in regular drills, so you find out before an incident does.

children: Write the plan down, and wrap-up
Model APIs go down. They rate-limit you at peak times. They slow down.
(Ch. 10, "Gateway") calls API failures “unfortunately common”. A production system doesn't get to choose whether it meets these failures, only how it behaves when it does.

children.question: Your only model provider has an outage. What's the worst thing your application can do?
options: Show a clear “we can't answer right now” message
Hang until the request times out, then show a generic error, for every user, for the whole outage
Send users to a help page

children.children: A slow, unexplained failure wastes every user's time and gives them nothing to act on. Each of the other options is a deliberate, degraded behaviour.

children: : an ordered list of things to try, each a bit worse than the last, ending in something honest rather than a hang.

's gateway section describes the first rungs: when the primary API is unavailable, route to alternative models, retry after a short wait, or handle the failure gracefully in other ways. Google's SRE book, "Addressing Cascading Failures", describes the middle rungs as
: reduce the work done by returning lower-quality, cheaper-to-compute results.

children.children: Which rungs exist, and in what order, is a product decision. A coding assistant might fall back to a smaller model; a medical summariser might prefer to say “unavailable” rather than risk a weaker model's answer.

children.question: For which application is “show the retrieved passages without a generated answer” a good degraded mode?
options: A documentation assistant: the passages still contain the answer, just unsummarised

children.children: The retrieval half of a RAG system (Module 05) often still works when the generator doesn't, and raw passages are far better than nothing.

children.children: Write the plan down, and wrap-up
Everything in this lesson is a decision best made before it's needed. During an incident, nobody has time to decide which model to fall back to, or what message users should see.

children.question: Which belongs in a written failure plan for an AI feature?
options: Timeouts, retry rules, the fallback chain, degraded modes, the overload response and the user-facing messages, plus how each is tested

children.children: Each is a specific behaviour your code implements. Writing them down makes them reviewable, and testable.

children: From this lesson, you can now:

children.children: design a ladder of fallbacks that ends in an honest response, not a hang;
compute what a fallback model buys, and why its failures must be independent of the primary's;
use circuit breakers so an outage doesn't cost every user a timeout;
degrade gracefully under load, and shed load with a fast, clear refusal;
treat fallback models as models to evaluate, and choose between retrying and parallel requests;
hand conversations to people when the system can't serve them well;
write the failure behaviour down, and exercise it before an incident does.

children.question: One sentence: what does “graceful” mean in graceful degradation?
options: When parts fail, users still get the best response the remaining parts can give, quickly and honestly, by design rather than by accident

children.children: The next lesson adds the other kind of limit: not what happens when things break, but what happens when things work and cost too much.

children.children: The first rung below the primary is usually another model: a second provider, a different region, or a self-hosted model. A gateway (lesson 1) makes the switch in one place. How much does it buy?

children.question: The primary is available 99% of the time; the fallback 99.5%. If their outages are independent, roughly how many minutes a month are both down at once?

children.children: Both down at once: 1% × 0.5% = 0.005% of the time, about 2 minutes in a 30-day month. The primary alone is down about 432 minutes.

Now drag “shared outages” up. If half the primary's outages also take down the fallback (the same provider's two models, the same cloud region, the same upstream dependency), the gap with no model grows to about 217 minutes. If they always fail together, the fallback adds nothing.

children: That's the most important property of a fallback:

children.children: it must fail for different reasons

children: . A different provider, a different region, or your own self-hosted model fails independently in a way a second model from the same API often doesn't.

children.children: Then switch on the last resort. A cached or static answer is always available, so nothing ends as an error, though some requests get a worse answer. The chain doesn't remove failure; it turns errors into degraded responses.

children.question: Your fallback is the same provider's smaller model. During the provider's last outage, both failed. What's the fix?
options: Add a third model from the same provider
Use a fallback that fails independently: another provider, another region, or a self-hosted model

children.children: Redundancy only helps against failures the copies don't share. Choose fallbacks by how they fail, not just by how well they answer.

children.children: A fallback is a different model

A fallback model is a different model. It may format answers differently, follow instructions differently, refuse different things, and need a different prompt. Switching to it silently can turn an outage into a quality incident.

children.question: Your primary model returns well-formed JSON 99.8% of the time with your prompt. During an outage you fall back to a model you've never evaluated with that prompt. What should you expect?
options: Unknown: its format reliability, quality and refusals have to be measured with that prompt before you rely on it

children.children: Prompts don't transfer perfectly between models. Lesson 1's rule applies: a model change is a release, including an automatic one during an outage.

children: So the fallback path needs the same treatment as the main one: its own

children.className: cursor-help underline decoration-muted decoration-dotted underline-offset-4 outline-none focus-visible:rounded focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring
absolute bottom-full left-0 z-50 mb-2 hidden w-72 max-w-[80vw] rounded-xl border border-border bg-surface p-3 text-sm leading-6 shadow-xl group-hover/term:block group-focus-within/term:block

children.children: One exact, named revision of a prompt. It is logged with every output it produces so results can be traced and compared; any edit, even a typo fix, makes a new version.

children: if needed, its own run of the evaluation and regression suite, and its own metrics in production, broken down by which model answered.
Some failures aren't outages at all but bad outputs: empty, malformed, or failing a guardrail.
(Ch. 10, "Output guardrails") notes that many of these can be fixed by retrying, because models are probabilistic, and describes the trade-off:
: cheap, but the user may wait twice as long.

children.children: Ask twice in parallel and pick the better response

children: : latency close to one call, but redundant calls on every request.

: transferring conversations containing certain phrases to human operators, using a model to decide when to transfer (one team does it when a sentiment model detects anger), or transferring after a certain number of turns so users don't get stuck in a loop.

children.question: Your latency budget is tight, cost is not, and 5% of responses fail a format check. Which approach fits?
options: Send two requests in parallel and use the first valid one

children.children: Parallel requests trade cost for latency: the user rarely waits for a second round trip. If cost were tighter, retrying after failure would be the better trade.

makes sure that when a change is bad, few people see it before you notice.

children.children: The Google SRE Workbook, "Canarying Releases", defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service, and its evaluation. The part that gets the change is the canary; the rest is the control; and you compare them. Its arithmetic for why it helps: a 5% canary with a 20% error rate adds only about 1% to the overall error rate.

children.question: A bad change raises bad answers from 4% to 9%, at 5,000 requests an hour. Shipped to everyone, it's noticed after 6 hours. As a 5% canary compared against the control, it's noticed after 2. How many extra bad answers does each give users?

children.children: Everyone for 6 hours: 1 × 5,000 × 6 × 5% = 1,500 extra bad answers. A 5% canary for 2 hours: 0.05 × 5,000 × 2 × 5% = 25. Smaller exposure, and faster detection because canary and control run side by side.

Faster detection isn't automatic: it comes from comparing canary with control at the same time, as in lesson 4's day 9–10 breakdown. The workbook's advice on what to compare: a few metrics, perhaps no more than a dozen, close to what users perceive, such as error rates and latency, and not noisy ones like CPU use. For an AI change, add the quality signals from lesson 4: format failures, guardrail triggers, thumbs-down and corrections.

children: goes one step earlier. The new version runs on a copy of real traffic, but users only ever see the old version's answers. You compare outputs, cost and latency with no user impact at all. It can't measure user reactions, since nobody sees the new answers, but it catches crashes, format failures, cost surprises and large output differences before any user is exposed.

children.children: The workbook also notes the trade-offs of canary size and length: big and long enough to be representative, short enough not to slow releases.

children.question: What can a shadow deployment not tell you that a canary can?
options: How users respond to the new answers: thumbs, corrections, abandonment

children.children: Shadow outputs are never shown, so there's no user feedback on them. Use shadow to catch technical failures safely, then a canary to see how real users respond.

children.question: Your assistant streams answers token by token. You add an output guardrail that checks the whole answer. What's the problem?
options: Either users wait for the whole answer plus the check before seeing anything, or the answer streams and an unsafe part may be shown before the check finishes

children.children: The book: output guardrails might not work well in stream completion mode, because partial responses are hard to evaluate, so unsafe content can reach users before the guardrail decides to block it.
Where the guardrails run also matters:

children: come with guardrails of their own, which the book notes can reduce how many you need to build. But a provider balances safety against flexibility for all its customers, not for your use case.
removes the need for many input guardrails (nothing leaves), but you build more of the rest.
(lesson 1) can apply guardrails centrally for every application behind them.
exist; the book lists Meta's Purple Llama, NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails, Azure's PyRIT and AI content filters, the Perspective API, and OpenAI's moderation API.

children.children: The choice can differ by feature. A casual chat feature might stream with light checks; a feature that gives medical or financial information might hold the answer until it's checked, and accept the wait.

children.question: Which feature most justifies holding back a streamed answer until an output check finishes?
options: An assistant that tells customers the terms of their insurance policy

children.children: When a wrong or harmful sentence can mislead someone about something important, a few hundred milliseconds of extra wait is a reasonable price.

(Ch. 10, "Step 2. Put in Guardrails") says they help mitigate risks to you and your users, and should be placed wherever there's exposure to risk. It sorts them into two groups: around inputs, and around outputs.

children.question: Which of these is an input guardrail's job rather than an output guardrail's?
options: Stopping a customer's card number from being sent to a third-party model API

children: The book gives input guardrails two jobs: preventing private information leaking to external APIs, and stopping bad prompts that compromise the system. Everything about what the model

children.children: Three earlier lessons already built parts of this:

children: . The book's warning applies to guardrails too: risks can be mitigated but never fully eliminated.

children.children: This lesson adds private data, output policies and their trade-offs, then the other half of safety in production: shipping changes so a bad one reaches as few people as possible.

children.question: Why does an output guardrail need a policy, not just a detector?
options: Detecting a failure isn't enough: the system must decide what to do with it (retry, repair, block, or hand to a person), and the right action differs by failure

children.children: The book names both jobs: catch output failures, and specify the policy for handling each failure mode. An empty response might be retried; a toxic one blocked; a billing dispute handed to a person.

(Ch. 10, "Input guardrails") lists ways private information ends up there:

children.children: an employee pastes a company secret or a user's private information into a prompt;

children: a developer puts internal policies and data into the

children.children: The developer's instructions, sent as the first message with the system role. The model gets it in the same sequence as the user's text; it carries more weight only through position and training.
a tool retrieves private information from an internal database and adds it to the context.

The book is frank that there's no airtight way to stop leaks to third-party APIs, but guardrails reduce them. Tools can detect sensitive data classes you specify, such as personal information (ID numbers, phone numbers, bank accounts), faces, and keywords tied to your intellectual property. When a query contains them, you can block it, or remove the sensitive parts.

children.question: A user's message includes their email and phone number, and the model needs to refer to them in its reply. How can you avoid sending the real values to the API?
options: Replace them with placeholders before sending, keep a reverse map on your side, and swap the real values back into the reply
Ask the model not to store them

children.children: That's the book's masking approach: mask a phone number as a placeholder, and if the response contains the placeholder, use a reverse PII map to restore the original.

children: The model never sees the email, phone or card number; it works with

children.className: rounded bg-surface-2 px-1 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

children: , and its reply still reads naturally once your code restores them. The lab's three regular expressions are a toy. Real detectors use trained models, cover many more classes, and still miss things, which is why the book stops short of calling any of it airtight.

children.children: The model can't use what it can't see.

children: If the task needs the actual value (checking a card's issuer, say), masking breaks it.

children.children: Private data also hides in retrieved context and tool results

children: , not just user messages, so the guardrail belongs where the whole prompt is assembled.

children.children: Self-hosting removes this whole risk class

children: , the book notes, since nothing is sent outside, at the cost of running the model yourself.

children.question: Where should the masking step sit in a RAG pipeline?
options: After the full prompt is assembled (user message, retrieved passages and tool results), just before it's sent to the external API

children.children: Private data can arrive from any part of the context. Checking the final prompt catches all of it in one place.

children: (Ch. 10, "Output guardrails") lists output failures in two groups.
: malformatted responses, factually inconsistent (hallucinated) responses, and generally bad ones.
: toxic content, private or sensitive information, responses that trigger remote tool or code execution, and brand-risk responses that mischaracterise your company or competitors.

children.children: Many are caught by a classifier that scores each output. Then you choose a threshold, and that choice is a trade-off.

children.question: Lowering the blocking threshold catches more harmful outputs. What does it also do?
options: Blocks more good outputs: false refusals that frustrate users with legitimate requests

children.children: The book stresses tracking false refusals alongside security failures: a system can be too secure, blocking legitimate requests and frustrating users.

Twenty illustrative outputs, six of them harmful. At a threshold of 0.3, all six are blocked, along with five fine answers. At 0.6, four are caught, two get through, and one good answer is blocked. At 0.8, nothing good is blocked and four harmful outputs get through. There's no threshold that does everything; there's the one whose mistakes you can best afford, and that depends on the harm.
What happens after a block is the policy:

children: The book notes many failures, such as an empty or malformatted response, can be fixed by trying again, because models are probabilistic.
Fix what's fixable, like a missing closing bracket.
, without exposing why in a way that helps an attacker.

children.question: Your guardrail's false-refusal rate is 8%, and users complain the assistant “won't help with anything”. What do you measure before changing the threshold?
options: Both sides on a labelled sample: how many harmful outputs the new threshold would let through, and how many good ones it would stop blocking

children.children: A threshold change moves outputs between two kinds of error. Count both before and after, as with any comparison in Module 04.

children.children: Put together, a change to an AI system goes through the same gates whether it's a new prompt, a new model or a new retriever setting.

children.question: You want to switch to a cheaper model. Offline evaluation looks good. What comes next?
options: Shadow it on real traffic, then a small canary compared with the current model on user-facing metrics, then widen in steps, with a flag to switch back

children.children: Offline evaluation can't see everything real traffic will throw at the model. Each later stage exposes more users only after the last one held up.

children: (Ch. 3, "Ranking Models with Comparative Evaluation") distinguishes A/B testing, where a user sees one candidate's output at a time, from comparative evaluation, where a user sees several side by side, and notes that for online evaluation, comparative evaluation can complement A/B testing. Both are ways to compare versions with real users once they've passed the earlier gates.
From this lesson, you can now:

children.children: place guardrails on inputs and outputs, each with a policy for what to do when it fires;
keep private data from leaving with masking and a reverse map, and know its limits;
choose an output-guardrail threshold by counting both missed harm and false refusals;
weigh guardrails against latency and streaming, and decide where they run;
ship AI changes behind flags, with kill switches for operators;
limit a bad change's reach with shadow deployments and canaries compared against control.

children.question: One sentence: what makes a deployment “safe” for an AI system?
options: Every change reaches users gradually, is compared against what it replaces on metrics users feel, and can be switched off in seconds

children.children: Tests reduce the chance of a bad change; gradual, measured, reversible releases limit the damage when one gets through anyway. The last lesson asks a different question: when is changing the model itself worth it?

children: Guardrails protect against bad outputs from a good system. The other risk in production is a bad
: a new prompt, model, retriever setting or guardrail that makes things worse. Lesson 4's incident was one. The goal is that when that happens, turning it off takes seconds.

children.question: A prompt change has made answers worse. Undoing it needs a code change, a review and a deploy, about 40 minutes. What would make it a few seconds?
options: Shipping the new prompt behind a feature flag, so turning it off is a configuration change, not a deploy

children.children: When release and deployment are separate steps, rolling back a release doesn't need a new deployment.
Pete Hodgson's "Feature Toggles" (2017), on martinfowler.com, describes four kinds:

children: ship unfinished or unproven code switched off, separating deployment from release.
send users down different paths to compare them.
let operators disable or degrade a feature in production. The long-lived ones are
, which Hodgson describes as something like a manually managed circuit breaker (lesson 2). They must be changeable quickly, without a new release.
decide which users get a feature: beta testers, paid plans, internal staff.
For AI features, a flag can switch the

children.children: One exact, named revision of a prompt. It is logged with every output it produces so results can be traced and compared; any edit, even a typo fix, makes a new version.

children: , the model, the retrieval settings or a guardrail. Every one of those is a change that can go wrong in ways tests didn't catch.

children.children: Hodgson's warning is the cost: each toggle adds conditional logic and testing burden. Keep the number low, and remove release toggles once they've done their job; he suggests they shouldn't stick around much longer than a week or two.

children.question: Which kind of toggle would you use to switch off an expensive optional AI feature during a traffic spike?

children.children: That's an ops decision made during an incident or a load spike. It's also lesson 2's graceful degradation, made a switch.

children.children: Cascades: cheap first, escalate on failure

children: A router decides before any model answers. A
lets the cheap model answer first and decides afterwards.

children.children: FrugalGPT, from Chen, Zaharia and Zou (2023), describes three ways to cut the cost of using language model APIs: adapting prompts, approximating expensive models, and cascades. Its cascade learns which models to try for different queries; on the paper's benchmarks it matched GPT-4's performance at up to 98% lower cost, or beat GPT-4's accuracy by 4% at the same cost. The paper also notes that API prices vary by up to about 100× between providers.

children.question: What can a cascade use to decide on escalation that a router can't?
options: The cheap model's actual answer: a scorer or validator can check it before deciding

children.children: A router guesses difficulty from the question. A cascade sees the attempt, so a failed format check, a failing test or a low score is direct evidence.

In the lab on the previous page, the cascade point gets 85% at 6.25 cost units per query: the small model answers all twenty, and a check sends 7 failed answers to the large model. The check is imperfect: it misses one wrong answer on a borderline query. At the same accuracy the router needs 7.3 units, so here the cascade is cheaper. But the lab treats the check as free; a model-based scorer isn't.
Most queries stop at the first step.

children: Every escalation pays for both models.
Missed failures ship wrong answers; false alarms waste the large model on answers that were fine.
Escalated queries wait for two models in sequence.
Cheap checks exist for many tasks: a JSON schema, a unit test, a regex, a

children.question: Your task produces SQL. Which check makes a good cascade gate?
options: Asking the small model if it's confident
Running the query against a test database and checking it executes and returns the expected columns

children.children: A deterministic, cheap check on the actual output is the best kind of gate: no judge model, no guessing.

children: Once you have several models, from several providers, used by several applications, something has to hold them together.
: an intermediate layer giving your organisation one unified, secure interface to different models, both self-hosted and commercial.

children.question: Ten teams each call a provider's API directly with a shared key. The provider changes its API. How many places need updating?
options: Ten, one per team, and the shared key is a leak waiting to happen; with a gateway, one

children.children: The gateway's most basic job is the unified interface: change providers or APIs in one place. The book also notes organisational keys are easily leaked if handed out to everyone.
The book lists what a gateway centralises:

children: : grant access to the gateway, not to provider keys, with fine-grained rules on who can use which model.
: monitor and limit API usage to prevent abuse and manage costs (lesson 3).
: when an API is down or rate-limited, route to an alternative, retry after a wait, or fail gracefully (lesson 2).
, load balancing, and in some gateways caching and guardrails.

children.children: The book names off-the-shelf examples such as Portkey's AI Gateway, MLflow AI Gateway, Kong and Cloudflare, and notes gateways are relatively easy to build.

children: From this lesson, you can now:

children.children: choose models by filtering on hard attributes, narrowing with public data, evaluating on your own, and monitoring;
account for licences and for API models that change underneath you, and pin versions;
route by intent, including cheap refusals for out-of-scope queries;
route by difficulty, and read the cost–accuracy curve a router traces;
use a cascade when a reliable, cheap check exists;
put a gateway between applications and models for access, cost control, fallbacks and logging.

children.question: One sentence: what's the production view of “which model?”
options: Pick the top of the leaderboard
Not one model but a policy: which model for which query, chosen by evaluation on your data, behind a gateway that controls access, cost and failure

children.children: The rest of the module fills in that policy: what happens when a model fails, what it may cost, how you know it's working, and what it's allowed to say.

children.children: Licences, and models that change underneath you

children: One hard choice comes early: call a provider's API, or host an open-weight model yourself.
(Ch. 4, "Model Build Versus Buy") adds two things that matter in production.

Open-weight models come under many licences, and the book suggests asking: is commercial use allowed? With what restrictions? Its example: Llama 2 and Llama 3 require a special licence from Meta for applications with more than 700 million monthly active users. And can the model's outputs be used to train other models?
With an API, the model is someone else's to update.

children.question: Your application calls a provider's model by a general name. Next month, quality on your test set drops 10%, though you changed nothing. What's a likely cause?
options: The provider updated the model behind that name

children: (Ch. 10, "Drift detection") warns that an API can stay the same while the underlying model is updated, and providers don't always say so. It cites Voiceflow reporting a 10% performance drop when moving from GPT-3.5-turbo-0301 to GPT-3.5-turbo-1106.

children.children: The book also cites Chen et al. (2023), who observed notable differences in benchmark scores between the March 2023 and June 2023 versions of GPT-4 and GPT-3.5. The production habits that follow:

children: where the provider offers dated or versioned model names, so changes happen when you decide.

children.children: Treat a model switch as a release
Self-hosting removes the surprise updates, but not the work: you take on serving, scaling and upgrades yourself.

children.question: A provider announces a new version of the model you use, cheaper and “better on benchmarks”. What do you do first?
options: Run your own evaluation and regression tests on the new version, then switch if it holds up on your data
Switch half your traffic without checking

children.children: Public benchmarks aren't your task. A model change is a change to your product, and gets the same checks as any other.

children: of query it is. A second kind of router decides

it is, and sends only the hard ones to the expensive model. RouteLLM, from Ong et al. (2024), trains routers that choose between a stronger and a weaker model for each query, learning from human preference data; the paper reports cost reductions of over 2× in some cases without compromising response quality.

children.children: The lab makes the trade-off concrete with twenty illustrative queries. The small model answers correctly up to a certain difficulty, the large one up to a higher difficulty, and the large model costs 15 times as much per query. The router doesn't know each query's true difficulty, only a noisy estimate.

children.question: Sending everything to the large model gets 90% right at 15 cost units per query. Can a router match 90% for less?
options: No: only the large model gets 90%
Yes: at a threshold of 0.5 the router sends half the queries to the large model and still gets 90%, at 8 units per query
Only by using a third model

children.children: The queries the router keeps on the small model are mostly ones the small model gets right anyway. Drag the threshold and watch accuracy and cost move together.

children: The curve is the router's whole range: a low threshold sends almost everything to the large model, a high one almost nothing. Read it like a
: which point gives the accuracy you need at the lowest cost?

children.children: Two cautions, both from the lab's shape:
The router's errors set the curve.

children: With a perfect difficulty estimate, every point would be better. Routers are evaluated like any classifier, on your own queries.

children.children: Accuracy can fall faster than cost.

children: Past 0.5, every step saves cost and loses accuracy. Where to stop is a product decision, not a technical one.

children.question: Your router sends 50% of traffic to the large model. You raise the threshold to cut costs. What must you check?
options: Accuracy on a representative test set at the new threshold, broken down by query type, since the queries newly sent to the small model are the borderline ones

children.children: Moving the threshold moves exactly the queries the router was least sure about. Measure them before shipping the change.

children: Most applications start with one model for everything. As they grow,
: send different kinds of query to different solutions.

children.question: A user asks your support bot who it would vote for in an election. What should the router do?
options: Send it to the largest model
Recognise it as out of scope and return a polite stock reply, without a model call

children.children: The book's example reply: “As a chatbot, I don't have the ability to vote. If you have questions about our products, I'd be happy to help.” No tokens spent, no risk of a bad answer.

The book gives two benefits. Specialised solutions, such as a model tuned for troubleshooting and another for billing, can beat a general model on their own queries. And routing saves money: simple queries can go to cheaper models instead of an expensive one for everything.

children: . The book notes many teams adapt small models (it mentions GPT-2, BERT and Llama 7B), and many train even smaller classifiers from scratch; either way, routers should be fast and cheap so that using several doesn't add much latency or cost. A router can also:
on ambiguous queries; the book's example is “Freezing”: the account, or the weather?
when models have different limits, truncating or choosing a model with a larger window;
in an agent, as in Module 06.

children.question: Why should a router be much smaller and faster than the models it routes to?
options: It runs on every query before anything else, so its latency and cost are added to all of them

children.children: A router that costs as much as the large model saves nothing. Its job is a quick, cheap decision.

children.children: The best model for your application

This module is about running AI applications for real users: choosing and routing models, surviving outages, controlling cost, watching what happens, guarding inputs and outputs, and deciding when to fine-tune. It starts with the first decision: which model.

children: (Ch. 4, "Model Selection") opens with a point that's easy to forget: you don't care which model is the best. You care which model is best
. And you'll make the choice more than once: prompt engineering might start with the strongest model to test feasibility, then work back to see whether smaller models will do.

children.question: A model tops a public leaderboard, but your company can't send customer data to that provider's API. Where does the model drop out of consideration?
options: It doesn't: leaderboard rank comes first
Immediately: that's a hard attribute, so it's filtered out before anything else

children: , which you can't or won't change (licences, training data and model size set by the provider; your own policies on privacy and control), from
, which you can improve (accuracy, toxicity, factual consistency). Hard attributes filter first.

children.children: Filter out models whose hard attributes don't work for you.

children: , benchmarks and leaderboards, to narrow down the promising ones, balancing quality, latency and cost.
to find the best: the pipeline of
to detect failures and collect feedback.

children.children: Within the shortlist, the book describes the choice in two parts: work out the best achievable performance, then map models on cost against performance and pick the one that gives the best performance for the money. What counts as hard depends on your situation: latency is soft if you host the model and can optimise it, hard if someone else hosts it.

children.question: Why might a soft attribute like accuracy be worth more effort than it first appears?
options: Prompting, decomposition or context can move it a lot: the book describes a model going from about 20% to 70% accuracy after splitting the task into two steps

children.children: The book is honest about the other side too: sometimes weeks of work don't make a model usable. Estimating how far a soft attribute can move is part of the judgment.

children.children: Here's a synthetic incident. Over two weeks, the thumbs-down rate on a help assistant rose from 3.7% to 8.2%. Nothing went down, there were no errors, and latency was normal. Release 2.4 shipped as a 10% canary on day 9, went to 50% on day 10, and 100% on day 11.

children.question: The aggregate starts rising on day 9 and keeps rising until day 11. What does that pattern most suggest?
options: Something tied to the rollout: the rise tracks the share of traffic on release 2.4

children.children: A rise that steps up with the rollout percentage points at the release. But “the release” is a big change. Breaking the metric down narrows it further.

children: : on days 9 and 10, when both releases served traffic side by side, 2.4 sat at 8.2% while 2.3 stayed at 3.7%. Same days, same users, different release: that's close to an experiment, and it's why canaries are valuable (lesson 5).
: billing and account questions didn't move. How-to questions went from 3% to 12%, from the best-performing type to the worst.
Together: something in release 2.4 broke how-to answers specifically. That's a far smaller search space than “quality dropped”. It's the same lesson as
in Module 04: aggregates hide where things go wrong, and sometimes hide that anything did.

children.question: Why was the day 9–10 comparison by release especially convincing?
options: Both releases served the same period's traffic, so time, user mix and outside events were held roughly constant

children.children: Comparing day 12 with day 5 mixes the release with everything else that changed in a week. Comparing releases on the same day isolates the release.

children: Not every problem arrives with a release.
(Ch. 10, "Drift detection") points out that the more parts a system has, the more things can change, and lists three kinds of change that can degrade an AI application quietly.

children.question: Over three months, average response length falls steadily by 30%. No release changed the prompt or the model. What's a plausible cause?
options: Users have learned to ask for shorter answers, changing the inputs, and so the outputs

children.children: The book's own example: users adapt to the technology, for instance learning to ask for concise responses, which causes a gradual drop in response length. Metrics show the trend; only investigation shows the cause.
The three sources, and how to catch each:

children.className: cursor-help underline decoration-muted decoration-dotted underline-offset-4 outline-none focus-visible:rounded focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring
absolute bottom-full left-0 z-50 mb-2 hidden w-72 max-w-[80vw] rounded-xl border border-border bg-surface p-3 text-sm leading-6 shadow-xl group-hover/term:block group-focus-within/term:block

children.children: The developer's instructions, sent as the first message with the system role. The model gets it in the same sequence as the user's text; it carries more weight only through position and training.

children: A template the prompt is built on was updated, or someone fixed a typo. The book notes simple logic is enough to catch this: version prompts (
) and alert when the deployed text changes.
Inputs drift: new topics, new phrasing, new languages. Watch input distributions and per-segment metrics over weeks, not just daily spikes.
An API's model can change behind the same name (lesson 1). Pin versions, and rerun your

children.className: cursor-help underline decoration-muted decoration-dotted underline-offset-4 outline-none focus-visible:rounded focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring
absolute bottom-full left-0 z-50 mb-2 hidden w-72 max-w-[80vw] rounded-xl border border-border bg-surface p-3 text-sm leading-6 shadow-xl group-hover/term:block group-focus-within/term:block

children.children: A fixed collection of inputs with known expected answers, run unchanged against every version so their results can be compared case by case.

children: on a schedule against what's deployed.

children.children: Drift is also why evaluation and monitoring have to work together. The book: evaluation metrics should translate to monitoring metrics, and issues found in monitoring should feed back into the evaluation pipeline.

children.question: Your quality metrics are stable, but the share of questions about a new product line has grown from 2% to 25%. Why might you still investigate?
options: Your evaluation set was built before that product existed, so stable aggregate metrics may hide poor quality on a quarter of traffic

children.children: When the input mix shifts, check the new slice directly and add it to the evaluation set. A test set that no longer looks like production can't vouch for it.

children.children: From a metric to a trace
The breakdowns narrowed the incident to how-to questions on release 2.4. The next question is which step of the pipeline failed. That's what traces are for.

children.question: Release 2.4 changed how help articles are chunked for retrieval. For a how-to question, which part of the trace would you inspect first?
options: The latency of the generation span
The retrieval span: what text actually reached the model

children.children: A change to chunking changes what retrieval returns. If the steps the user needs never reach the model, no prompt or model will produce them.

Open the three traces. Same question on both releases; on 2.4 the top retrieved chunk stops after step 2 of a four-step procedure, so the answer gives two steps and the user replies “No, that didn't work. What do I do after Data?”. On 2.3 the chunk holds all four steps. The billing question on 2.4 is fine, because its article is short enough to fit in one chunk either way.

children: arriving as a production incident: a boundary landed inside the thing users needed whole. And it's
in practice: the answer was wrong because the evidence was incomplete, not because the generator misbehaved.

children.children: Notice how the user's reply helped. “No, …” followed by a rephrase is one of the implicit feedback signals two pages on, and here it's direct evidence of what was missing.

children.question: After rolling back 2.4, what should the fix include so this can't silently happen again?
options: Fix the chunking (for example, split by structure so numbered steps stay together) and add how-to questions with multi-step answers to the retrieval evaluation set

children.children: The fix addresses the cause; the new test cases make sure the next chunking change is caught before release, not by users.

children.children: Put together, this lesson's tools make an incident process: detect, mitigate, diagnose, fix, learn.

children.question: You've confirmed release 2.4 is breaking how-to answers, but you don't yet know the exact cause. What should you do next?
options: Keep investigating until you find the root cause, then fix it
Mitigate first: roll back 2.4 (or switch it off), then diagnose without users suffering in the meantime

children.children: Diagnosis can take hours. Rolling back takes minutes if releases are built for it, which is lesson 5's subject.

children: The last step is learning. Google's SRE book, "Postmortem Culture", defines a postmortem as a written record of an incident: its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, its root causes, and follow-up actions to prevent it happening again. It should be

: identify the contributing causes without indicting any individual or team, assuming everyone acted in good faith with the information they had. The questions are why the system allowed the mistake and why people had incomplete information, not who erred.

The SRE book lists triggers for writing one, including user-visible degradation beyond a threshold, an on-call engineer having to roll back or reroute traffic, and an incident found manually because monitoring didn't catch it. For an AI system, add: a failure mode your

From this lesson, you can now:

children.children: use metrics, logs and traces in sequence, and judge your setup by MTTD, MTTR and change failure rate;
design metrics around the failures you want to catch, across format, quality, safety, user behaviour, latency and cost;
break metrics down to find where a problem lives;
go from a metric to the traces of affected requests, and find the failing step;
watch for drift from prompts, users and models;
read explicit and implicit user feedback;
run an incident: mitigate first, then diagnose, fix, add tests, and write a blameless postmortem.

children.question: One sentence: what makes an AI system observable?
options: Enough recorded about every request, broken down by enough dimensions, that you can find what went wrong and why without shipping new code to investigate

children.children: The next lesson is about the checks that run before and around every response, and about shipping changes so that mitigation is a switch.

(Ch. 10, "Monitoring and Observability") says the goal of monitoring is the same as the goal of evaluation: to mitigate risks and discover opportunities, and that observability should be designed in from the start rather than added afterwards.

children.question: An alert says the thumbs-down rate jumped in the last hour. What's the right order of investigation?
options: Read random conversations until something stands out
Ask the model what went wrong
Metric first to see when and where, then logs from that window, then the traces of affected requests to find the failing step

children.children: The book's debugging sequence: metrics tell you something went wrong but not what; logs from around that time tell you what happened; correlating them confirms you've found the right issue. Traces then pinpoint the step.

children: , tracking a system's outputs to see when something is wrong, from

, which assumes you can work out the system's internal state from its outputs without shipping new code. That only holds if you've logged enough: in Module 06's words, log everything, with IDs that tie each record to its request.

children.children: How good is your observability? The book borrows three measures from DevOps:

children: (mean time to detection): when something goes wrong, how long until you know?
(mean time to response): once detected, how long until it's resolved?

(change failure rate): what share of changes or deployments cause failures that need fixing or rolling back? The book's advice: if you don't know your CFR, redesign the platform to be more observable.

children.question: Your team found out about last week's quality drop from a customer email, three days in. Which number does that hurt most?
options: Mean time to detection: users noticed before your monitoring did

children.children: Three days of degraded answers is the detection gap. The fix is a metric and alert on the failure users noticed. The SRE book lists “found manually because monitoring failed” as a reason to write a postmortem.

children: Users tell you how the system is doing, whether or not you ask.
: what users give when asked: thumbs up or down, star ratings, “Did we solve your problem?”.
: what's inferred from what they do. The book notes conversational interfaces make this richer, because users correct and redirect the model the way they would a person.

children.question: A user's next message after an answer starts with “No, I meant…”. What does that most likely tell you?
options: The previous response missed the user's intent: an error-correction signal
The user wants a longer answer

children.children: The book lists follow-ups starting “No, …” or “I meant, …” as error correction: the model's response was likely off the mark.
The book's natural-language signals worth tracking in production:

children: : stopping a generation halfway, leaving the app, or leaving an agent waiting for an answer.
: “No, …”, “I meant, …”, or rephrasing the same request.
: “Are you sure?”, “Check again”, “Show me the sources”: not proof of a wrong answer, but a sign answers lack detail or trust.
: a user rewriting generated code or text is a strong signal it wasn't right, and the edit itself is preference data.
The book names three uses for feedback:
. And it adds a caution: feedback is user data. Respect privacy, and tell users how their data is used.

children.question: Why track implicit feedback when you already have a thumbs-down button?
options: Few users press buttons; corrections, rephrasing and early stops happen in far more conversations, so they show problems sooner and more broadly

children.children: Explicit feedback is clear but sparse. Implicit signals are noisier but plentiful. Together they're a better detector than either alone.

children: Sooner or later someone asks: shouldn't we fine-tune a model on our own data? Sometimes yes.

(Ch. 7, "When to Finetune") is clear about the order, though: compared with prompt-based methods, fine-tuning needs significantly more resources (data, hardware, and machine-learning expertise), so it's generally attempted after extensive experiments with prompting. And the two aren't exclusive: real problems often need both.

children.question: A team says prompting “doesn't work” and wants to fine-tune. What does the book suggest checking first?
options: Whether a bigger GPU is available
Whether the prompt experiments were systematic: clear instructions, representative examples, well-defined metrics

children.children: The book describes a pattern many practitioners report: someone insists on fine-tuning, and on investigation the prompt experiments were minimal and unsystematic. Once the prompting process was fixed, the prompts were often good enough.
The book's workflow, which pulls the course together:

children: in the prompt: the book suggests anywhere from 1 to 50, depending on the task.
, if failures come from missing information, starting simple, such as term-based search (
: more advanced retrieval for information failures, fine-tuning for behaviour failures.
RAG and fine-tuning where it measurably helps.
And before all of it: evaluation criteria and a pipeline (
), present at every step, not only the first.

children.question: Why does the book put evaluation before the first adaptation step?
options: Without it you can't tell whether prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning actually improved anything, or which failures remain

children.children: Each step up the ladder is a bet that it will help. The evaluation pipeline is how you know whether the bet paid off, and which failures are left to fix.

children: (Ch. 7, "Finetuning and RAG") says the choice between RAG and fine-tuning depends on what kind of failures you see.

: the output is factually wrong or outdated, because the model doesn't have the information (it's private to you) or has an old version of it (it changed after the model's training cut-off). RAG gives the model the missing facts.
: the facts may be right, but the output is irrelevant to the task, ignores the expected format, or uses the wrong syntax or style. Fine-tuning can teach the behaviour.

children.children: fine-tuning is for form, and RAG is for facts.

children.question: The book cites Ovadia et al. (2024) on questions about current events. For Mistral-7B, which scored highest: the base model, the base model with RAG, or fine-tuned versions?
options: The base model with RAG, by a wide margin

children.children: In the table the book reproduces, Mistral-7B scored 0.481 alone, 0.875 with RAG, and 0.504 and 0.588 with two fine-tuning approaches. For facts the model doesn't have, giving it the facts beats training on them.

children: Sort the twelve illustrative failures. Seven are information failures: prices, policies, error codes the model was never told about. Five are behaviour failures: a query language written with invalid syntax, ignored section headings, the wrong tone. With both kinds, the book's advice is to

children: : for an AI feature you're building or running, what's in place, and what isn't yet.

children.question: What's the most useful output of a readiness review?
options: A short list of specific gaps, each with an owner and a date, linked to how to close it

children.children: A score hides which gaps matter. A list of named gaps is something a team can act on.

Each line maps to a lesson in this module. Tick what your system genuinely has, with evidence, not memory: a dashboard you can open, a flag you've actually flipped, a fallback you've seen serve traffic. What's left is your plan.
To turn it into a document, add for each open line:

children: of leaving it open: what failure would it let through, and how often;
that closes most of the risk (often a day's work, not a project);
that will show it's done: a test, a metric, a drill.
Then rank the lines the way
ranked failures: by how likely and how harmful each gap is, against what it costs to close.

children.question: Your plan has eleven open items and two weeks. How do you choose?
options: By risk: how likely and how harmful the failure each gap allows, against the effort to close it
Whatever the newest team member prefers

children.children: The same prioritisation as error analysis: frequency times severity, against cost. A missing kill switch on a feature that issues refunds outranks a missing dashboard on a low-traffic internal tool.

children.children: A piece of text from a model's fixed vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a character or a byte sequence. Models read and write tokens, not characters.

children.question: Which statement best sums up this module?
options: Pick the best model and ship it
Treat the model as one fallible, metered, changeable component, and build routing, fallbacks, budgets, observability, guardrails and safe releases around it

children.children: Each lesson added one of those layers. None of them makes the model better; all of them make the system dependable.

children: : the best model for your application, pinned versions, routers, cascades and a gateway.
: independent fallbacks, circuit breakers, degraded modes and load shedding.
: cost models, safe caching, rate limits, quotas and latency budgets.
: metrics from failures, breakdowns, traces, drift, feedback and postmortems.
: input and output guardrails, flags, shadow and canary releases.
: form against facts, the ladder of adaptations, the real costs, and a readiness plan.

children.children: From this lesson, you can now:
place fine-tuning after prompting and retrieval, and say why;
name good reasons to fine-tune, and the costs that argue against it;
classify failures as information or behaviour, and pick RAG or fine-tuning accordingly;
estimate fine-tuning memory, and explain what parameter-efficient methods like LoRA save;
write a production-readiness plan as a ranked list of gaps.

children.question: One sentence for the whole course: what does an applied AI engineer actually do?
options: Turns a model into a dependable product: understands what it does, measures it honestly, gives it the right context and tools, bounds what it can do, and runs it so failures are rare, small and quickly fixed

children.children: Modules 01–02 explained the model, 03–05 gave it context and measured it, 06 let it act within limits, and 07 put it in front of users. The interview hub collects the questions that test all of it.

children.children: Model output in a fixed machine-readable format, such as JSON with known keys or one label from a list, so code can parse and use it.

children: . Then it lists what fine-tuning costs.

children.question: You fine-tune your support model on order-change conversations, where it was weak. What might happen to its other tasks?
options: They may get worse: fine-tuning for one task can degrade performance on others

children.children: The book's example is exactly this: a model fine-tuned to fix order changes may get worse at product recommendations and general feedback. Its remedies: fine-tune on all the tasks you care about, use separate models per task, or merge separately fine-tuned models.
The other costs the book lists:

children: : annotated examples can be slow and expensive, especially for tasks needing expertise.
: choosing a base model, training knobs, overfitting, evaluating during training.
: hosting your own model, or a provider's service, with
: new base models arrive fast and may improve faster than your fine-tuned one. When does a new base model justify switching, or re-fine-tuning?

: a 50-billion-parameter model for finance, trained with about 1.3 million A100 GPU hours, an estimated $1.3–2.6 million in compute. In the same month, GPT-4-0314 was released, and research by Li et al. (2023) found it significantly outperformed BloombergGPT on financial benchmarks: 87.15 against 75.07 weighted F1 on FiQA sentiment analysis, and 76.48 against 43.41 accuracy on ConvFinQA, zero-shot. The book is careful to add that benchmarks don't capture real-world use, and that the team gained valuable experience.

children.question: What's the strongest argument against fine-tuning as a first step?
options: It's a large up-front and ongoing investment, and the improvements may be reachable with prompting and RAG, which are cheaper to try and change

children.children: The book's advice: start with prompting, explore more only if it proves inadequate, and make sure the prompt experiments were thorough before concluding they were.

children.children: What fine-tuning takes: memory and LoRA

children: If the failures say fine-tune, the first practical question is memory.

(Ch. 7, "Parameter-Efficient Finetuning") works an example: a 7-billion-parameter model in a 16-bit format needs 14 GB just for its weights. Full fine-tuning with the Adam optimizer, also in 16-bit, needs another 7B × 3 × 2 bytes = 42 GB for gradients and optimizer states. That's 56 GB before activations, more than most consumer GPUs, which the book notes have 12–24 GB.

children.question: What's the main way to cut that 42 GB?
options: Train fewer parameters: gradients and optimizer states are only needed for the parameters you update

children.children: The book: the more trainable parameters, the more memory, which is the motivation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Quantization reduces the rest.
Drag the trainable share down. At 1%, the gradients and optimizer states shrink from 42 GB to 0.42 GB; the 14 GB of frozen weights remain.

children: (Hu et al., 2021), which the book covers in detail, is the best-known way to train a tiny share. For a weight matrix, it trains two small matrices whose product is added to the frozen original, and those can be merged back afterwards, so unlike some adapter methods it adds no inference latency.

children.children: None of this removes the larger costs from the last page: the data, the evaluation, and the maintenance. LoRA makes fine-tuning cheaper to run, not cheaper to get right.

children.question: LoRA cuts training memory dramatically. Which cost does it not change?
options: The need for good training data and an evaluation pipeline, and the work of maintaining the fine-tuned model

children.children: Efficient training makes experiments feasible on smaller hardware. Whether the result is better, and stays better, is still decided by data and evaluation.

children.children: Dropping by age keeps the troubleshooting and discards the one sentence that says what the user wants. This is exactly the failure the book warns about. (Illustrative scenario.)

Selection under a budget is compression too: the packer's "over budget" and "below top k" passages are dropped whole. Whatever the method, write down what must survive (the goal, IDs, numbers, constraints) and test with cases where that fact appears early, late, or buried in a detail.

children.question: Which compression method can introduce a statement that was never in the original context?

children.children: Dropping and truncating only remove text. A summary is new text written by a model, so it can omit, merge or misstate details. Check summaries against the original on the cases that matter.

children: : How Language Models Use Long Contexts" (arXiv:2307.03172, TACL; read 21 October 2026). Each question from NaturalQuestions-Open came with one Wikipedia passage containing the answer plus retrieved passages that didn't, and the authors moved the answering passage from first to last. If models used their context evenly, accuracy would be flat.

children.question: GPT-3.5-Turbo, 20 passages (about 4K tokens). Where was its accuracy lowest?
options: With the answer in the middle

children.children: In the middle. The paper calls it a U-shaped curve: performance is "often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context" (abstract), and drops in between.

children.children: A piece of text from a model's fixed vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a character or a byte sequence. Models read and write tokens, not characters.

The paper's own suggestion (Liu et al., Section 5) is reranking that pushes relevant information closer to the start of the context, or retrieving fewer documents when appropriate. The same section found that more context stops paying off early: using more than 20 retrieved documents improved GPT-3.5-Turbo by only about 1.5% and Claude-1.3 by about 1%, while the input grew a lot.

children: (Ch. 6, "Reranking") points out that for context, exact position matters less than it does in search results: as long as a document is included, its order has a smaller effect. Inclusion is the first decision; order is the second.

children.question: Query “how do I stop paying every month”, rank by Embedding, top 14, budget 300: all 14 articles go in. Where does the answer land in each order?
options: Best first: 1. Best last: 14. As stored: 10
Best first: 14. Best last: 1. As stored: 7

children.children: The cancellation article is ranked #1, so best-first puts it at the start and best-last at the end, right before the question. Stored order puts it 10th of 14, because it is the 10th article in the collection: the middle, by accident.

"Best last" is worth trying because the question usually follows the passages, so the best passage ends up next to it. In the paper's Figure 5, every model did better at the ends than in the middle, but which end was best varied: in Table 6, GPT-3.5-Turbo and LongChat did best with the answer first, Claude-1.3 and MPT-30B-Instruct with it last. Which order works for your model is an empirical question. The order to avoid is the accidental one: stored order, or a fused list nobody looked at.

children.question: Your pipeline concatenates passages in the order the database returns them. What's the cheapest improvement to try first?
options: Buy a model with a longer window
Sort passages by relevance (best first, or best next to the question) and compare the two on a needle-style test
Shuffle them randomly on every request

children.children: Reordering costs no tokens. Measure both arrangements on questions with known answers before you pick one.

children.question: Query: “how do I stop paying every month”. Rank with Both (RRF), keep only the top 1. Which article does the model get?
options: “Cancel your subscription”: embeddings rank it first

children.children: The Wi-Fi article. BM25 returns only one passage for this query, Wi-Fi, because it shares a single word, “every” (“every few minutes”). Embeddings rank it third. Fusion rewards appearing in both lists, so Wi-Fi (1/61 + 1/63) beats the cancellation article (1/61, embeddings only). The answer is ranked #2, and with k = 1 it never reaches the model.

children: The answer goes to #1. Now rank by BM25: it isn't retrieved at all, because it shares no word with the query.
The only match is the two-factor article, through the word “phone”.

children.children: “is this toy safe for a two-year-old”, Both, top 3, budget 40.

children: Two passages fit (18 + 21 = 39 tokens); the third, at 21, would make 60, so the packer stops.

children.question: What's the general lesson from the “stop paying” case?
options: A combined ranking can promote a keyword coincidence; check selection on real queries before trusting any rule, and give k enough room for the answer
Fusion is broken and shouldn't be used
BM25 is always better than embeddings

children.children: No rule wins on every query here: each one ranks the answer below first for at least one of the six. Raising k to 2 would have included the answer, for 25 more tokens. Measure your selection on queries with known answers.

children.children: Relevant is not the same as similar
Every rule in this lesson ranks by a score. None of those scores measures what you actually need: does this passage answer the question?
Take the toddler query in the help centre, “is this toy safe for a two-year-old”. Two articles are about it:
“This toy is safe for children over three.”
“This toy is not safe for children under three because it has small parts.” This is the one that answers: a two-year-old is under three.

children.question: Which of the two does each retriever rank first?
options: Both rank the “not safe” article first
Both rank the “safe for children over three” article first

children: Both put the reassuring article first, and so does their fusion. Both articles share “toy” and “safe” with the question; BM25 favours the shorter one, and as
showed, embeddings barely register “not”. With top 1, the model gets only the passage that leads to the wrong answer.

children.children: Raise k to 2 and both go in; then the order decides which one the model reads first. That is the pattern of the whole lesson:
