children: Wrap-up, and the rest of the module
A model only knows what was in its training data and what's in its prompt.
adds a step before generation: search your own data for the passages most relevant to the question, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them.
The pattern is older than the name.

(Ch. 6, "RAG") traces it to Chen et al. (2017), "Reading Wikipedia to Answer Open-Domain Questions": the system retrieved the five Wikipedia pages most relevant to a question, and a reader model pulled the answer out of them. (The paper's retriever used bigram hashing and TF-IDF.) Lewis et al. (2020) coined the term
, for knowledge-intensive tasks where all the knowledge can't be given to the model directly.

children.question: Your support assistant answers from a model trained a year ago. The pricing page changed last week. What does RAG change?
options: Nothing: the model still only knows its training data
The model is retrained on the new page
The answer can use this week's pricing page, because the page is retrieved at question time and put in the prompt
The model's weights are updated with the new price

children.children: Retrieval happens per question, from the data as it is now. Update the document and the next answer can use it, without touching the model.

children: describes RAG as building context specific to each query, instead of using the same context for every query. That gives three things a bigger model alone doesn't:
Updating a document updates what the model can draw on. Lewis et al. list updating a model's knowledge as an open problem for models that store knowledge only in their weights.
A query about one customer can include that customer's records and nobody else's.
Retrieved passages can be cited, so a reader, or an evaluator, can check the answer against its source. Lesson 5 measures this.

children.children: The book also compares context construction to feature engineering in classical machine learning: both give the model the information it needs to handle an input.

children.question: Which is a reason to use RAG rather than relying on a model's training data?
options: It removes the need for a prompt
Answers can draw on current, per-user data, and can cite where they came from
It guarantees the answer is correct

children.children: RAG changes what's in the context. It doesn't guarantee correctness: the right passage still has to be retrieved, and the model still has to use it. That's the rest of this module.

children: Wrap-up, and the rest of the module

children.children: The simplest RAG system searches the same index for every message. Real questions don't all need that.

children: (Ch. 8, "Advanced RAG Techniques") lists improvements that hand more of the decision to the model:
: choose the source. HR questions go to the HR system; customer questions go to the CRM.
: let the model decide when a question needs no retrieval and can be answered directly.
: split a question that needs several searches ("compare 2023 and 2024 results") into one search each.
: search, read the result, then search again based on what came back.

children.children: The book notes that each step gives the model more responsibility, until the system starts to look like an agent: Module 06.

children.question: A user asks your shop's assistant: “How many Fruity Fedoras did we sell in the last 7 days?” The sales data is in a SQL table. What should retrieval do?
options: Write a SQL query from the table schema, run it, and give the result to the generator
Embed the question and search the product descriptions
Put the whole sales table in the prompt

children: That number isn't written in any document: it has to be computed.
(Ch. 6, "RAG with tabular data") describes the workflow: text-to-SQL from the question and schemas, execute the query, then generate the answer from the result.

children.children: With many tables, the book adds a step before text-to-SQL: predict which tables a query needs, since all their schemas may not fit in the context. The same applies to document collections. Searching the right source is the first retrieval decision, and a wrong route fails before any ranking happens.

children.question: Why let the system skip retrieval for some messages?
options: For messages like “thanks!” or “say that more briefly”, a search adds latency and irrelevant passages without adding information

children.children: A search on “thanks!” returns something, because retrievers always return their nearest matches, and that something then competes for the model's attention.

children: Comparing a query with every vector is fine for thousands of chunks;
(Ch. 8, "Nearest neighbor search versus vector databases") says plain NumPy is reasonable up to tens of thousands. Beyond that, systems use
search, which looks at only some of the vectors.

children.question: An ANN index is much faster than comparing with every vector. What does it give up?
options: The ability to use cosine similarity
Some recall: occasionally a true nearest neighbour isn't among the vectors it looks at

children.children: Approximate means exactly that. The trade is speed against the fraction of true nearest neighbours found, and every ANN method makes it differently.

(inverted file index): k-means clusters; search only the clusters nearest the query. Together with product

children.children: Storing a model's numbers in a format with fewer bits, such as FP16, INT8 or INT4, to cut memory and the bytes each step reads. Strictly it means converting to integers, but in practice it covers any precision reduction.

children: , the book calls it the backbone of FAISS.
(Hierarchical Navigable Small World): a multi-layer graph of similar vectors, searched by walking its edges.
(locality-sensitive hashing): hash similar vectors into the same buckets.
: compress each vector into smaller sub-vectors so distances are cheaper.
: several random binary trees, searched together.

children.children: There's a second trade, between indexing and querying. In "Comparing retrieval algorithms", the book contrasts HNSW, which gives high accuracy and fast queries but takes significant time and memory to build, with LSH, quicker and lighter to build but slower and less accurate to query. It points to the ANN-Benchmarks site, which compares algorithms on recall, queries per second, build time and index size.

children.question: Your documents change every hour, so the index is rebuilt constantly. Which ANN metric matters more than usual?
options: None: ANN indexes never need rebuilding
Build time (and how easily the index takes additions and deletions)

children.children: The book singles out build time as especially important when data changes often. Hands-On LLMs adds that vector databases let you add or delete vectors without rebuilding the whole index.

children.children: A keyword-search scoring function that ranks documents by the query words they contain, weighting rare words more and long documents less.

children: , developed by Robertson and colleagues in the 1980s, is a refinement of TF-IDF, and
(Ch. 6, "Term-based retrieval") notes that it and its variants are still widely used and are formidable baselines for newer methods. It changes the term-frequency part in two ways:
The fourth mention of a term adds less than the first. A parameter, k1 (1.2 here), sets how quickly it saturates.

The book's reason: longer documents are more likely to contain a term, and to contain it more often. BM25 shrinks the term-frequency factor for documents longer than average. A parameter, b (0.75 here), sets how much; b = 0 turns it off.

children.children: The lab computes BM25 live on the fourteen help-centre articles from Module 01. Each term in the query adds IDF × a term-frequency factor.

children.question: Query: “is this toy safe for a two-year-old”. Two articles both contain “toy” twice and “safe” once. One has 10 terms; the other has 14 and is the one that answers the question (“not safe for children under three”). Which does BM25 rank first?
options: The 14-term article: it has more words
The 10-term article: same matches, shorter document

children.children: Same terms, same counts, so the only difference is length. Length normalisation favours the shorter article, 4.539 to 4.066. Turn normalisation off (b = 0) and they tie at 4.255. Either way, BM25 has no idea that “not” is the word that matters.

Now try “my internet keeps cutting out”. The Wi-Fi article matches “keeps” and the slow-speeds article matches “internet”. Both words are in one article each, so both get the same IDF, 2.303. The slow-speeds article is shorter, 13 terms against 15, so with length normalisation it wins, 2.249 to 2.112. Neither score has anything to do with which article answers the question.

children.question: Why does BM25 normalise by document length?
options: Long documents contain more terms by chance, so raw term counts would favour them regardless of relevance
Because short documents are always better

children.children: It's a correction for an unfair advantage, not a preference for short documents. The parameter b controls how strong the correction is, and the right value depends on the collection.

children.children: A vector of numbers that represents a token or a text, arranged so that similar meanings end up close together.

children.question: You embed your documents with model A. A new query arrives. What must happen before you can search?
options: Embed the query with any good embedding model
Nothing: search on the raw text
Embed the query with the same model A, so query and documents share one vector space

children.children: Each embedding model has its own space, so similarity between vectors from two models is meaningless. Module 01 called this one of the two rules that are easy to break.

children: The book describes the query in two steps: embed the query with the same model used during indexing, then fetch the k chunks whose embeddings are closest. The naive way is
: compute the query's similarity to every stored vector, sort, return the top k. It's exact, and the book recommends it only for small datasets because it's slow on large ones.
One behaviour to design for: embedding search always returns k results.

(Ch. 8, "Caveats of dense retrieval") points out that a query with no answer in the collection still gets results with distances, and suggests a maximum-distance threshold as one heuristic. The book also warns that dense retrieval can struggle in domains its model wasn't trained on: a model trained on web text may do poorly on legal documents.

children.question: A user asks your help-centre search about something the docs don't cover. What does embedding retrieval return?
options: The k nearest articles anyway, ranked by similarity, whether or not any is relevant

children.children: There's always a nearest neighbour. A similarity threshold, or a generator instructed to say when the passages don't answer the question (lesson 5), has to handle the rest.

children: Term-based retrieval is fast because of the data structure behind it.

used by Elasticsearch, which is built on Lucene: a dictionary from each term to the documents that contain it. It can also store each term's frequency and document count, which help in computing TF-IDF scores.

children.question: With an inverted index, how many of the 14 help articles does BM25 have to score for “is this toy safe for a two-year-old”?
options: Only the articles listed under the query's terms: 3
None until the query is embedded

children.children: “toy” and “safe” point to the two toy articles, “two” to the two-factor article, and “year” and “old” point nowhere. Three candidates; the other eleven are never looked at.

The same structure explains a behaviour you've already seen: a document that shares no term with the query isn't on any list, so it isn't returned at all. For “how do I stop paying every month”, the only match in the collection is “every”, in the Wi-Fi article, and the cancellation article never appears.

children: The book also mentions an alternative: score documents by n-gram overlap with the query, the lexical similarity of

. It works best when queries and documents are similar in length. When documents are much longer, many of them overlap with the query by chance, and the scores stop separating relevant from irrelevant.

children.question: A document contains the answer but uses none of the query's words. What does an inverted index return for it?
options: Nothing: it's on none of the query terms' lists, so it's never a candidate

children.children: That's term-based retrieval's blind spot: paraphrase. Embedding-based retrieval, two pages on, has the opposite strengths.

Term-based is generally much faster, both indexing and querying: extracting terms is cheaper than computing

children.children: A vector of numbers that represents a token or a text, arranged so that similar meanings end up close together.

children: , and an index lookup is cheaper than a nearest-neighbour search.

Term-based works well out of the box but has few knobs to improve it. Embedding-based retrieval can be improved over time, for example by fine-tuning the embedding model, until it beats term-based, and it handles natural, paraphrased queries.

Embeddings cost money to generate and regenerate when data changes, and vector storage and search can be expensive. The book says it's not uncommon for a company's vector database spending to be a fifth to half of what it spends on model APIs.

children.question: On the six help-centre queries, which retriever ranks the right article first more often?

children.children: Embeddings rank it first for 5 of 6; BM25 for 2 of 6, and returns nothing at all for two of the queries. But this collection is mostly paraphrase, which favours embeddings. On a collection full of error codes and product names, the picture can change.

children: The book's warning about embeddings: they can blur exact keywords such as error codes (it uses

children.className: rounded bg-surface-2 px-1 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

children: ) or product names. Here MiniLM still finds the

children.className: rounded bg-surface-2 px-1 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

children: article, but that's the case where term matching is most reliable and embeddings are least. Neither family handles negation: both rank “safe for children over three” above “not safe for children under three”.

children.children: Different strengths suggest using both. That's hybrid search, the next lesson.

children.question: Your users search mostly by exact part numbers like “AX-2201-B”. Which retriever is the safer default?
options: Term-based (BM25), possibly alongside embeddings: exact identifiers are where term matching is strongest and embeddings least reliable

children.children: A part number is a rare, exact string with a high IDF. Embeddings may place similar-looking numbers close together. If users also ask paraphrased questions, combine the two.

children.children: The simplest term-based idea: retrieve documents that contain the query's words. The book points out two problems. Many documents may contain them, and some query words matter far more than others.

children.question: Query: “easy-to-follow recipes for Vietnamese food”. Which word should count most when matching documents?

children.children: A word that appears in nearly every document can't tell documents apart. A word that appears in few of them is informative. That's the idea behind inverse document frequency.
Two measurements, as the book defines them:

children: : how many times a term appears in a document. More mentions suggest the document is more about it.

: the total number of documents, divided by the number that contain the term. With 10 documents and 5 containing the term, IDF is 10 / 5 = 2. In practice you take the log of that ratio, so very rare terms don't swamp everything else.
sums IDF × TF over the query's terms. It ranks a document higher the more often it uses the query's rare words.

children.question: A term appears in every document in the collection. What's its IDF, using log(N / count)?
options: 0: log(N / N) = log 1 = 0, so it adds nothing to any score

children.children: A term in every document can't separate them, so it contributes nothing. The BM25 in this lesson's lab uses a smoothed IDF that stays positive, but the ordering is the same: rarer terms weigh more.

children.children: The component that cuts text into tokens and maps each to an integer ID, and turns IDs back into text.

children: : the goal is units that should match, not units a model can read.

children.children: Common choices: lowercase everything, remove punctuation, and drop stop words like “the”, “and” and “is”. Term-based search engines usually do this for you.

children.question: This lab's tokenizer splits on anything that isn't a letter or digit. What does BM25 match for the “two” in “two-year-old”?
options: The two-factor authentication article, which contains “two” twice

children.children: “two-year-old” becomes “two”, “year” and “old”. No article contains “year” or “old”, but “Two-factor authentication. Turn on two-factor…” contains “two” twice, so it ranks third for a question about a toddler's toy.

Splitting can destroy meaning. The book's example is “hot dog”: as “hot” and “dog”, neither word means the food. One fix is to treat common n-grams as single terms, so the bigram “hot dog” is indexed as one term.

children: The same choices cut both ways for identifiers. This tokenizer keeps

children.className: rounded bg-surface-2 px-1 py-0.5 font-mono text-[0.9em]

children: whole, so a query for that error code finds its article with a high score. A tokenizer that split it into “0” and “80070005” would also match any stray “0” in other articles.

children.question: Your product is called “Note”. Users search “Note export”. Why might term-based retrieval do badly?
options: Lowercased, “note” is a common word that appears all over the help docs, so it carries little IDF and matches many irrelevant articles

children.children: Term-based retrieval sees spelling, not meaning. Indexing product names as distinct terms, or adding them as metadata (lesson 4), keeps them from blending into ordinary words.
